title: Agentic World Action Models
authors: Zhuoyang Liu,Dantong Niu,Botong Zhang,Boning Shao,Jing Wang,Ruijie Zheng,Yuvan Sharma,Runyu Lu,Jiaming Liu,Renrui Zhang,Roei Herzig,Yutong Bai,Ken Goldberg,Danfei Xu,Yuke Zhu,Guanzhi Wang,Linxi "Jim" Fan,Trevor Darrell
abstract:
Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics.
We introduce AW-0,
an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture.
Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands.
Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution.
We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries.
Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness,
demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
introduction:
Learning-based robotic manipulation has progressed from small task-specific visuomotor policies over a decade ago
to broadly supervised foundation models that connect perception, language, and action (Levine et al., 2016; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).
In parallel, self-supervised video prediction has long been valued as a learning signal to model the world: image inpainting extended to video prediction led to action-conditioned video predictors that can imagine the future before committing to an action (Pathak et al., 2016; He et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022; Finn et al., 2016; Assran et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026).

World Action Models (WAMs) couple visual prediction with visuomotor policies, grounding control in representations of how the physical world evolves (Ye et al., 2026; Kim and others, 2026; Yuan and others, 2026).
This predictive grounding is particularly valuable for complex manipulation, where successful execution depends on anticipating object motion, contact, and the consequences of low-level actions. Yet predicted video and action chunks do not by themselves specify how a long-horizon task should be decomposed: which reusable skills to invoke, how to parameterize them, or how to compose them across subtasks.
Predicting the world and/or actions in general can also be expensive, especially as it can be difficult to establish limits on how many degrees of freedom need to be “world modeled” (or teleoperated, in the supervised setting).

Agentic robot systems provide complementary structure to WAMs: a programmatic harness that selects reusable skills and tools, binds them to the current scene, tracks progress, and replans as observations change (Liang et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). This programmatic representation makes the structure of multi-step tasks explicit, specifying which skills and tools to invoke, with what arguments, and in what sequence.
Yet agentic robotics often lacks predictive grounding in real-world physical dynamics and does not leverage a learned model of how the world will change as the robot acts.

We advocate for an architecture that combines the foresight and action execution of WAMs with the cognitive efficiency, reusable skills, and potential for future self-improvement of agentic robotics.
We propose AW-0, an agentic WAM framework that incorporates code-based planning and generation directly into world action modeling via a grounded code expert that harnesses broad programming priors to synthesize modular skills featuring explicit parameters and control logic. Code guides synchronized video and control modules within a mixture-of-transformers architecture, simultaneously denoising discrete code structures, predicted visual observations, and low-level motor commands.

We first show that such agents can be realized by adding a code expert to a WAM, leveraging multisensor action and code generation in a planning stage.
We develop a modular generation framework: planning via code generation significantly improves WAM performance, by appropriately conditioning the long-horizon generations required for complex robotic tasks. An automated curation pipeline extracts systematic routines into reusable program libraries, mapping code segments directly onto robotic and human video trajectories. This approach bridges high-level semantic reasoning with predictive physical dynamics, establishing a unified language for compositionality across distinct environments and tasks.
We further demonstrate agentic skill reuse via a hybrid deployment strategy that selects between raw action chunk execution and programmatic skill invocation. Empirical evaluations across RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and physical bimanual setups show substantial performance gains compared to standard VLA and WAM baselines, highlighting programmatic code as an effective structural backbone for predictive planning, skill discovery, and embodied robotic control.

Our primary contribution is the conceptualization and realization of agentic robotic skills within a world action model framework, showing that code generation improves action prediction in the world model, and that the code generated from the world model can be re-used in an agentic framework. Specific novel contribution elements include: a mixture-of-transformers framework integrating a code expert into world action models via simultaneous denoising of code, video, and control; an automated agentic pipeline designed for program annotation and skill discovery; a dataset of such structured skill programs; and a hybrid execution policy that dynamically toggles between programmatic skill invocation and direct deployment of action chunks from the WAM action expert.

title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
authors: Yunhao Luo,Wentao He,Yinpei Dai,Hyelin Nam,Hongze Fu,Joyce Chai,Nima Fazeli,Jeong Joon Park
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object’s mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes.
To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene’s actual physical behavior.
PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead.
We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate.
The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
Project page at https://physical-world.github.io/.
introduction:
World models predict how a scene evolves given its current state and
the intended actions of the agents within it.
Trained on internet-scale data, video-based world
models (Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Team et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026)
are now able to generate photorealistic visual predictions of complex scene dynamics that are difficult to model with traditional physics engines.
Modeling the world in image space is thus becoming a promising alternative to hand-built physics modeling in such areas as robotics (Hou et al., 2026) and autonomous driving (Feng et al., 2025).

Existing world models usually generate predictions from the current frame or a short visual history. However, such observations may leave the underlying physical properties unconstrained, forcing the world models to guess a future state among multiple possible ones. For example, an opaque bottle appears identical whether or not it is filled with water, yet it will respond differently under identical actuation. A world model that relies only on empirical priors over object category or appearance will produce incorrect predictions in such scenarios, limiting its applicability in downstream applications that require accurate dynamics (Zhou et al., 2025; Quevedo et al., 2026). This motivates calibrating the world model to the hidden physical properties of each scene.

A natural way to resolve this physics ambiguity is to physically interact with the scene to infer its hidden properties, similar to how we humans would do for an object with unknown properties.
Inspired by this,
prior system identification methods (Wu et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2021) attempt to construct accurate physical models with closed-form equations and fit the predefined physics parameters to the in-situ interaction data. However, real-world systems exhibit complex, coupled physics factors, thus building a geometric model or formulating closed-form equations can be challenging.
Hence, to adapt to each deployment setting, existing world models (Gao et al., 2026) are typically finetuned on a small set of in-house data, which is computationally expensive.

To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, a method for in-context Physics Calibration for World models.
Inspired by the in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models (Brown et al., 2020; Bar et al., 2022), we prompt world models with a sequence of observation-action pairs
collected in the test environment (i.e., an environment whose physics configuration is unknown) for physics calibration.
Our in-context prompting method sidesteps both the need for human effort to build analytical physics simulators for system identification and expensive model finetuning. Our method requires only an exploratory interaction clip without any gradient descent steps.
PhysiCalWorld compresses the interaction sequence into a compact physics descriptor token that conditions the world model. The entire system is trained end-to-end with only a video prediction objective, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

At test time, PhysiCalWorld first extracts the descriptor from a few exploratory interactions with the test scene (e.g., via random exploration or scripted policies).
This descriptor then conditions all subsequent rollouts in that scene, enabling the world model to generate physically consistent predictions in novel configurations without any test-time weight updates.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

In-Context Physics Calibration: We formulate physics calibration of generative world models as in-context conditioning: from a short interaction sequence, the model adapts zero-shot to instance-specific dynamics, with no test-time weight updates.

Physics Descriptors Learned from Video Alone: We introduce a physics descriptor token that grounds the world model in hidden physical properties. It is learned end-to-end from video prediction alone, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

Performance and Analysis: Across four environments with single and coupled physics variations, PhysiCalWorld consistently improves rollout accuracy and planning success on two world model backbones. Its single-token descriptor matches or exceeds raw-context conditioning at a fraction of the cost. Without physics labels, the descriptors form a physically structured latent space and extrapolate beyond the training parameter range.

2. Physics Descriptors Learned from Video Alone: We introduce a physics descriptor token that grounds the world model in hidden physical properties. It is learned end-to-end from video prediction alone, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

3. Performance and Analysis: Across four environments with single and coupled physics variations, PhysiCalWorld consistently improves rollout accuracy and planning success on two world model backbones. title: CW-WAM: A Structured Contact-Wrench World Action Model for Force-Sensitive Manipulation
authors: Houzhu Ding,Xinda Qi,Luqi Wang,Ming Yang
abstract:
Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by
visual observations.
We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact
wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion–force control, it contains a unified
interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned
motion–wrench chunks as control references.
A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion–wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length
wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a
force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow–fast control system
that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact
prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side
and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input.
It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads.
Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE
from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively,
with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution.
Project website: cw-wam-project.github.io.
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual observations and actions,
providing coherent motion plans for manipulation [1].
Yet a square peg jammed during insertion may appear fully seated, and
visually similar objects may differ substantially in weight. Such force-sensitive
tasks require physical interaction information that wrist force–torque sensing can provide.

Force feedback improves contact-rich manipulation by complementing visual
observations [2, 3] and enabling rapid motion correction [4].
Joint action–wrench prediction extends these benefits: predicted forces guide
learned feedback correction [5] or help evaluate contact
outcomes [6]. These advances motivate WAMs that predict the wrench associated with
each action and use it to guide execution.

Contact depends on commanded motion, prior interaction, and the environment.
To capture these dependencies, we design an interaction module inspired
by hybrid motion–force control.
The module pairs past commands with measured wrenches
(Fig. ) and predicts future motion and wrench
using separate tokens, prediction heads, and training losses.
High-rate wrench encoding captures contact changes within motion intervals, while
longer memory retains earlier wrench measurements.

CW-WAM integrates this module into a DreamZero-style video–action
backbone [1].
During execution, paired predictions provide nominal motion and
an expected wrench reference for admittance feedback.
A slow–fast system applies corrections and tracks continuous motion between model
queries. During contact, this keeps force feedback active while the model
computes the next motion–wrench chunk.
Our work makes three contributions:

Structured action–wrench modeling. We introduce a unified
interaction module with paired motion–wrench history,
separate future output streams and modality-specific losses.
Across four real-robot tasks, CW-WAM achieves the strongest overall
performance among the evaluated methods.
It improves insertion and release success, tracks force more accurately
in peg insertion and wiping, and adapts motion to sensed load.

Predicted wrench references for feedback. We use the predicted
wrench trajectory to guide admittance corrections without requiring a separately
trained corrective policy. During successful trials, this feedback reduces
the error between predicted and measured forces and lowers contact-force variation.

A slow–fast execution system. We combine low-rate CW-WAM inference
with faster admittance feedback and continuous trajectory tracking.
The admittance controller computes pose corrections at 20 Hz.
The corrected motion waypoints
are then interpolated into smooth trajectories for a 1-kHz robot controller.
We demonstrate this interface on four real-robot tasks.

1. Structured action–wrench modeling. We introduce a unified
interaction module with paired motion–wrench history,
separate future output streams and modality-specific losses.
Across four real-robot tasks, CW-WAM achieves the strongest overall
performance among the evaluated methods.
It improves insertion and release success, tracks force more accurately
in peg insertion and wiping, and adapts motion to sensed load.

2. Predicted wrench references for feedback. We use the predicted
wrench trajectory to guide admittance corrections without requiring a separately
trained corrective policy. During successful trials, this feedback reduces
the error between predicted and measured forces and lowers contact-force variation.

3. A slow–fast execution system. We combine low-rate CW-WAM inference

The admittance controller computes pose corrections at 20 Hz.

are then interpolated into smooth trajectories for a 1-kHz robot controller.
We demonstrate this interface on four real-robot tasks.

title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
authors: Yanzhe Chen,Ziyi Yang,Jifeng Zhu,Qiming Huang,Ruihe An,Peiyao Xu,Hesen Yang,Runda Liu,Chang Gong,Zhijun Cao,Zechen Bai,Wenzheng Zeng,Yiqi Lin,Guoqiang Liang,Kevin Yuchen Ma,Kevin Qinghong Lin,Mike Zheng Shou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Multimedia (cs.MM)
abstract:
Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use?
We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions:
Perceive the current state,
Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome.
Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs.
Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors.
Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success.
These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.
introduction:
Multimodal agents (MMAs) have grown from one-shot generation into systems that interact over time, use external tools, and revise decisions from feedback, and they now operate browsers, desktops, and phones as computer-use agents [217, 213, 168, 171, 186, 239, 198]. Robotic systems (RSs) have followed a complementary path: foundation models and generalist policies increasingly connect language and perception to physical action across a widening range of tasks [4, 79, 108, 37, 14, 13, 88, 150, 149, 12]. Robotics offers a mature account of how to close the loop under physical dynamics [69, 91, 46, 41, 92, 17, 50], while agent research offers ways to sustain the loop through longer interactions [217, 171, 186, 98, 29, 67, 28, 31].

We use multimodal embodied agent (MMEA) for a goal-directed system that uses multimodal evidence to guide physical action and feedback from that action to revise later decisions. Bringing the two traditions together changes more than the action interface. Computer-use agents can draw on structured state and direct feedback supplied by software, while conventional robotic systems can rely on constraints chosen for a known operating setting [239, 198, 216, 17, 50]. Open-ended physical interaction offers neither in full: the same loop becomes less predictable and less forgiving, and more decisions move into the interaction itself. This motivates our central question:
What changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use?

Survey taxonomies still tend to follow the field in which they were developed. Surveys of computer-use agents foreground computational architectures and digital interaction [40, 197, 181, 215, 16], whereas surveys of embodied AI, VLA models, and robot autonomy emphasize physical tasks and execution [120, 133, 164, 185]. Several recent accounts cover both computer-use and robot-use [40, 120, 164, 215, 16, 143], but covering both is different from drawing the analogy between them (Table 1): existing categories describe systems within each setting and do not show how the same function changes when its actions acquire physical consequences. The need for such an analogy is growing. Foundation models, world models, and broader robot datasets now connect capabilities that were once developed separately [37, 13, 15, 64, 209, 150, 97], yet strong components do not by themselves form a coherent physical agent. Coherence depends on coordination across the full loop as the environment changes, which calls for a unit of comparison that remains stable across both settings. Figure 2 traces the two research paths and their recent convergence.

We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric perspective built around five functions in a recurring task loop, the cycle through which an agent advances a task one step at a time. Perceive establishes the current state; Anticipate estimates the effects of candidate actions; Plan selects a feasible course; Act realizes that course through an interface or body; and Verify judges the outcome and whether further interaction is needed. Each function is defined by what it contributes to the loop rather than by the component that implements it: one model may support several functions, and one function may be distributed across several models or tools. A click, a skill call, and a robot trajectory differ in form, but PAPAV asks what each contributes to the same task loop rather than whether the systems share an architecture or action space. PAPAV also sharpens two boundaries often folded into a standard observation–decision–action loop: Anticipate asks what a candidate action may cause before Plan chooses a course, and Verify asks whether post-action evidence supports the intended outcome rather than merely recording another observation. These distinctions make prediction and outcome judgment visible as separate functions while remaining compatible with existing agent and control-loop taxonomies [215, 120, 164, 143, 185].

The shared coordinate then isolates what embodiment changes. We study five constraints that recur in physical interaction: partial observability, limited simulatability, irreversibility, real-time coupling, and unverifiable outcomes. Together they make the loop less predictable and less forgiving, increasing the weight of what the agent decides during interaction rather than what the interface or system design fixes in advance. Memory and orchestration keep the five functions connected across time; we call this coordinating substrate the agentic harness rather than a sixth capability.

Our scope spans MMAs, conventional RSs, and their intersection. We borrow computer-use and robot-use as shorthand for the two ends of this transition [198, 83], and use digital and physical throughout the body for the interaction settings along it. Robot-use here covers any configuration in which multimodal task reasoning acts through a robot body, by remote tool-style control or by an end-to-end policy, and is thus broader than cloud-controlled robots alone. The MMA and RS categories are system classes rather than settings, and they overlap. MMAs commonly operate through software interfaces, including games and simulated worlds [151, 186], whereas RSs center body-specific sensing and control, even when evaluated in simulation. We include virtual embodied work when it informs a capability, while whole-system MMEA membership follows the physical task-loop criteria in Section 2.3. The task loop is therefore the unit of comparison: evidence for one capability does not by itself classify an entire system as an MMEA. Table 1 compares related surveys in terms of computer-use and robot-use coverage, benchmark analysis, and digital–physical analogy, highlighting PAPAV’s emphasis on a shared capability perspective across settings.

This survey makes three contributions:

A unified capability-centric perspective. PAPAV enables unified comparison of MMAs, RSs, and MMEAs through five functional roles in a task loop, spanning computer-use and robot-use.

A three-way capability comparison. For each capability, we identify what MMAs, RSs, and MMEAs share, then separately analyze MMEA–MMA and MMEA–RS differences.

A capability-level benchmark analysis. We analyze PAPAV coverage in 64 benchmarks, distinguishing explicit capability evaluation from evidence available only through task outcomes. Explicit evaluation concentrates on Act, with few benchmarks isolating Anticipate or Verify.

Figure 3 summarizes the research landscape: its capability branch organizes representative evidence by PAPAV relation and literature lineage, and its benchmark branch organizes the curated corpus by primary evaluation target. Neither placement is a shortcut for whole-system MMEA membership.

Section 2 defines the shared task-loop setting and PAPAV. Section 3 compares the five capabilities across digital and physical systems, with particular attention to the five physical constraints. Section 4 analyzes benchmark coverage at the capability level, Section 5 discusses open challenges for reliable physical interaction, and Section 6 concludes.

title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
authors: Sriyash Poddar,Yanda Bao,Jacob Krantz,Matthew Chang,Xavier Puig,Roozbeh Mottaghi,Natasha Jaques,Abhishek Gupta
abstract:
Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively.
Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student–teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student’s on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ∼\sim2×\times higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses up to ∼\sim100×\times fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40%+40\% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.
introduction:
Sequential decision-making under partial observability is a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) [34, 53]. In the real world, from robotics to embodied AI, agents receive only partial, noisy observations of the environment. To act successfully, agents must first explore to uncover hidden, task-relevant information [31, 79, 42, 74, 46, 71]. For example, a household robot searching for an object must use onboard sensing to infer likely object locations, track locations it has already searched, and adapt future exploration based on prior attempts [12, 11, 30]. These problems are formalized as partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) [34].

Solving these tasks requires policies with memory [28, 50]. Learning them from scratch via recurrent RL is sample-inefficient, since the agent must learn to gather information and exploit it at the same time [5, 79, 21]. One way to improve sample efficiency is to assume training-time access to a privileged expert that observes the hidden state and acts accordingly. For example, in household navigation, an oracle planner could use the full map of the training environments, which is unavailable at deployment. In practice, these teachers can be trained in fully observed tasks using RL, imitation learning, or hybrid approaches [78, 75, 60, 27, 52]. This expert can teach the student how to act once the hidden state is known, but not how to find it [44]. As a result, naively copying the expert does not teach the student to explore [70]. Interactive imitation [65] offers a natural fix by relabeling student mistakes with expert actions. However, standard approaches [59] train the student to predict the average expert action across possible hidden states, so it dithers between hypotheses instead of resolving them [37, 70]. Other approaches propose to address the student-teacher mismatch using expensive online RL [74], differentiable experts [73], or offline coverage assumptions [42].

In this work, we propose ASTEROID (Asymmetric Student Teacher Roll-Out In-context Distillation), a framework that shows that privileged experts can teach exploration through interactive imitation. The idea is simple: the student generates the history online, and the expert provides the labels. ASTEROID rolls out the current student under partial observability, producing a history of observations, actions, and rewards, then asks the expert what it would do from the state the student has reached. The expert does not explore; it only labels the student’s histories. As a result, failed searches and probes become useful context: they specify evidence accumulated so far, while the expert provides next actions given the hidden state. With on-policy history, the policy can identify inconsistent hypotheses and adapt its exploration and action distribution accordingly.

Why does this teach exploration? A partial history represents uncertainty over the hidden state. Returning to household navigation: suppose the object could be in location AA, BB, or CC. If the student searches AA and finds nothing, its history rules out AA but is still consistent with BB and CC. A privileged expert would label this history with search(B) when the object is at BB, and search(C) when it is at CC. The student therefore learns to act and explore the remaining valid actions: if it fails at AA, it samples search(B) or search(C). If it then fails at BB, every label is search(C), since only CC remains. Unlike random sampling of locations, the policy conditions on its history and never retries hypotheses it has ruled out. Across many training tasks, ambiguous histories are labeled with a distribution of potential, consistent expert trajectories. The student samples from this distribution to explore, and each new observation and feedback eliminates additional hypotheses. The key insight: the set of histories that the student needs to learn to adapt from (e.g., failing at AA, failing at BB and then moving to CC) is entirely covered by on-policy behavior. This is in-context exploration, i.e., searching while uncertain, and exploiting once the hidden state is revealed. Additionally, we show that a curriculum over the student rollout horizon improves sample efficiency and enables longer-context adaptation (Section 5). Overall, ASTEROID incorporates very simple changes into standard online student-teacher distillation to enable test-time exploration behavior.

We show both empirically (Section 6) and theoretically (Appendix H) that ASTEROID approximates Bayesian posterior sampling, a provably efficient exploration strategy [53]. However, posterior sampling has been hard to scale: prior approaches maintain an explicit posterior [3] or assume infinite offline data [42], which are intractable in realistic settings. ASTEROID avoids both: it does not maintain an explicit posterior, and on-policy supervised learning avoids impractical data costs. Because it is a simple extension of student–teacher distillation, ASTEROID works with modern architectures and existing sim-to-real frameworks [75]. In summary, we make the following contributions:

We present ASTEROID, a simple student–teacher distillation framework that enables in-context exploration and test-time improvement learned solely from privileged experts.

We evaluate our method across 11 environments, including navigation in realistic household simulators and real-world robot manipulation, where it outperforms RL and supervised baselines under fixed exploration budgets while using two orders of magnitude fewer training interactions.

We show that learned policies exhibit efficient real-world exploration and, under appropriate assumptions, recover posterior sampling with error linear rather than quadratic in context length.

title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
authors: Likui Zhang,Zhe Zhu,Zhihao Zhan,Yibo Bai,Hanlin Wang,Dongwei Li,Bin Wang,Tianle Zhang,Xiaodan Liang,Liang Lin
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision–language–action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.
introduction:
Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Beyer et al., 2024; Deitke et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025) have established Vision–Language–Action (VLA) (Intelligence et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b) models as a prominent paradigm for robotic manipulation. Although imitation learning (IL) from large-scale robot demonstrations enables VLA models to acquire diverse manipulation skills, its performance is inherently constrained by the coverage of the demonstration data. Reinforcement learning (RL) overcomes this limitation by directly optimizing policies with task feedback obtained through environment interaction, and recent work (Li et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026) has successfully applied RL to VLA models. However, existing VLA-RL methods still face substantial challenges in long-horizon manipulation tasks.

First, most methods rely on terminal-only success rewards. In an episode that completes the first kk subtasks but fails at subtask k+1k+1, the absence of a terminal success reward causes generalized advantage estimation (GAE) to propagate failure-related temporal-difference (TD) residuals backward to t0t_{0}, suppressing the advantages of correctly executed actions. We refer to this as credit contamination, where useful behavior in failed trajectories is systematically devalued, with the effect worsening as the horizon grows.
Prior work (Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Tan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2025) mitigates reward sparsity through stage-level preference optimization or subtask-level intermediate rewards, but these approaches alter reward density without resolving credit contamination.
Second, subtask mastery is uneven, with failures increasingly concentrated in a few bottleneck subtasks during later training. Uniform task sampling and fixed exploration then waste interaction budget on saturated subtasks while providing insufficient exploration for the bottlenecks.

To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, as illustrated in Fig. 1, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure. Our key insight is that semantic subtasks provide a unified basis for both the propagation of learning signals and the allocation of exploration resources. AtomicRL couples Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO) with Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE), supported by a lightweight Progress–Completion Critic (PCC) that estimates atomic subtask progress and completion boundaries. PCC also provides progress estimates for constructing dense progress-based shaping rewards (PBSR).
SAPO modulates TD-residual propagation in advantage estimation with a soft gate conditioned on semantic boundaries. Within each atomic subtask, it preserves standard GAE trace decay; across subtask boundaries, it maintains propagation between successful subtasks while attenuating residuals from failed subtasks. By leaving one-step TD residuals and value bootstrapping unchanged, SAPO reduces failure interference while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and successful subtask dependencies.
BATE tracks the mastery of each subtask via a moving average of its completion rate, jointly adjusts the sampling weight of full tasks and the strength of subtask-level entropy regularization, directing interaction and exploration resources toward bottleneck subtasks.
Finally, to support physical deployment, we develop an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline. Given a single real-world multimodal demonstration and the required auxiliary information, the pipeline reconstructs an interactive simulation environment. It connects simulation-based RL with real-robot deployment, shifting costly physical trial-and-error to parallel simulation with reproducible resets.

We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation and the real world. On LIBERO-LONG (Liu et al., 2023) AtomicRL achieves success rates of 99.0% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025b) and 98.8% with OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025), improving over PPO by 3.6% and 4.0%. On CALVIN ABC-D (Mees et al., 2022), the average completed sequence length improves from 3.56 to 4.56, while the success rate of completing full five-subtask chain improves by 9.5% over PPO.
Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further yields an average improvement of 21.3% on real-robot long-horizon tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of AtomicRL for long-horizon VLA reinforcement learning. Overall, our contributions are as follows:

We introduce AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

We propose SAPO to mitigate cross-subtask credit interference and BATE to adaptively direct task sampling and exploration toward bottleneck subtasks.

We develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that streamlines simulation construction and RL training for efficient real-robot deployment.

We validate the effectiveness of AtomicRL through extensive experiments conducted in both simulated environments and real-world robots.

1. We introduce AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

2. We propose SAPO to mitigate cross-subtask credit interference and BATE to adaptively direct task sampling and exploration toward bottleneck subtasks.

3. We develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that streamlines simulation construction and RL training for efficient real-robot deployment.

4. We validate the effectiveness of AtomicRL through extensive experiments conducted in both simulated environments and real-world robots.

title: Do Earth-Trained Humanoid Controllers Walk on the Moon? Gravity, Terrain, and Soil Transfer
authors: Guillem Casadesus Vila,Sri Aditya Deevi,Grace X. Gao
comment: . Supplementary material () included as an ancillary file
abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 °20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.
introduction:
Walking on the Moon is hard for people. Suited Apollo crews often loped [1], fell 27 times across the Apollo surface missions [2], and paid a metabolic cost that limits how long astronauts can work outside [3, 1]. Humanoid robots could take mundane and dangerous surface tasks off the crew [4], and their form suits tools and interfaces designed for people, a premise of NASA’s Robonaut 2 [5]. Learned humanoid controllers now walk over rough, deformable, and sloped terrain on Earth [6, 7], but lunar operation changes several of these conditions at once (Fig. 1). Gravity falls to 1.62 m s−21.62\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-2}, craters and rocks, with measured size statistics [8, 9], change the available footholds, and regolith yields under contact [10]. A controller can stay upright under these changes yet make little commanded progress, and adapting it to one condition can cost performance in another.

Prior learned-locomotion studies mostly adapt one task-specific recipe to one of these conditions, reduced gravity on rigid ground [11, 12] or granular media at Earth gravity [13]. A quadrupedal manipulator trained at lunar gravity has been tested on compliant ground contact withheld from training, with friction calibrated to a regolith simulant [14], and a quadruped has been trained with granular contact for the lunar surface [15]. Only two of these study a humanoid, each under a single condition. To our knowledge, no study has tested a pretrained generalist humanoid controller, such as SONIC [16], under reduced gravity, or compared fine-tuning, training from scratch, and gravity randomization for the Moon by Earth performance and compute.

We ask how much of an Earth-trained humanoid controller’s performance survives lunar gravity, terrain, and soil, and what it costs to close the gap. We train 12 G1 policies with one recipe (Fig. 2). Eight are trained from scratch and cover every combination of Earth or Moon gravity, flat or rough terrain, and rigid or granular ground. The other four are two Earth-to-Moon fine-tunes and two gravity-randomized policies. Granular ground uses three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT) [17, 18], and we call training on it soil training. The released SONIC controller is a frozen reference. Every policy faces the gravity change, so we study gravity first, then whether rough or soil training widens or narrows the remaining gap.

The contributions of this letter are:

A two-way study of gravity transfer for learned humanoid locomotion, testing 12 policies and the pretrained SONIC controller at Earth and lunar gravity, which shows that transfer is asymmetric.

An analysis of training on rough terrain and on 3D RFT soil at each gravity, on held-out terrain, slopes, and soils.

A comparison of training strategies for the Moon, namely training from scratch, fine-tuning, and gravity randomization, finding that the gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain keeps a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 °20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}.

An evaluation on three soil models held out of training: the material point method (MPM) [19, 20], the soil contact model (SCM) [21], and the continuous representation model (CRM) [22].

2. An analysis of training on rough terrain and on 3D RFT soil at each gravity, on held-out terrain, slopes, and soils.

A comparison of training strategies for the Moon, namely training from scratch, fine-tuning, and gravity randomization, finding that the gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain keeps a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 °20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}.

4. An evaluation on three soil models held out of training: the material point method (MPM) [19, 20], the soil contact model (SCM) [21], and the continuous representation model (CRM) [22].

title: Test-Time Motion Steering for Perceptive Humanoid Fall Recovery
authors: Osher Azulay,Cheng-Lin Hsieh,Stella X. Yu
abstract:
Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time.
It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: RISE.
introduction:
For a fallen humanoid, standing up is only part of recovery: the robot must also choose
how to stand. Fig.  shows that even the same fallen pose
admits several ways to stand, such as rolling to either side or rising
directly. The scene and next task
determine which fits: a wall can obstruct a recovery route, a step can
change the available support, and the task may require the robot to face a
particular direction. Steering lets task objectives select among feasible
recoveries, preparing the robot to continue its task.

Prior work has achieved reliable fall recovery and controllable whole-body
motion, but combining onboard perception with test-time steering remains under-explored, as Fig. 2 shows. Recovery
controllers now stand up from diverse postures and manage falls
[1, 2, 3], and VIGOR adapts
recovery to uneven ground using egocentric depth [4].
In these methods, the learned policy alone decides how the robot stands.
Other whole-body controllers,
including perceptive ones, are often directed through commands such as
joystick or heading inputs [5, 6]. These
commands work well for trained behaviors, but each must be defined, with
labeled data, before training. Guided motion generation is more flexible: it
expresses task objectives as test-time costs that can be designed after
training and combined as needed [7, 8].
We bring this flexibility to perceptive fall recovery.

Steering fall recovery is harder than steering from an upright pose. The
robot starts from varied fallen configurations and must shift support among
its hands, knees, feet, and torso to rise, so its motor actions must adapt to
its configuration and contacts. Uneven terrain compounds the difficulty:
steps, slopes, and nearby obstacles change the available supports and routes,
so a request feasible in one scene can fail in another. Yet this is the
practical setting, as humanoids rarely operate on flat ground with clear
space. Steering here needs several feasible ways to stand from each pose, but
each recorded recovery shows only one. It also needs to anticipate how a
requested movement will unfold under changing contact with the surrounding
terrain.

We introduce RISE (Perceptive Recovery via Intent Steering),
which addresses these needs with two insights (Fig. 3).
First, diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movement
patterns, providing several ways to stand from each pose. We compose
compatible recorded segments and adapt them to terrain, building a
multimodal recovery repertoire. From the repertoire’s physical
executions, we learn a recovery vocabulary: motion latents that a
feedback decoder turns into motor actions using proprioception and egocentric
depth. Second, a planner trained on the robot’s own executions can
anticipate how recovery will unfold, so steering its predictions shapes the
executed recovery. Our visual diffusion planner
predicts this unfolding as motion intent: a sequence of
future body states. Prior planners denoise future
states jointly with actions or motion
latents [9, 8]. Our planner is
instead state-first: task costs steer the predicted states, then motion latents
are generated conditioned on them, making the requested recovery an explicit
condition for execution.

In
simulation, RISE recovers more reliably and with lower contact forces
than prior work while offering several ways to stand from the same pose.
A single trained model follows heading, speed, and path objectives across
terrains without retraining.
Planning with egocentric depth improves recovery even when the decoder already
uses depth. The state-first design tracks these objectives more accurately than
joint generation of states and motion latents.
Real-world demonstrations show perceptive and steerable recovery.

Our contributions are threefold:

We
introduce RISE, to our knowledge the first framework for humanoid fall recovery
that combines perception with test-time steering by task objectives.

We propose a motion-matching pipeline that builds a multimodal
recovery repertoire by composing recorded motions, coarsely adapting them
to terrain, and collecting their physical executions.

We introduce a visual state-first diffusion planner that steers
predicted body states toward task objectives, then generates motion latents
conditioned on those states to realize the requested recovery.

title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks
authors: May Espinola,Qifan Zhang,Yu Xiang
comment: . May Espinola and Qifan Zhang contributed equally. Project page:this https URLCode:this https URL
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Recent advances in frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use Arena AI [2026]. In particular, recent demonstrations of GPT-6 Astra have shown impressive robot manipulation behaviors, including interpreting visual observations, generating robot actions, and correcting mistakes through closed-loop interaction Zhang et al. [2026], Su et al. [2026], Team et al. [2026]. NVIDIA’s Astranomy report Yang et al. [2026a] further demonstrates the potential of frontier AI models for robot manipulation through different control configurations, including direct action generation, agentic tool use, and supervision of pretrained robot policies. These results suggest that general-purpose AI models may be capable of performing robot manipulation without task-specific policy training.

Despite these promising demonstrations, an important question remains: How well do frontier AI models perform on established robot manipulation benchmarks? Existing evaluations often use different tasks, robot platforms, and control interfaces, making systematic comparisons difficult. Connecting frontier AI models to standardized benchmarks is essential for understanding their capabilities, identifying limitations, and comparing their performance with conventional robot learning approaches.

Motivated by this question, we develop a unified manipulation pipeline to evaluate frontier AI models on LIBERO-10 (also known as LIBERO-Long) Liu et al. [2023], a subset of LIBERO-100 containing ten held-out, long-horizon manipulation tasks. LIBERO-10 has been widely adopted for evaluating robot learning methods, including generalist robot policies and vision-language-action models such as Octo Team et al. [2024], OpenVLA Kim et al. [2024], π0.5\pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. [2025], UniVLA Bu et al. [2025] and UniAct Zheng et al. [2025]. Built upon the open-source Inspect Robots framework Robocurve [2026], our pipeline enables frontier AI models to interact with the simulation environment through visual observations and structured tool calls, allowing closed-loop manipulation without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We evaluate multiple frontier AI models, including GPT and Claude models, under a common protocol, exploring different reasoning modes to investigate the impact of reasoning effort on manipulation performance. Beyond task success rates, we analyze API calls, inference latency, token usage, and monetary cost to understand the tradeoffs between reasoning capabilities, manipulation performance, and efficiency.

Our work provides a standardized evaluation of frontier AI models on robot manipulation tasks, offering insights into their capabilities and limitations. By releasing our code and evaluation results, we provide reproducible, ready-to-use baselines for future research, reducing the need to repeatedly evaluate these computationally expensive models and lowering evaluation costs.

title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Zhaohui Yang,Quanbao Lin,Chengqi Shi,Zhenglang Weng,Jicheng Lin,Boyu Chen,Tengjie Zhu,Guanzhu Ren,Jiahao Xu,Yang Feng,Xiaokang Yang,Yao Mu
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our project page.
introduction:
The motion interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control
is an important design choice in humanoid loco-manipulation
 [1, 2, 3]. Existing interfaces emphasize different aspects of humanoid motion. Joint-space actions [4, 5, 6] directly specify joint configurations, but can require the high-level policy to model whole-body coordination alongside task intent. Task-space actions provide a compact, task-grounded representation, yet sparse targets alone do not fully specify coordinated whole-body motion. Token-space actions [7] can encode reusable coordination patterns, while task-critical spatial targets may remain implicit. These trade-offs motivate an interface that combines representations of spatial intent and whole-body coordination, rather than encoding both in a single form.

We argue that task-critical spatial intent and whole-body coordination should instead be represented in complementary forms. Spatial intent remains explicit, specifying where task-relevant body parts should move, whereas whole-body coordination is encoded implicitly as a learned motion prior describing how the body should move. Following this principle, we expose only five task-critical body poses—the pelvis, two wrists, and two ankles—as explicit spatial constraints and complement them with a latent whole-body motion representation. This interface preserves direct task-space control while avoiding the need for the high-level policy to explicitly specify full-body coordination.

Following this formulation, we present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. At its core, SP-GMT performs whole-body control by jointly conditioning on sparse task-space targets and a learned motion latent. We pretrain a motion variational autoencoder (VAE) to encode full-body motion into a compact latent representation. This latent provides coordination information not fully specified by the sparse targets while enabling efficient policy training.

To obtain this implicit motion prior from sparse task-space targets at deployment, we introduce SP-MGM, which reconstructs coordinated full-body motion from five-point pose targets in real time. Starting from a pretrained motion generation model, SP-MGM reduces network depth and denoising steps and employs two-stage distillation to improve sparse-pose adherence and temporal consistency.

The proposed interface also reduces the burden of high-level action prediction. SP-VLA predicts only task-relevant sparse body poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions, without directly predicting full-body configurations. We further adopt asynchronous action-chunk inference for responsive closed-loop execution. Together, SP-VLA specifies task-space intent, SP-MGM recovers coordinated whole-body motion, and SP-GMT integrates the explicit sparse targets and implicit motion prior for whole-body control.

We separately evaluate SP-GMT, SP-MGM, and the complete SP-HLM system. SP-GMT achieves competitive motion-tracking performance against representative state-of-the-art baselines. SP-MGM improves sparse-pose adherence over the motion-generation baseline while achieving a 1.45×\times higher generation rate. For loco-manipulation, SP-HLM achieves a 52.75% overall success rate across eight simulated tasks, outperforming the token-space and joint-space baselines. We further validate SP-HLM on four real-world tasks, demonstrating its feasibility for humanoid loco-manipulation. Our main contributions are:

We propose a sparse-pose-driven motion interface for humanoid loco-manipulation, combining five task-critical body poses with a learned motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms.

We develop SP-GMT, a whole-body tracker conditioned jointly on sparse targets and a pretrained motion representation, and SP-MGM, a real-time sparse-conditioned motion generator trained through two-stage distillation.

We present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework that integrates the above two components with SP-VLA, which uses asynchronous action-chunk inference to predict task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint-position targets from multimodal inputs. The resulting system achieves higher overall success than the evaluated baselines across eight simulated tasks and is further validated on four real-world tasks.

1. We propose a sparse-pose-driven motion interface for humanoid loco-manipulation, combining five task-critical body poses with a learned motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms.

2. We develop SP-GMT, a whole-body tracker conditioned jointly on sparse targets and a pretrained motion representation, and SP-MGM, a real-time sparse-conditioned motion generator trained through two-stage distillation.

3. We present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework that integrates the above two components with SP-VLA, which uses asynchronous action-chunk inference to predict task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint-position targets from multimodal inputs. The resulting system achieves higher overall success than the evaluated baselines across eight simulated tasks and is further validated on four real-world tasks.

title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
authors: Yicheng Xu,Zhikai Xu,Ziyuan Chen,Yuhang Dong,Tao Zhang,Zhucun Xue,Yong Liu,Jiangning Zhang
comment: . Project page:this https URLCode:this https URL
abstract:
Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs.
Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world.
We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents.
TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue.
An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes.
TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions.
On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes.
Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks.
Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult.
Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.
introduction:
Robots operating in everyday environments must account for physical constraints [11], human safety, appropriate interaction, and social norms [19, 23].
As the world evolves, sensory conditions, physical access, and people’s actions and needs can change during execution [9, 23, 8].
Long-horizon tasks therefore require tracking world states, interpreting human intentions, and adjusting plans using execution feedback [34, 4, 9] (Figure 1).

Vision-language-action (VLA) models [3, 10] and world-action models (WAMs) [38] have advanced robot control,
yet they often lack the ability to adapt to dynamic and uncertain environments.
Large language models (LLMs) provide broad knowledge for reasoning yet lack the ability to perform complex, real-world tasks [1, 9, 8].
This complementarity motivates embodied agents that connect reasoning to action [1, 9, 37, 14].
However, Harness VLA [39], RoboClaw [13], and HumanCLAW [14] focus on tasks with specified goals, leaving an evolving world with human involvement largely unexamined.
Other settings, including EmbodiedBench’s high-level tasks [37], LoTa-Bench [5], ALFWorld’s text environments [28], and Embodied Agent Interface [12], abstract physical execution into discrete symbolic actions.
GRBench [35] combines robot execution with virtual NPC dialogue, while PARTNR [4] evaluates embodied human-robot collaboration with temporal task constraints. These gaps motivate a physically and socially grounded foundation for benchmarking robotic agents in an evolving world, with task outcomes tied to execution and human interaction.

Insight. Studying embodied intelligence requires physically and socially grounded execution and tasks revealing capabilities across varied situations in a changing world (Sections 4.2, 4.3.2 and 4.3.4).

Challenge 1: Embodied execution is not symbolic [Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4].

A valid action call does not guarantee successful execution: the robot must contend with contact, friction, balance, and human responses.
The agent must therefore revise decisions using physical execution feedback.

Challenge 2: The world changes during execution [Sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3].

Physical conditions, human activity, and task requirements can change while a plan unfolds.
The agent must interpret the current situation and reconsider what to do next.

Challenge 3: Evaluation must assess diverse capabilities [Section 4.2].

Within this setting, evaluation must reveal how agents handle varied situations across multiple capability dimensions.
Aggregate success alone can mask different capability gaps across task families (Section 4.2).

We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for embodied agents under physical and social constraints.
TARSphere-Infra couples robot controllers with embodied NPCs in a physics simulator (Challenge 1).
An event-driven FSM maintains world and task states, while TARSphere-Harness combines observations, memory, skills, and execution feedback for replanning (Challenge 2).
We build TARSphere-Bench through agent-in-the-loop curation, pairing navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks with five capability conditions: perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding (Challenge 3). Paired variants retain their Base scene and task family.

Across 8 MLLMs, general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, with capability gaps varying by task family (Section 4.2).
Planning credit does not ensure successful execution, and collisions and falls remain common (Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4).
These findings call for agents that combine general reasoning, adaptation to world changes, and safe execution (Sections 4.2 and 4.3.2).

Our contributions are three-fold.

We formulate long-horizon embodied tasks under physical and social constraints, where execution outcomes and world changes continually shape the agent’s decisions.

We develop TARSphere Framework, where physical execution and interaction with embodied humans update task states and supply evaluation evidence; an embodied brain harness uses observations, memory, executable skills, and world feedback to guide model decisions.

We introduce agent-in-the-loop curation for 360 TARSphere-Bench episodes in 30 scenes and five paired capability conditions, aligning task semantics, geometry, and execution.

1. We formulate long-horizon embodied tasks under physical and social constraints, where execution outcomes and world changes continually shape the agent’s decisions.

2. We develop TARSphere Framework, where physical execution and interaction with embodied humans update task states and supply evaluation evidence; an embodied brain harness uses observations, memory, executable skills, and world feedback to guide model decisions.

3. We introduce agent-in-the-loop curation for 360 TARSphere-Bench episodes in 30 scenes and five paired capability conditions, aligning task semantics, geometry, and execution.

title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations
authors: Mingze Sun,Ziang Cao,Yuan Fei,Qiankuan Tao,Zihan Wang,Tianqi Liu,Junhao Chen,Haiwen Diao,Fangzhou Hong,Zhaoxi Chen,Ziwei Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,5751{,}575 sequences spanning 229229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without fine-tuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79%86.79\% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32%57.32\% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.3677.36 and 45.7345.73 percentage points.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation supports household assistance, industrial assembly, and assistive care. Unlike gripper-based manipulation, it requires precise coordination of finger motions and changing hand–object contacts to grasp, reorient, and reposition objects [28, 2, 8, 33]. Generalizing across objects and behaviors is challenging, especially when human demonstrations must be retargeted to robot hands with different kinematics [26, 19, 38]. Simulation-ready objects [4, 5, 6] and synthetic trajectories [12, 40] enable large-scale interaction data, but may not fully capture natural human manipulation. Recent trackers therefore learn from human hand–object motion [19, 38, 1], yet remain largely limited to single-hand tasks. Many everyday tasks instead require asymmetric bimanual coordination: one hand stabilizes an object while the other opens, rotates, or repositions it [9, 41, 43]. This motivates a generalist bimanual reference tracker that learns from diverse human motion to control different objects and tasks with one policy.

Developing such a tracker poses two challenges. First, public datasets include bimanual manipulation [9, 41, 20, 10], but fully tracked hand–object sequences with sustained two-hand contact remain scarce, limiting the available coordination patterns. Second, a shared policy must learn trajectories with changing hand roles and contact timing. Hand-pose accuracy alone does not ensure successful object manipulation, while requiring both hands to satisfy contact conditions can mask one hand’s progress. Unequal clip difficulty also creates advantage offsets that can weaken updates for useful actions in harder sequences. Shared training therefore needs feedback grounded in object motion and each hand’s reference contacts, alongside advantages that preserve differences among transitions within each clip.

We address these challenges with DONIC, a generalist bimanual reference tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view hand–object interaction dataset. BiHOI contains 1,5751{,}575 sequences spanning 229229 objects and 14.7714.77 hours, captured from 3232 calibrated RGB views. It covers symmetric manipulation and asymmetric coordination. We reconstruct both hands and the object, then retarget hand motion to robot references paired with the object trajectory. Combined with public references, BiHOI broadens the training objects and coordination patterns. DONIC learns one policy for both hands through proximal policy optimization (PPO) [31] and behavioral cloning (BC) on verified demonstrations. Trajectory-specific policies optimize screened references, while successful shared-policy executions are verified and reused. At inference, one checkpoint tracks new references without further training. Our object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback and supervises each hand’s reference contacts, including asynchronous engagement. Our Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA) subtract each clip’s mean estimated advantage before PPO updates, removing clip-dependent offsets while preserving within-clip differences. On held-out trajectories and objects from public datasets, DONIC exceeds the stronger bimanual baseline by 77.3677.36 and 45.7345.73 percentage points in success rate, respectively.

Our contributions are:

To our knowledge, DONIC is the first bimanual reference tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human motion datasets; a single checkpoint is evaluated on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.

We introduce BiHOI, a multi-view hand-object interaction dataset emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, and reconstruct its recordings into robot motion references.

We propose an object-centered per-hand reward and CCA to support joint PPO training across bimanual references with different contact roles and difficulty.

On our two public-data evaluation splits, DONIC outperforms bimanual adaptations of DexTrack and Dexplore in success rate and completion, reaching 86.79%86.79\% and 57.32%57.32\% success on unseen trajectories and objects, respectively.

1. To our knowledge, DONIC is the first bimanual reference tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human motion datasets; a single checkpoint is evaluated on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.

2. We introduce BiHOI, a multi-view hand-object interaction dataset emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, and reconstruct its recordings into robot motion references.

3. We propose an object-centered per-hand reward and CCA to support joint PPO training across bimanual references with different contact roles and difficulty.

4. On our two public-data evaluation splits, DONIC outperforms bimanual adaptations of DexTrack and Dexplore in success rate and completion, reaching 86.79%86.79\% and 57.32%57.32\% success on unseen trajectories and objects, respectively.
