title: Object- and Task-Aware Active Perception for Safe Navigation of Mobile Manipulators in Semi-Static Environments
authors: Jingxing Qian,Xintong Du,Jun Yang,Siqi Zhou,Steven L. Waslander,Angela P. Schoellig
abstract: Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.
introduction:
Mobile manipulators have gained increasing interest in a wide range of applications, including household assistance, logistics, and industrial automation. In these settings, robots are often required to execute navigation tasks across large workspaces over extended periods of time [1]. However, many deployment sites are cluttered, partially unknown, and semi-static, where objects may appear, disappear, or shift between robot visits. Clutter introduces frequent occlusions, blind corners, and narrow passages, while semi-static scene changes cause previously observed regions to become outdated. These challenges are particularly pronounced when the robot must perceive the environment through a limited field of view (FoV). In such cases, occlusions and blind spots can prevent changes from being detected until the robot is in close proximity, leaving new obstacles in previously traversable areas undetected. This can lead to delayed reactions, increased collision risk, and reduced navigation efficiency.

To operate safely and robustly in such cluttered, semi-static environments, a mobile manipulator must not only navigate toward its desired goal but also maintain an up-to-date, consistent understanding of the scene over time. However, this requirement is not well supported by most existing navigation pipelines, which typically assume a static world with an offline-constructed map for downstream planning and control [2], or only track short-term, highly dynamic objects between consecutive frames. Recent research on long-term and semi-static mapping has made important progress toward maintaining consistent environment representations across repeated traversals [3, 4]. By incorporating semantic and object-level reasoning, these approaches can detect scene inconsistencies and accommodate long-term changes, thereby improving map quality and robustness over time. Nevertheless, such methods remain fundamentally passive: they depend on observations collected along the robot’s nominal trajectory, and thus can only update the regions that the robot happens to observe. In cluttered environments, this is often insufficient, especially in occluded regions where up-to-date scene knowledge is most needed.

This limitation is especially critical because not all map regions affect navigation equally. Outdated knowledge in task-relevant and safety-critical regions, such as areas along the planned path, narrow passages, and blind corners, has a disproportionate impact on the robot’s ability to move safely and efficiently. As seen in Figure 6, when the robot makes a sharp turn around the boxes, it is most important for the robot to observe the region around its navigation path behind the orange-shaded blind corner, which is not immediately observable by the fixed camera on the robot base. An outdated or incomplete map in these regions can lead to overly conservative behavior, unnecessary replanning, getting stuck, or collisions. Therefore, map maintenance is particularly valuable in regions where it improves the robot’s ability to make safe task decisions. In this work, we refer to this principle as task-awareness: observations should be prioritized according to their relevance to the robot’s current navigation task, especially when they reduce uncertainty in map regions that affect safe progress toward the goal.

Active perception provides a means to acquire these observations during task execution. Related approaches couple perception and motion planning for control and collision avoidance [5, 6]. Next-best-view (NBV) planning has also been studied for exploration [7], object seeking [8], inspection [9], pose estimation [10], and grasping [11]. A camera mounted on the manipulator hand provides a natural mechanism for viewpoint control. However, many NBV methods target short-horizon operation in static scenes [12, 13] or geometric completeness [14, 15]. They generally do not jointly consider long-term scene changes, object-level map consistency, and relevance to the current navigation task.

For semi-static environments, this omission is particularly important because scene changes often occur at the level of objects: furniture may be moved, shelves may be added, or obstacles may partially block previously traversable space. A partial mismatch at the visible edge of a cabinet can indicate that the cabinet has moved, making its previously mapped region worth checking again. As a result, identifying which objects or occupied structures are likely to have changed and which of them matter more for the robot’s navigation task is critical for effective map maintenance and safe task execution. This motivates an object-aware active perception strategy in which viewpoint selection is informed by uncertainty in the maintained semi-static map, especially when such uncertainty may affect path clearance. Task awareness then determines whether this potential change matters to the next maneuver.

Moreover, because the hand camera is mounted on a manipulator, viewpoint selection cannot be treated independently from navigation. The robot must realize informative camera motions without compromising progress on its primary navigation task. We therefore use hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC) as the mechanism for enforcing this priority structure and realizing the selected viewpoints through the robot’s kinematic redundancy [16, 17].

In this work, we aim to enable safe mobile manipulation in cluttered, semi-static environments over extended periods of time through integrated active perception and whole-body control. Specifically, we develop an object- and task-aware active perception framework that combines the planned navigation path with uncertainty in the maintained semi-static map. Our approach enables a mobile manipulator to exploit its kinematic redundancy to direct a hand camera toward uncertain, occluded, and safety-critical regions while continuing to execute its primary navigation task. By actively updating the map where it matters most, the robot can better detect and adapt to incremental scene changes and improve map consistency in task-relevant areas. We deploy the system on a real mobile manipulator and evaluate reconstruction accuracy, task-dependent map entropy, and navigation safety against passive and task- or object-unaware baselines. Figure 2 illustrates the resulting behavior in cluttered scenes. Our main contributions are as follows:

We formulate a probabilistic next-best-view (NBV) objective that uses task-dependent map entropy and path-conditioned grid weights to prioritize uncertain or potentially changing regions along the planned path.

We formulate a probabilistic next-best-view (NBV) objective that uses task-dependent map entropy and path-conditioned grid weights to prioritize uncertain or potentially changing regions along the planned path.

We introduce a hierarchical-task control framework that assigns higher priority to navigation than to active perception within a two-stage optimization problem. This allows the robot to exploit its kinematic redundancy to gather informative observations while bounding the base-tracking cost during camera-task optimization.

We demonstrate the system on a mobile manipulator with a hand camera in cluttered indoor environments. In the tested static scenes, the proposed system reduces task-dependent map entropy, improves map consistency, and lowers navigation risk compared with passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional scene-change sequences demonstrate the closed-loop map-maintenance behavior.

1. We formulate a probabilistic next-best-view (NBV) objective that uses task-dependent map entropy and path-conditioned grid weights to prioritize uncertain or potentially changing regions along the planned path.

2. We introduce a hierarchical-task control framework that assigns higher priority to navigation than to active perception within a two-stage optimization problem. This allows the robot to exploit its kinematic redundancy to gather informative observations while bounding the base-tracking cost during camera-task optimization.

3. We demonstrate the system on a mobile manipulator with a hand camera in cluttered indoor environments. In the tested static scenes, the proposed system reduces task-dependent map entropy, improves map consistency, and lowers navigation risk compared with passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional scene-change sequences demonstrate the closed-loop map-maintenance behavior.

title: HuMiT: Low-Latency Whole-Body Humanoid Teleoperation via Compact Reference Tracking
authors: Liu Cao,Botian Xu,Ruoqu Chen,Jiajun Liu,Mingzhi Pei,Zihao Wang,Zhongyu Li,Mengdi Xu
abstract:
Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning.
Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules.
In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames.
Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of ∼\sim20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types.
We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/.
introduction:
Humanoid robots hold unique promise for operating in human-centric environments due to their morphology that naturally matches the workspaces and tools designed for people.
Teleoperation is a practical paradigm for human-in-the-loop robot control.
It provides a scalable mechanism for collecting diverse demonstration data to train autonomous policies,
and also allows human operators to intervene in high-risk scenarios or situations where autonomous systems are likely to fail.

However, building an effective whole-body teleoperation system remains challenging. A primary issue is large teleoperation latency, which arises from two sources. First, optimization-based retargeting [1] introduces substantial per-frame delay and can suffer from numerical instability. Second, existing learning-based tracking policies rely heavily on full reference states as inputs, including complete joint positions, body-part transformations, and their velocities [2, 3].
Moreover, many of these methods condition the policy on future reference frames to enable anticipatory control [4, 5], which further exacerbates the latency problem.
A secondary challenge is limited whole-body coordination, as many approaches decouple upper- and lower-body control [6, 7, 8], which is particularly restrictive for dynamic tasks.
In addition, hardware-centric solutions based on exoskeletons [9, 10, 11] or marker-based motion capture [12, 13] further constrain deployment flexibility.

In this work, we investigate a simple but consequential question: does high-fidelity whole-body motion tracking truly require a full reference state at deployment?
We find that a compact reference target (CRT), consisting only of a root height, root linear and angular velocity commands, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints (bilateral wrists and ankles) at the current frame, is sufficient as the deployment-time input of a unified whole-body tracking policy that achieves competitive tracking performance compared to methods relying on full reference states (i.e., complete joint positions, dense body-part states, their velocities, and future frames).
This compact reference design dramatically reduces the information that the upstream sensing module must provide, and it removes the retargeting pipeline from the online control loop entirely, resulting in significantly lower end-to-end latency.

We present HuMiT, a low-latency whole-body teleoperation system for humanoid robots.
HuMiT employs lightweight human motion sensing to produce compact reference targets, which are then tracked by a whole-body policy trained in parallel simulation.
As shown in Fig. 1, HuMiT enables a wide range of dynamic whole-body skills that are difficult to achieve with high-latency or decoupled systems.

Our contributions are as follows:

Compact reference suffices at deployment.
Through cross-method comparison and ablations under identical conditions, we show that a compact reference target matches full-reference policies.

Low-latency teleoperation system.
By removing optimization-based retargeting and future-frame conditioning from the online loop, HuMiT achieves a communication-to-inference latency of ∼\sim20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) between operator and robot motion, while maintaining robust tracking performance.

Dynamic whole-body teleoperation for humanoids.
We validate HuMiT on a Unitree G1 humanoid executing reactive catching and coordinated loco-manipulation, confirming that the unified compact-reference design supports tightly coupled whole-body control under low-latency constraints.

1. Compact reference suffices at deployment.
Through cross-method comparison and ablations under identical conditions, we show that a compact reference target matches full-reference policies.

2. Low-latency teleoperation system.
By removing optimization-based retargeting and future-frame conditioning from the online loop, HuMiT achieves a communication-to-inference latency of ∼\sim20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) between operator and robot motion, while maintaining robust tracking performance.

3. Dynamic whole-body teleoperation for humanoids.
We validate HuMiT on a Unitree G1 humanoid executing reactive catching and coordinated loco-manipulation, confirming that the unified compact-reference design supports tightly coupled whole-body control under low-latency constraints.

title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation
authors: Samuel Foo Enze,Manthan Patel,Fan Yang,Linus Kramer,Pascal Roth,Marco Hutter,Cesar Cadena
abstract: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require 360∘360^{\circ} perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird’s-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation enables mobile robots to operate in challenging real-world domains, from negotiating dense pedestrian crowds in last-mile delivery to inspecting unstructured industrial and construction sites. A major driver of recent progress in learning-based navigation has been the use of pretrained visual representations. Rather than requiring the policy to learn perception from scratch, a frozen or lightly fine-tuned encoder supplies rich geometric and semantic features. This approach has proven effective for RGB-based navigation [1, 2] and depth image-based policies [3, 4].

However, both RGB and depth cameras inherit limitations. RGB features degrade under poor lighting and appearance shifts, and depth cameras return noisy or missing values beyond a few meters, in sunlight, and on reflective or textureless surfaces. Crucially, both are limited to a narrow field of view (FoV). Obstacles approaching from the side, pedestrians overtaking from behind, and routes outside the current view are simply invisible until it is too late to react. LiDAR addresses these weaknesses with 360∘360^{\circ} coverage, metric range up to tens of meters, and invariance to illumination, making it the natural sensor for the crowded, outdoor, and industrial settings that motivate this work. Yet pretrained representations for LiDAR-based navigation remain underexplored. Although point-cloud foundation models (FMs) such as Sonata [5] and Utonia [6] learn strong geometric and semantic features, their computational cost limits their use in massively parallel reinforcement learning (RL), and their effectiveness as pretraining sources for compact navigation encoders remains an open question. A navigation-ready LiDAR encoder should therefore be lightweight enough for large-scale RL, pretrained so the policy does not have to learn perception from sparse rewards, and generalizable across scenes and to the real world.

To this end, we present a compact LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained specifically for navigation. Exploiting the fixed scan pattern of spinning LiDARs, we spherically project each scan onto a 2D range image [7]. This representation is cheap to compute and batches predictably across parallel environments, but its geometry differs from a perspective image: it has many more azimuthal columns than elevation rows, and the image wraps around at the 0∘/360∘0^{\circ}/360^{\circ} seam. We account for both with a fully convolutional encoder that uses anisotropic kernels and circular convolutions along the azimuth. We pretrain the encoder on range images rendered from
TartanGround [8] with three navigation-aligned objectives: range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and BEV prediction, which preserve object semantics, obstacle boundaries, and top-down traversability information. The frozen latent representation then feeds an RL navigation policy using spatially-enhanced recurrent units (SRUs) [3] (Fig. 1).

In simulation, our pretraining recipe improves navigation success rate (SR) over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution test environments, respectively. Compared with the depth-based policy of [3], our LiDAR policy achieves comparable average SR, shorter navigation times, and higher success weighted by path length (SPL), and surpasses it in crowded and densely cluttered environments, highlighting the benefits of a wider FoV. Deployed zero-shot on a Unitree B2-W robot, the policy navigates obstacle-rich environments, unlit spaces, dense crowds, and cluttered construction sites, settings in which limited-FoV depth policies struggle.

In summary, our contributions are:

A navigation-aligned pretraining recipe combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and BEV prediction that significantly improves downstream navigation.

A lightweight (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder with anisotropic and circular convolutions, suitable for large-scale RL.

Extensive simulation and zero-shot real-world evaluation demonstrating the advantages of LiDAR-based navigation policies over limited-FoV depth-based policies.

title: Spacetime Splines for Adaptive Robot Motions
authors: Boxuan Zhang,Ante Marić,Sylvain Calinon
abstract:
Movement primitives commonly represent robot motions through basis
functions indexed by time or phase. Inspired by spacetime representations employed in physics,
we propose a spline-based formulation in which spatial geometry and
temporal progression are represented within a common set of continuous variables. The proposed method jointly estimates a shared Bézier
curve, while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adapted independently (e.g., demonstration-specific phase modulation). As use case, we consider an alternating optimization process that simultaneously estimates path intervals observed in partial demonstrations. Simulation experiments demonstrate accurate joint
recovery, refinement through modifications in model complexity and continuity, and improved robustness to variance in the demonstration set. Finally, we demonstrate online retiming and synchronization capabilities in a patient-turning task assisted by a robot, evaluated with a physical manikin.
introduction:
To adapt and coordinate robot motions, we need to consider both spatial and temporal information. For example, human-guided demonstrations may produce recordings of different durations that can speed up or slow down in different parts of the motion. The recorded paths and sampling rates may also differ, and some recordings may contain only part of the overall motion, starting and stopping at different points of the full path.

Spline representations provide compact continuous models of robot motion [1, 2, 3, 4]. Bézier curves provide one such representation that allows for easy modification of through geometrically-interpretable control points and favorable mathematical properties. For example, De Casteljau’s algorithm can be used as a stable method for evaluating and subdividing these curves [5, 6].
Temporal alignment and phase-based methods account for nonlinear timing differences or separate path geometry from timing [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], while others learn from incomplete or partial demonstrations [13, 14, 15, 16]. A common thread is that temporal and spatial aspects are encoded and
optimized separately.

Inspired by spacetime representations in physics, we propose a continuous dynamic curve representation that homogeneously encodes spatial geometry and motion timing as an augmented state space.
Figure 1 shows an example in which different phase modulations produce different spacetime curves preserving a spatial path. We consider in this paper a use case in which we jointly estimate a shared geometric path with a demonstration-specific modulation of the phase function that describes progress along that path.
We utilize and alternating optimization process that adapts path geometry by modifying spatial coordinates of the control points,
and motion timing through the temporal coordinates of the control points. This allows us to estimate path intervals in partial demonstrations of a longer motion.

The main contributions of this work are:

Spacetime dynamic curve representation: a modular continuous
spline encoding that homogeneously couples path geometry and phase, while allowing independent spatial and temporal adaptation.

Coverage estimation in partial demonstrations: joint inference of path intervals observed in partial demonstrations.

Spatial and temporal adaptation: adaptive refinement of shared Bézier geometry and demonstration-specific phase for online retiming and synchronization of robot motions.

1. Spacetime dynamic curve representation: a modular continuous
spline encoding that homogeneously couples path geometry and phase, while allowing independent spatial and temporal adaptation.

2. Coverage estimation in partial demonstrations: joint inference of path intervals observed in partial demonstrations.

3. Spatial and temporal adaptation: adaptive refinement of shared Bézier geometry and demonstration-specific phase for online retiming and synchronization of robot motions.

title: Robot Generalization Beyond Volume: The Diversity Path via Zero-Shot Capabilities
authors: Rafael Felix
abstract: General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning; As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.
introduction:
In recent years, several reports have projected strong growth for robotics through 2050. McKinsey estimates a $370B general-purpose robotics market by 2040 [59], Japan has set a national target of 10 million AI robots by 2040 [64], and Morgan Stanley projects a $5T humanoid market by 2050 [61]. These projections are driven by falling hardware costs, growing AI capabilities, and adoption that starts with developers and spreads through society. However, to achieve the true return on investment in physical AI, robot generalization is a major hurdle, and existing research has not yet found scalable solutions [100, 4].

The idea that an individual, on a given day, arrives home with a new appliance and hands it to their home robot, which has never seen the object before, is the promise of general-purpose robotics, as illustrated in Figure 1. A general autonomous system should be capable of inferring the new object’s affordances, selecting a suitable grasp, and completing tasks with it [3, 46]. Current robotic systems perform poorly at this capability, known as zero-shot generalization [100, 4]. Zero-shot generalization has been the target of extensive studies over the past decades in the field of digital AI such as computer vision [50, 92], large language models [71, 8], audio [70] and multi-modal learning [23, 22, 21]. We argue that it determines whether robots remain confined to controlled settings or become general-purpose economic assets.

In digital AI, zero-shot generalization has progressed as a function of the volume and diversity of data [16, 23]. As illustrated in Figure 2 volume is the density with which each situation is represented in the latent space, and diversity is the footprint those situations cover. This mirrors a familiar result for Gaussian processes: posterior uncertainty shrinks only near observed inputs, so spreading samples across the input space reduces uncertainty far more than repeating them in one region [76]. Volume helps AI systems recognize patterns accurately, but diversity allows them to interpolate within the latent space and act on concepts they have never seen. Seminal research and industry efforts have demonstrated zero-shot capabilities in large language models (LLMs) [8, 47], computer vision [69], and other fields [70, 32]. Robotics has yet to show comparable zero-shot capability. Moreover, the problem of diversity has been largely overlooked, as industry and research efforts have prioritized demonstrations of robots performing single tasks [13, 98]. Industrial and early-stage robots are typically deployed for a single, repetitive task, and each new task requires reprogramming or new training data [6, 100]. A robot able to perform an array of tasks within the same facility, adapting to new parts, layouts and procedures, would amortize its cost across many functions and lower the integration cost of each new task. For instance, in a warehouse, a robot trained to pick a given type of product could take on new types of object, or develop new tasks. In elderly care, a robot that delivers meals could assist carers with preparing food, a new task with new handling demands [78]. Further examples of zero-shot settings are depicted in Figure 1,

In this paper, we propose a novel approach based on our prior work in zero-shot and noisy-label learning applied in physical AI. Our approach combines a crowd-sourced data collection with recent advances in zero-shot generalization, generative AI, learning from noisy labels and scalable trust and safety [23, 28, 19]. We argue that generalization will emerge from structured data acquisition combined with community-driven crowd-sourcing. This combination allows us to acquire large volumes of data safely, while widening the range of scenarios, objects, situations and environments far beyond what any single engineering team could cover. Unlike digital AI, robots must also transfer what they learn in simulation to the physical world, where simulation never fully matches reality, a challenge known as the sim-to-real gap [99, 81]. A community running the same robotic platform in both simulation and reality exposes that gap at scale, and provides the tools to close it.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews how digital AI reached zero-shot behavior, what builds a latent space, how each training stage has drawn on crowd-sourced data, and how learning from imperfect data can absorb noisy contributions. Section 3 presents our approach. We first formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, showing why more data from the same collectors closes the gap only slowly, while each new contributor can widen it. We then describe a shared latent space for robot actions built from multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label and uncertainty learning, in which safety is part of the space from pre-training onward and seen/unseen detection lets the robot hand control to a human (Section 3.2). Real2Sim2Real treats simulation and reality as noisy teachers of each other across a community running the same robot (Section 3.3), and a community of developers building on one standard, approachable robot provides the data, with a cost model for each contributed hour (Section 3.4). Section 4 sets out a testable hypothesis and evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data. Section 5 discusses limitations and open questions, and Section 6 concludes.

title: OMAR: Open-World Multi-Attribute Reasoning for Scene-Conditioned Shelf Organization
authors: Benedikt Kreis,Rohit Menon,Benno Wingender,Muhammad Ehsan Ullah,Nils Dengler,Maren Bennewitz
abstract:
With the advent of foundation models, robots are increasingly capable of understanding and executing explicitly specified human tasks.
Extending these capabilities to open-ended tasks, however, requires robots to infer appropriate actions from the observed scene.
Household organization exemplifies this challenge, as robots must often act without detailed instructions, predefined object vocabularies, or known object-receptacle associations.
While robots may follow instructions or learn organization preferences from demonstrations, inferring the latent organization of an occasionally changing scene and placing a novel object consistently with it remains challenging.
We propose an open-world multi-attribute reasoning pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and constructs an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.
First, a vision-language model proposes labels together with attributes such as content and packaging type, which are grounded through segmentation, depth, and multi-view association.
Then, an LLM reasons over this representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements without explicitly user-provided preferences.
The resulting placement rankings guide subsequent geometric and kinematic feasibility checks for execution.
Our experimental evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines, enabling autonomous placement of previously unseen objects without predefined object-receptacle mappings or class-specific retraining.
introduction:
Households are constantly changing environments, and their organization reflects implicit and evolving human conventions.
To effectively organize objects in such environments, service robots must act beyond explicitly specified tasks.
When storing groceries, a robot must determine where a previously unseen object belongs, even without detailed instructions or user-provided preferences.
As object locations change, predefined object vocabularies and object-receptacle mappings cannot fully specify appropriate placements.

We study scene-conditioned shelf organization, in which the robot must infer the latent organization from the observed arrangement and place a novel object consistently into it.
This task requires reasoning over multiple object attributes, including content, packaging type, edibility, and orientation.
These attributes can suggest competing placements, and their relative importance depends on the organization of the particular scene.
Category labels alone therefore provide insufficient context.
Placement reasoning requires object-level descriptions grounded in the observed shelf.
Multi-view grounding provides this object-level context by associating instances across views and revealing occluded objects.

Vision-language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) offer semantic knowledge beyond predefined object sets, supporting the prediction of semantically plausible placements [1, 2, 3], but plausibility alone does not ensure geometric or kinematic feasibility.
Joint pick-and-place pipelines address grasp-placement compatibility through task-aware 6-DoF grasp selection and feasibility evaluation [4, 5, 6], but do not infer the shelf’s latent organization from semantic object attributes.
The resulting challenge is to connect grounded, scene-dependent semantic reasoning with feasibility-aware planning so that placements of unseen objects preserve the observed organization and remain executable in confined shelf spaces.

We address this gap via open-world, multi-attribute reasoning (OMAR), which places previously unseen objects consistently with the observed shelf organization.
As shown in Fig. 1, our pipeline grounds VLM-generated object descriptions across views in an instance-level 3D scene graph, capturing content, packaging type, edibility, and orientation rather than category labels alone.
An LLM reasons jointly over these attributes and their scene-dependent relevance to infer the latent shelf organization and propose placements that preserve its coherence, without user-provided preferences, predefined object-receptacle mappings, or class-specific retraining.
These proposals guide grasp prediction and geometric and kinematic feasibility checks, linking multi-attribute shelf coherence to executable placements.
To summarize, the main contributions of our work are:

An open-world multi-attribute mapping pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and creates an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.

An open-world multi-attribute mapping pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and creates an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.

An LLM-based reasoning pipeline leveraging instance-level scene representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements.

Our evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines.

2. An LLM-based reasoning pipeline leveraging instance-level scene representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements.

title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Johannes Keller,Albrecht M. Bloße,Adrian Lindenmeyer,Thomas Neumuth,Daniel Schneider
abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly.
Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies.
We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy.
Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations.
Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged.
In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance.
For SmolVLA, the head on the vision–language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs.
We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings.
Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs.
With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement.
These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
Code available at https://github.com/post-hoc-vla-uncertainty/post-hoc-vla-uncertainty.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models bring pre-trained visual and linguistic representations to robot control [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
After deployment, such a policy keeps encountering tasks, scenes and instructions that its training demonstrations cover only partially.
In tasks where failures may be costly, when facing difficulties due to insufficient training knowledge, the robot should respond adaptively by deferring tasks to seek human assistance or by requesting relevant additional training demonstrations [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14].
Both responses are effective only if guided by the policy’s epistemic uncertainty, that is, by how poorly its training data support a situation.
Unlike aleatoric ambiguity, epistemic uncertainty shrinks with more relevant demonstrations [15, 16].

Flow-based VLAs do not provide such an estimate by themselves.
This motivates dedicated methods for quantifying epistemic uncertainty in these policies.
For example, Römer et al. [14] derive velocity-field disagreement (VFD), an ensemble estimate of the divergence between flow-matching policies.
They use VFD in SAVE, an active fine-tuning procedure that they evaluate on LIBERO [17], a simulation benchmark of language-instructed household manipulation tasks.
In each round, SAVE requests a few new demonstrations, preferring situations that VFD rates as uncertain, and then fine-tunes the policy.
In their evaluation, VFD correlates more strongly with task success than six alternative uncertainty scores, including other ensemble-based measures and entropy-based scores.
SAVE with VFD needs at least 22% fewer demonstrations than the compared acquisition strategies.
The price is an ensemble of at least two policies: every additional member must be pre-trained, fine-tuned alongside the deployed policy in every adaptation round, and integrated jointly with it whenever a score is computed.

We ask whether this ensemble is necessary to obtain comparably useful estimates of epistemic uncertainty.
Ensemble disagreement reflects differences between the predictions of independently trained policies, which can arise where the demonstrations leave their behaviour weakly constrained.
Their disagreement can therefore serve as an indirect signal of demonstration coverage.
This motivates assessing coverage directly in the embedding space of a single trained policy, using lightweight uncertainty estimation heads.
Each head reads embeddings that the policy already computes and compares a queried observation with support observations from its training demonstrations (Figure 1).
The approach assumes that the embeddings keep unfamiliar observations apart from familiar ones [18], a property that we do not enforce during training.
Its practical usefulness further depends on whether unfamiliarity helps identify situations where the policy may fail or benefit from assistance or additional demonstrations.
We assess these relationships empirically across our experiments.
The measure is the posterior variance of a Gaussian process (GP) with a Gaussian kernel, conditioned on the support embeddings [19].
It needs no regression targets and no gradient update and does not alter the policy’s predicted actions but can inform decisions such as when to request help or new demonstrations.
Fitting it post hoc to a trained policy takes one feature extraction pass over the support observations and one Cholesky factorization.
Since the heads are this cheap, several of them can be attached to different embeddings of the same policy.
Heads on modality-specific representations, such as the camera or instruction tokens, can then indicate which part of an input is unfamiliar.

title: Sufficient and Necessary Causal Explanations for the Analysis of Autonomous Systems
authors: Tom Yaacov,Khen Elimelech,Hana Chockler,Moshe Y. Vardi
abstract: Understanding failures of autonomous systems is challenging, particularly when their behavior depends on black-box components such as neural networks. In this work, we make a distinction between two objectives of failure analysis: reproduction, which seeks to identify conditions sufficient to reproduce an observed failure, and avoidance, which seeks to identify the changes required to prevent it. Previous work on causal explanations of system failures is based on the concept of sufficient explanations and naturally supports reproduction. Nevertheless, we observe that it does not address the problem of avoiding the failure. In this paper, we introduce and formalize the concept of necessary explanations for system analysis as the correct formalism for failure avoidance. We place necessary explanations in the framework of actual causality and show that, together with sufficient explanations, they provide a unified causal framework for addressing both objectives of failure analysis. We present an efficient approximation algorithm for generating necessary explanations based on the notion of causal responsibility. We evaluate the efficiency of our approach across multiple environments. We demonstrate the practical utility of necessary explanations for failure avoidance through counterfactual generation and show that it outperforms existing methods.
introduction:
Autonomous systems rely on algorithms and digital computation to control real-world machines and achieve complex objectives autonomously [1]. As these objectives become increasingly challenging, modern systems have come to rely heavily on black-box components, such as neural networks [2, 3]. The opacity of these components, combined with the complexity of systems and the variability of their operating environments, makes it difficult to interpret system behavior and gain insight into how decisions were made.
This difficulty has motivated the rapidly growing interest in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), which is widely regarded as crucial for the widespread adoption of autonomous systems [4, 5].

Explainability becomes even more vital when failures happen. Understanding failures, known as failure analysis, is crucial for the development and debugging of systems, and it is especially challenging when systems rely on black-box components, often provided by a third party.
An explanation should help us gain insight into what affected the system behavior that led to the failure outcome. Addressing this goal requires answering two questions: (1) what counts as an explanation? (2) how to generate the right one?
Post-hoc XAI, where explanations are based on the analysis of the outcome rather than the process,
is a suitable paradigm for analyzing black-box systems, as it does not require any changes or even access to
the internals of the system, and it is the one we follow in this paper.

To position this work clearly, we first mention the underlying conceptual contribution of this paper (which we discuss in detail in Sec. IV), with which we identify the two complementary explanation objectives: outcome avoidance, and outcome reproduction. In the first case, our concern is changing the outcome (with minimal effort), e.g., when we wish to repair the failure; the explanation should hence provide insight on which elements in the scenario should be changed (and how), in order to change the (failing) outcome.
In the second case, our concern is generating additional scenarios, in which the same (failing) outcome is maintained, e.g., as part of a debugging process; the explanation should hence provide insight on which elements in the scenario are sufficient to recreate the outcome, regardless of the rest. The two forms of explanation are complementary, but one cannot be deduced from the other.

A recent work [6] suggested using the framework of “actual causality” [7, 8]
to formally define and generate causal failure explanations (for CPSs).
According to our categorization, that work addressed the objective of failure reproduction, by focusing on the generation
of “sufficient explanations” (an established concept in actual causality). Roughly speaking, a sufficient explanation is a subset of elements
of the failure execution that is, by itself, sufficient to result in a failure, even if all other elements are changed or removed.
Such explanations are not suitable for failure avoidance, as removing or changing such a sufficient subset does not guarantee that the failure
is avoided. Intuitively, this is because multiple sufficient subsets may exist.

This work seeks to extend the foundations laid in [6] to address the objective of failure avoidance by introducing and applying the concept of “necessary explanations”. Roughly speaking, a necessary explanation is a subset of elements of the failure execution such that
removing them avoids the failure. Together, this provides, for the first time, a unified (causal) formal framework for failure analysis, allowing to address both objectives. As exact computation of such causal explanations quickly becomes intractable when the number of inputs increases [9], we also develop a practical, scalable algorithm
for generating necessary explanations based on the notion of causal degree of responsibility [10].

The paper contributions:
(i) We suggest a conceptual categorization of the objectives of failure explanation—avoidance and reproduction—providing a basis for understanding,
comparing, and advancing work in this field.
(ii) We introduce the notion of necessary explanations for autonomous system failures and discuss its application to failure avoidance.
(iii) We develop a practical, scalable algorithm for generating necessary explanations and provide an experimental evaluation demonstrating its efficiency across multiple environments.
Finally, to demonstrate the superiority of this framework for explanation for failure avoidance, (iv) we provide a study comparing
with prior work on failure avoidance not based on causal reasoning. We show that our approach achieves a higher success rate, lower computation time, and better quality.
For clarity, the paper is presented (and contributions (iii) and (iv) are evaluated) using a setup of an autonomous car with a black-box neural controller, trained to avoid collisions (as in Fig. 1). In our evaluation, we use two autonomous driving simulators, of both high and low fidelity, showing that the benefits of our approach are simulator- and system-independent.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows.
After overviewing the related work,
Sec. II provides preliminaries on the autonomous system testing model and introduces the running example.
Sec. III gives a brief overview of actual causality and introduces our setup.
Sec. IV introduces the conceptual framework of failure analysis.
Sec. V presents our theoretical contributions, extending the framework with necessary explanations. Sec. VI presents the approximation algorithm for computing necessary explanations. The experimental performance evaluation is presented in Sec. VII. Sec. VIII demonstrates the practical utility of necessary explanations for failure avoidance, comparing it with existing work. Sec. IX concludes the paper.

Related Work:
In explainable AI, actual causality has been used in various domains, such as images [9], audio [12], and process mining [13]. Since computing actual causes is generally hard, these approaches introduce efficient approximations [14]. Similarly to us, they treat the AI model as a black box.

Existing explainability approaches for failure reproduction include sensitivity analysis [15, 16], which examines neighborhoods around falsifying traces, identifying regions where a property is violated. As mentioned, actual causality has also been proposed for failure reproduction, providing a more structured, high-level alternative by identifying minimal subsets of elements that reproduce the observed failure [6].

Failure avoidance methods focus on modifications to a failing scenario that change its outcome. Existing approaches for failure avoidance primarily generate counterfactuals, passing examples similar to the original [17, 18].
While counterfactuals can provide valuable insight into the observed behavior, they focus on input-output changes rather than the underlying causal mechanisms, potentially attributing importance to downstream effects and including modifications that are not necessary for avoiding the failure.
Autonomous systems work on explainability also use counterfactual attribution for root-cause analysis [19]. This approach relies on causal discovery, which infers causal relationships from data,
a fundamentally different approach from
the one we adopt in this paper, which allows reasoning within an abstract model.

title: Reconstruction-Augmented Visuomotor Pre-Training of 3D-Grounded Bimanual Dexterity from RGB-Only Human Videos
authors: Xingyi He,Zhiwen Qiu,Adhitya Polavaram,Yunhao Cao,Cory Fan,Julius Samwer,Saleh Kalantari,Kuan Fang
abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone. Project page and video: https://spatial-dex.github.io/
introduction:
Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires coordination between both hands to stabilize, reorient, and transfer objects while adapting to their shapes and changing positions in the surrounding environment. Geometric representations support this coordination by capturing spatial relationships between hands and objects [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], while pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) can provide complementary visual and semantic priors [6, 7, 8]. Learning such coordination therefore demands both spatial grounding and diverse experience of how the two hands act across objects and scene configurations. Robot demonstrations supply the former through depth sensing and executable commands, but collecting them through teleoperation is costly, which limits the range of tasks, objects, and configurations they cover.

Human videos on the web provide an alternative source of rich everyday activities and physical interactions with diverse environments at scale. However, these RGB-only recordings lack explicit scene geometry or robot-compatible action labels. Learning from these videos therefore calls for recovering the demonstrated hand motion and the scene geometry at a consistent scale and keeping them aligned across time.

Recent methods pre-train vision-language-action (VLA) models on human videos with explicit wrist and finger motion supervision, and transfer learned skills to robots through action-space alignment [9, 10, 11]. Other approaches exploit 3D cues by predicting point tracks [12], adopting shared hand-object keypoint representations [13], combining calibrated geometry with spatial-language and wrist-motion supervision [14], or reconstructing hand-object interactions to synthesize robot trajectories [15]. However, recovering scene geometry at a scale consistent with the recovered hand motion from RGB-only videos remains challenging, as scale errors misalign reconstructed geometry with hand trajectories and compromise spatial supervision. Although some studies integrate geometric and visual features [3] or combine spatial and human-motion supervision [14], their training objectives provide limited direct supervision for how fine-grained hand behavior relates to changes in the surrounding scene. How to effectively incorporate these cues into human-video pre-training therefore remains underexplored.

In this work, we present SpatialDex, a framework for pre-training 3D-grounded visuomotor policies from large-scale RGB-only human videos. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry alongside hand motion and using both to supervise policy pre-training. To make reconstructed hand-object distances consistent with the demonstrated motion, we use the hand-size prior in 3D hand estimates to calibrate scene geometry with a shared scale across frames and both hands, as illustrated in Figure 1. The reconstructed geometry then serves the policy in two roles. As an input, it is combined with the image-patch features of a pre-trained VLM through progressive dual-gated fusion, which adds spatial information while retaining the visual priors of the VLM. As a target, future scene geometry is supervised alongside wrist and finger actions, so that the policy captures spatial relationships and scene dynamics. The policy generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists, and it is fine-tuned to bimanual dexterous tasks with a small number of robot demonstrations.

In summary, the contributions of this work are threefold:

We introduce a data pipeline that aligns reconstructed scene geometry with human hand motion at a shared video-level scale, producing 1M video clips with aligned geometry and motion annotations for policy pre-training.

We develop a reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training framework that combines progressive dual-gated fusion of geometric and visual features with future geometry prediction, and generates finger motion conditioned on both wrist trajectories.

We evaluate SpatialDex on nine simulated tasks across two embodiments and six real-world tasks, reaching mean success rates of 76.3% and 81.7% compared with 59.8% and 43.3% for the state-of-the-art methods.

1. We introduce a data pipeline that aligns reconstructed scene geometry with human hand motion at a shared video-level scale, producing 1M video clips with aligned geometry and motion annotations for policy pre-training.

2. We develop a reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training framework that combines progressive dual-gated fusion of geometric and visual features with future geometry prediction, and generates finger motion conditioned on both wrist trajectories.

3. We evaluate SpatialDex on nine simulated tasks across two embodiments and six real-world tasks, reaching mean success rates of 76.3% and 81.7% compared with 59.8% and 43.3% for the state-of-the-art methods.

title: CausGround: Causal Interaction Grounding for Adaptive Embodied Planning
authors: Yijun Shen,Diqi He,Jinbang Guo,Wanyue Zhang,Jiaming Mi,Huan Yang,Zhongyuan Wang,Zhiwei Yu,Kai Zhang
abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising reasoning capabilities, but deploying them for physical interaction requires reliable planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world.
These preconditions and effects are often environment-dependent and are not fully captured by MLLMs, making adaptation to new environments challenging.
Yet existing adaptation approaches either update model parameters through costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to ground and reuse.
To address this challenge, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge.
CausGround learns from experience by identifying action preconditions and effects, and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations.
At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in the current observation, supporting backward reasoning over action preconditions and forward reasoning over action effects for action selection and multi-step causal planning.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of CausGround across diverse long-horizon embodied settings spanning simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation.
Evaluated on the adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround consistently improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, improving average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa.
Consistent gains are also observed on SWITCH benchmark, with average interaction reasoning accuracy improving from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating stronger reasoning over action selection, recovery, and verification.
Moreover, real-world experiments further show that CausGround can reason backward from MLLM-interpreted goal states to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation.
These results demonstrate that explicit action preconditions and effects provide a reusable causal grounding mechanism for long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.
introduction:
Embodied agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising reasoning capabilities for high-level planning (Chen et al., 2025; Driess et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2025b). Yet successful embodied interaction requires more than knowing what to do: agents must know when an action is executable and how it changes the world. Such interaction knowledge is often environment-dependent, involving available actions, object states, action preconditions, and effects (Kim et al., 2025; Han et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). As illustrated in Fig. 1, a planner may correctly infer that an object should be placed into a fridge, yet attempt the action before satisfying the precondition that the fridge be open. Such precondition violations can accumulate over long-horizon execution, leading to invalid actions, repeated attempts, and costly trial-and-error (Raman et al., 2024; Zhi et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2025). Effective embodied planning therefore requires agents to account for task semantics while adapting their planning to the interaction dynamics of the environment in which the task is executed.

Existing approaches still fall short in enabling efficient environment adaptation. A direct strategy is to specialize embodied agents through fine-tuning or reinforcement learning (Xu et al., 2026; Zhai et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025a), but such parametric adaptation requires substantial environment-specific interaction data and repeated optimization, making it costly to deploy across diverse environments, particularly in real-world settings.
Non-parametric approaches instead incorporate interaction feedback or episodic memory at inference time (Anwar et al., 2025), but such experience is often retained as unstructured trajectories or task-level memories (Ginting et al., 2025; Buoso et al., 2025). This makes it difficult to identify which parts of an experience are causally relevant rather than incidental, reuse them across tasks, or ground them in the current visual scene.
Moreover, existing representations do not always jointly capture the fine-grained object attributes and inter-object relations required to determine whether an action’s preconditions are satisfied (Chen et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026).
This raises a central question: Can interaction experience be distilled into reusable causal knowledge that tells an embodied agent both what must be true before an action and what changes as a result?

To this end, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework for adaptive embodied planning. As illustrated in Fig. 1, CausGround abstracts interaction experience into action-centered causal knowledge, representing each action through its relevant preconditions and resulting state effects. Rather than storing complete trajectories, it organizes reusable action-centered causal knowledge over a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations.
At planning time, the current observation and task are grounded into the same representation to construct a task-relevant local causal graph from reusable causal knowledge. This allows the planner to reason backward over action preconditions to determine what must happen before an action becomes executable, and forward over state effects to anticipate how the world should change after execution. Composing such causal dependencies provides a structured reference for multi-step planning without updating model parameters.

We evaluate CausGround across heterogeneous long-horizon embodied settings.
In simulation, we adapt VirtualHome (Puig et al., 2018) and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2026) for visually grounded high-level planning and observe consistent improvements under both one-shot and closed-loop planning, including an increase in average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and from 43.0% to 57.0% under closed-loop planning on RoboCasa.
Beyond simulation, we evaluate interaction reasoning on SWITCH (Cheng et al., 2025), a real-world egocentric long-horizon interaction benchmark, where CausGround improves average accuracy from 25.8% to 31.9%.
We further validate the framework on real-robot manipulation, where CausGround reasons backward from interpreted goal states to derive executable high-level action sequences and successfully complete multi-step interactions.
Together, these results show that explicit causal interaction knowledge provides a reusable grounding substrate for long-horizon embodied reasoning across diverse environments.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate embodied interaction knowledge around action preconditions and state effects, and introduce a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations, enabling interaction knowledge to be grounded in current visual observations.

We introduce CausGround, a non-parametric framework that distills interaction trajectories into reusable action-centered causal knowledge and dynamically grounds task-relevant causal dependencies for planning. This enables reasoning over both what must hold before an action and how the world changes after it without parameter updates.

We evaluate CausGround across long-horizon embodied settings spanning VirtualHome and RoboCasa simulations, the real-world egocentric SWITCH benchmark, and real-robot manipulation, demonstrating consistent gains in planning and interaction reasoning across environments and MLLM backbones.

1. We formulate embodied interaction knowledge around action preconditions and state effects, and introduce a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations, enabling interaction knowledge to be grounded in current visual observations.

2. We introduce CausGround, a non-parametric framework that distills interaction trajectories into reusable action-centered causal knowledge and dynamically grounds task-relevant causal dependencies for planning. This enables reasoning over both what must hold before an action and how the world changes after it without parameter updates.

3. We evaluate CausGround across long-horizon embodied settings spanning VirtualHome and RoboCasa simulations, the real-world egocentric SWITCH benchmark, and real-robot manipulation, demonstrating consistent gains in planning and interaction reasoning across environments and MLLM backbones.

title: AirPlayground: Benchmarking Aerial Navigation across Diverse Reconstructed Environments
authors: Rangya Zhang,Yujing Shang,Zhuoyuan Yu,Mingsheng Li,Qingsong Yan,Chao Yan,Yuhang Zhang,Mir Feroskhan
abstract: Large-scale aerial resources provide a foundation for learning navigation across diverse environments. However, existing resources remain limited in providing (1) densely sampled flight demonstrations for learning different policy formulations and (2) broad environment coverage for standardized closed-loop evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for training and evaluating aerial navigation policies across diverse environments. We first construct 94 photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) environments spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation settings, with aligned collision geometry. Building on these environments, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline for automated expert flight collection, yielding 94K demonstrations and 46.5M synchronized observation–state–action samples at 50 Hz. We further provide an extensible API that supports training different policy formulations on this shared corpus and evaluating them under unified protocols in the corresponding environments. We benchmark seven baselines spanning four policy paradigms across three navigation settings in seen and unseen environments, and further examine scaling behavior with ACT. Scaling ACT’s training corpus from 5 to 70 scenes raises median success rates on seen and unseen environments from 30.6%30.6\% and 16.8%16.8\% to 41.2%41.2\% and 29.4%29.4\%, respectively. Through this shared training and evaluation framework, AirPlayground supports analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes. Our analyses highlight the roles of prediction errors, execution protocols, and scene interactions in closed-loop performance.
introduction:
Learning-based aerial navigation depends on large-scale, diverse experience to generalize across environments (Zheng et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Acquiring experience through online interaction can be costly and difficult to scale. Offline demonstrations support scaling policy learning without environment interaction during training (O’Neill et al., 2024). Yet policies trained on demonstrations learn from expert states, whereas deployment exposes them to states shaped by their actions (Seo et al., 2024). Small errors can compound through feedback, so accurate imitation does not guarantee reliable navigation. Assessing reliability therefore requires systematic closed-loop evaluation across diverse environments, where policies must respond to the consequences of their actions.

To meet these learning and evaluation needs, aerial navigation research has produced both flight datasets and interactive environments. Large-scale datasets such as CityNav and OpenFly provide aerial trajectories for navigation and vision-language learning (Lee et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026), substantially increasing the scale and diversity of reusable flight experience. In parallel, 3DGS-based embodied platforms make reconstructed real-world scenes available as photorealistic, geometrically grounded environments for interactive navigation (Liu et al., 2026b; Miao et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026). Recent benchmarks further combine reconstructed environments, collision-aware interaction, and flight trajectories for policy learning and evaluation (Guo et al., 2026).

Despite this progress, two limitations remain in the resources for aerial policy learning and evaluation. (i) Limited dense flight experience. Densely sampled observation–action demonstrations remain limited across diverse real-world environments. Dense supervision captures continuous flight control for learning different action representations, while coverage across scenes exposes policies to varied visual conditions and spatial structures. (ii) Limited standardized evaluation across diverse environments. Standardized closed-loop evaluation remains limited in its coverage of environments with diverse appearances and spatial structures. Indoor spaces, urban outdoor areas, and vegetation present different visibility and obstacle configurations, making evaluation across these settings important for assessing how consistently policies perform beyond a narrow set of scenes.

To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for aerial navigation that pairs dense flight experience with photorealistic 3DGS reconstructions and executable geometry. AirPlayground comprises 94 reconstructed scenes spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation environments, with nearly 100K flight demonstrations and 46.5M RGB frames under 50 Hz observation–action supervision. To scale collection, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline, reusable across reconstructed scenes, that models navigable space, samples navigation tasks, and generates expert demonstrations. We further introduce an extensible cross-policy API that adapts the shared corpus to each policy’s native representation and maps its outputs to a common control interface under unified evaluation protocols. By linking recorded trajectories to executable scene geometry, AirPlayground also enables analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes.

Specifically, AirPlayground makes three main contributions.

(i) Dense flight experience paired with executable reconstructions of real-world environments. We pair dense flight demonstrations with photorealistic reconstructions and aligned navigation and collision geometry for policy learning and matched closed-loop execution.

(ii) A unified benchmark across navigation policy paradigms. Our extensible API supports shared-data policy training and unified closed-loop evaluation across three navigation settings, while preserving each policy’s native representations and inference structure through adapters.

(iii) Cross-policy evaluation and deployment diagnosis. We benchmark seven baselines and analyze offline predictions and closed-loop behavior. These studies show that offline accuracy alone does not fully explain deployment performance and examine how execution horizons and scene geometry affect navigation, demonstrating the benchmark’s value beyond performance comparisons.
