title: FlowVLA: Learning Flow-Aware Physical Completion for Quantitative Robotic Pouring
authors: Liwen Yang,Yutian Zhang,Jiaqi Zhai,Li Yang,Tutian Tang,Qiwei Shan,Yancheng Bi,Qiankuan Shangguan,Yangkun Zhu,Ce Hao,Dong Wei,Qiaojun Yu,Dibo Hou
abstract: During steady pouring, images and robot pose may remain nearly unchanged while transferred mass accumulates, making the return decision ambiguous for a whole-task vision–language–action (VLA) policy. We present FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from physical-completion estimation. A shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert learns approach, pour, and return with boundary-aware supervision. A target-independent estimator fuses visual, joint, wrist-wrench, and recurrent force-belief histories to maintain an estimate of transferred mass. The controller initiates return when this estimate plus predicted residual outflow reaches the requested mass. In coffee-pot/water experiments, FlowVLA achieves 13.1 g goal-balanced mean absolute error (MacroMAE), lower than all tested VLA baselines. Across all attempts, 53.7% both complete the task and finish within ±10%\pm 10\% of the requested mass. The same model interpolates to held-out 150/250-g targets without retraining. Independently trained models further evaluate the formulation in three additional container–fluid settings.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models connect visual and language understanding to robot control, enabling a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks [1, 2, 3]. Quantitative pouring adds a requirement beyond executing the manipulation sequence: the transferred mass must match a requested amount. This matters in food preparation [4] and household drink-serving tasks [5] (Fig. 1). Without online electronic-scale feedback, the robot must infer how much liquid has been transferred and when to return the container upright. During steady pouring, images and robot pose can remain nearly unchanged while mass accumulates, so visually similar states may require either continued pouring or return. We call this ambiguity physical-completion aliasing. Understanding “pour 200 g” specifies the goal but does not reveal physical progress, and initiating return does not stop liquid transfer immediately.

Whole-task VLA policies typically learn completion implicitly alongside motion. Policies use force or tactile feedback to guide action generation [6, 7, 8], while FM-VLA encodes force histories as memory tokens [9]. Wrist wrench is informative about liquid transfer, but it also varies with arm motion, container pose, grasp geometry, and liquid dynamics [4]. Force conditioning therefore does not by itself define the accumulated physical quantity needed for a stopping decision. Precision-pouring controllers make this quantity explicit by closing the loop on fill level [10, 5], source-mass loss [4], or predicted overpour [11]. Their feedback formulations offer a useful starting point, but generally assume prescribed grasps or constrained motions. The remaining challenge is to integrate quantitative completion into a learned whole-task policy that must also grasp, transport, pour, return, and place the container.

Our insight is to treat physical completion as a persistent state separate from motor generation. FlowVLA couples a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert with explicit flow and mass estimation. Boundary-aware supervision distinguishes continued pouring from return at action-chunk boundaries. A recurrent force observer provides temporal belief to the action expert and a dedicated completion head, which fuses this belief with visual, joint, and wrist-wrench histories to estimate transferred mass. The physical estimators are target-independent, while the requested mass conditions the POUR prompt and completion threshold. The controller accounts for liquid transferred during return by triggering return when predicted terminal mass reaches the target. Real-robot comparisons with whole-task VLA and load-based baselines, mechanism ablations, and held-out target interpolation evaluate this formulation, alongside additional container–fluid regimes with independently trained models.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate physical-completion aliasing in quantitative pouring and introduce FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from estimation of the hidden physical progress needed for quantitative stopping.

We develop boundary-aware action learning that combines multirate force observations and recurrent belief with stage-specific prompts in a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert. Row-wise masking and exact-return-boundary sampling jointly supervise the transition from steady pouring to return.

We design a target-independent completion module that maintains flow and accumulated mass from causal multimodal histories and predicts residual outflow, enabling return decisions based on predicted terminal mass rather than current transferred mass.

1. We formulate physical-completion aliasing in quantitative pouring and introduce FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from estimation of the hidden physical progress needed for quantitative stopping.

2. We develop boundary-aware action learning that combines multirate force observations and recurrent belief with stage-specific prompts in a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert. Row-wise masking and exact-return-boundary sampling jointly supervise the transition from steady pouring to return.

3. We design a target-independent completion module that maintains flow and accumulated mass from causal multimodal histories and predicts residual outflow, enabling return decisions based on predicted terminal mass rather than current transferred mass.

title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI
authors: Meng Luo,Zechen Bai,Shanqing Xu,Yanlin Li,Kaixin Li,Mengchen Qian,Weifeng Lu,Ran Zhang,Yingtian Zou,Ziyang Luo,Wei Chen,Hongzhan Lin
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves the process by which it improves, not only its behavior. The idea goes back to I. J. Good’s speculation about machines that design better machines (Good, 1966) and to self-referential learners such as the Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003), and recent digital agents have begun to approach it (Chen et al., 2026d). STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024) applies a program that improves code to its own source, and the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2026c) lets improved coding agents modify themselves; both judge each candidate with executable tests. Yet a system can get better at a task, and a fixed procedure can keep producing better versions of it, without anything recursive happening. RSI requires two further links (Section 2.2): what the system retains from earlier improvements must make its next revision better, and the improver, the component that revises the learning procedure, must in turn use what it has gained to help produce its own next improvement.

Physical RSI asks the same question of systems that learn by acting in the physical world, such as robots. Digital RSI supplies the mechanisms (language models that write reward code or controllers, archives of earlier variants, and automated experiment loops); physical RSI tests how these mechanisms use physical experience and whether they hold under physical constraints (Figure 1). The physical setting changes the experimental conditions in four ways (Table 1). First, physical outcome checks depend on sensors and task-specific verifiers, people, or learned detectors whose reliability must be established; even an automated grasp-success check can miss what it does not sense, and an error in that judgment can be reinforced and then executed on hardware. Second, every candidate costs robot time, resets, supervision, and wear, so a revision must pay off within few trials. Third, practice changes its own conditions: objects move, grippers wear, calibration drifts, and rolling back software does not repair a damaged object. Fourth, what can be improved extends beyond prompts and code to controllers, dynamics models, and the interface to a particular body. Each difference bears on the central question of RSI, whether what one round of revision teaches the improver makes the next revision better.

Consider a robot arm that keeps missing the same grasp. The failure can have several causes, and each calls for a change kept in a different place; these places organize Sections 3.1 and 3.2. The robot’s policy, the learned controller that turns observations into motor commands, may never produce the recovery motion; an expert correction can teach it, as RECAP (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) learns from deployment experience and corrections (Section 3.1.1). The robot may mistake a light touch for a stable hold because its model of contact is wrong; a world model refitted to contact data can correct the prediction and give the policy a place to practice, as in PlayWorld (Yin et al., 2026b) (Section 3.1.2). The robot may have recovered from this failure before without keeping what worked; external knowledge, such as a saved recovery or program, can be called the next time, as Zetta (Ding et al., 2026) grows code-based critics and recoveries around a frozen policy in simulation (Section 3.1.3). Finally, the robot may keep choosing the wrong kind of repair; then the learning procedure must change: which attempts to collect, how to judge them, and how to turn them into updates (Section 3.2). Eureka (Ma et al., 2024a) rewrites reward code from simulated training results, and ENPIRE (Xiao et al., 2026b) lets coding agents modify the training infrastructure from robot experiments. The first three routes improve what the robot does; the fourth improves how it learns, and it is where physical RSI would begin. Recursion would further require that knowledge of why earlier repairs worked, which we call repair knowledge, improves how the next procedure revision is made. Figure 2 contrasts this route with applying a fixed training recipe to new experience.

Our central argument is that physical experience can improve task competence, the learning procedure, and the improver that revises this procedure, and that four recurring conditions, each sharpened by the physical setting, decide whether such gains carry forward. Each can fail: the new signal may not address what the learner still lacks, because sensing shows only part of a failure; the receiving component may be unable to absorb it on its body; its value may not survive later changes in behavior or hardware; or further practice may become unsafe or unaffordable. For the grasping robot, this could mean collecting more of the grasps it already makes well, refining a contact model that its controller cannot use, relying on a fix that stops working once the gripper is replaced, or practicing until the gripper wears out. A change can improve execution and still fail to help later learning: added autonomous data often yield modest gains that saturate and can even regress (Mirchandani et al., 2025).

Several research traditions supply pieces of this progression. Self-supervised grasping showed that physical outcomes alone can supervise behavior at scale, first by learning from tens of thousands of real grasp attempts (Pinto and Gupta, 2016) and then through large-scale real-robot reinforcement learning (RL) with QT-Opt (Kalashnikov et al., 2018). Interactive imitation learning, as in DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) and HG-DAgger (Kelly et al., 2019), showed how an expert can correct the learner in the states that the learner itself reaches. Lifelong robot learning (Thrun and Mitchell, 1995) asks how knowledge gained on earlier tasks can reduce the real-world experimentation needed for later ones; model-based RL, from Dyna (Sutton, 1990) and PILCO (Deisenroth and Rasmussen, 2011) to Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020), asks how recorded transitions can support practice inside a learned model; and skill-based approaches, such as options (Sutton et al., 1999) and the shared RoboEarth knowledge base (Waibel et al., 2011), ask how an extended behavior can be stored and called again. Each tradition widened what one learning episode can pass on to the next.

Recent generalist and foundation-model-based systems widen both what can change and what role the change plays. RoboCat (Bousmalis et al., 2024) turns a policy adapted to a new task into a source of training data for the next generalist, and SILVR (Luo et al., 2026a) revises a video-based planner using its own executions. In RoboCat, Eureka (in simulation), and ENPIRE, experience reaches the machinery that produces future updates (a data collector, a reward function, the training infrastructure) as well as the policy that receives them. This brings the physical problem close to the long-standing aspiration of learning to learn (Thrun and Pratt, 1998), and several reviewed systems already contain the components that a demonstration of recursion would need. The open question is how to realize that aspiration with limited trials, imperfect sensing, and a body that changes over time.

Our scope is the improvement of policies, world models, memories, skills, and the software procedures that update or use them, whenever their evidence or evaluation is connected to physical action. We discuss hardware change when it affects compatibility, maintenance, or continued experimentation. Autonomous morphology design and physical self-reconstruction are adjacent topics outside our scope.

Recent surveys cover neighboring ground (Table 2). Some focus on agents and embodiment: recursive self-improvement in AI systems (Chen et al., 2026d), self-evolving agents (Gao et al., 2025), weights versus executable skills as stores of improvement (Jena et al., 2026), self-evolving embodied AI (Feng et al., 2026) and humanoids (Nguyen et al., 2026), and levels of physical recursive self-improvement (Zhou et al., 2026a). Others analyze world models for robot learning (Hou et al., 2026) and manipulation (Wang et al., 2026a), joint world–action models (Lu et al., 2026b), actionable simulators (Chen and Zhu, 2026), verifiers for robot policies (Wan et al., 2026), and physical AI broadly (Xiang et al., 2025). Our organizing question is different: after a change has been acquired, who uses it next, and what does that use improve? Component names alone cannot answer it, because two data collectors with similar task success can yield training data of very different value; a more accurate predictor can still produce less useful training data for a policy; and the same kind of retrieved memory can change either how a program is repaired or how an outcome is judged.

The review makes three connected contributions. First, it positions RSI within robot learning by separating method paradigms and problem settings (from reinforcement learning and meta-learning to AutoML) from a ladder of claims (behavioral improvement, later-learning benefit, procedure improvement, and the two links of recursion), each defined by the comparison that would establish it. It organizes physical self-improvement along that ladder according to where experience leaves its change and which decision of the learning procedure it revises, showing that data volume and component accuracy are unreliable proxies for progress. Second, it separates mechanisms that change an improver’s knowledge or tools from evidence that the improver has improved: existing studies support the first three claims, while recursive gains still need dedicated verification. It reviews digital precedents and physical boundary cases and specifies a two-round experiment that could isolate the recursive relation, together with its controls and an estimate of its hardware cost; Table 13 records where the reviewed studies stand on each claim. Third, it names the four breakdowns above as recurring conditions (informative feedback, usability, robustness to distribution shift, and continued practice) and shows how each fails and which capability would restore it. Four research questions organize the review.

Section 2 lays the foundations: a primer for newcomers (Section 2.1), where improvement is kept, the ladder from self-improvement to recursion, the position of RSI relative to neighboring learning paradigms (Section 2.3), and the benchmarks and metrics used in the reviewed studies (Section 2.5); Figure 3 maps the review, and Appendix C collects the terms. Section 3 climbs the ladder, from improving the learner (Section 3.1) and the learning procedure (Section 3.2) to improving the improver (Section 3.3) and closing the recursive loop (Section 3.4). Section 4 turns to what current evaluation cannot yet measure, why gains stop compounding, how practice can stay safe, and which problems remain open, including the two-round test that recursion would require.

title: From Acceptance and Avoidance to Affective Viscosity: Designing Social Agents Intermediating in Human Relationships
authors: Tomoko Yonezawa
comment: The 2nd International Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies (TBSA_2nd) in HAI 2026
abstract:
As social agents become embedded in human relationships, they are expected not only to provide smooth assistance but also to handle rejection, discomfort, jealousy, persistence, and other forms of social tension. This paper connects two research directions: acceptance and avoidance in response to an agent’s gaze, approach, and contact, and affective viscosity as a model of how negative affect accumulates, persists, is suppressed, and is expressed over time. We argue that avoidance should not be treated merely as a failure of interaction, but as a relational signal that indicates boundaries between humans and agents. Building on this view, affective viscosity provides a design perspective for agents that maintain, suppress, or express negative states depending on social relationships and interaction histories. We discuss several ongoing design cases, including triadic jealousy, discomfort suppression, patience timing, and spatiotemporal stickiness, and consider how these cases lead to broader questions of blame and accountable intervention. Rather than designing agents as simple scapegoats or artificial villains, we ask
how agents can intermediate in problematic social situations
while making their intervention traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable.
introduction:
Social agents are often designed to be polite, helpful, and smoothly cooperative. However, agents embedded in human relationships may need to do more than maintain pleasant interaction. They may be approached or avoided, accepted or rejected, welcomed or perceived as intrusive. They may also need to express hesitation, discomfort, jealousy, or limits of patience when social tension arises. These reactions should not be treated only as breakdowns of interaction. They may indicate relational boundaries and provide important cues for how agents should intervene in social environments.

Our previous and ongoing work on acceptance and avoidance focuses on how users respond to an agent’s gaze, approach, and contact, and how such responses can be estimated and reflected in the agent’s behavior. This perspective treats avoidance not simply as a negative outcome, but as a signal that the agent has entered a boundary-sensitive region of interaction. The next step is to model how such boundary-sensitive states persist and transform over time. In particular, discomfort, jealousy, annoyance, and reluctance may accumulate, remain latent, leak through behavior, or suddenly become explicit. We refer to this temporal and relational property as affective viscosity.

This perspective also leads to questions of blame and responsibility. Once an agent detects social tension and intervenes, it may change the trajectory of the relationship. If the intervention fails, becomes annoying, or exposes a tension that participants preferred to ignore, the agent may become a target of blame. However, assigning blame to an agent should not simply mean placing an artificial scapegoat or villain in the environment. A more productive question is how to design agents whose interventions are traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable. In this sense, affective viscosity is not only a model of negative emotion, but also a basis for discussing how agents can take part in socially risky intervention.

Prior work on trust in automation and human–robot interaction has
emphasized that trust is not simply a positive attitude, but a basis
for appropriate reliance under uncertainty (3, 4). Reviews of trust in AI and human–automation
trust further suggest that trust depends on both system properties
and the user’s interpretation of agency, reliability, and risk
 (7, 6). However, when agents
are embedded in social relationships, the issue is not limited to
whether users rely on them. Agents may also affect interpersonal
boundaries, social norms, and the distribution of responsibility.

In socially embedded HAI, trust, blame, and responsibility may be
distributed across users, agents, developers, institutions,
bystanders, and broader social contexts. This makes it necessary to
consider not only whether an agent is trusted, but also how the
agent is treated as a social participant when it refuses, avoids,
asserts a boundary, or becomes involved in socially disruptive
interaction.

title: Reading the Room: Scale-ambiguous Semantic Registration of Sparse VSLAM Maps to Floor Plans in Partially Built Environments
authors: Bjorn Stragier,Emilia Szymańska,J. Micah Prendergast,Lukas Rosenberger Schmid
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Many robotic construction applications, such as progress tracking, require registering a sensor trajectory to a prior 2D floor plan.
Visual capture is attractive for its low cost and availability, but aligning a visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) map to a floor plan is difficult; VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, the sparse point cloud is cross-modal to the symbolic floor plan, sites are only partially built during capture, and construction sites are visually repetitive, degrading map quality while removing distinctive features.
Existing methods address at most two of these challenges.
We thus introduce Reading the Room (RR), a global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous, sparse, semantic VSLAM maps to partially built floor plans.
Our key idea is to define a single robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function that governs all stages of the pipeline.
We develop two global initialization schemes, leveraging a single inaccurate user-provided correspondence if provided, or estimating the initialization globally using a cross-modal matching network.
Both schemes are designed to find initial candidates with respect to the energy function, which is then directly optimized for local refinement.
We evaluate RR on 33 sequences across three active construction sites against classical and learning-based baselines, achieving a 4.5× improvement in mean absolute trajectory error over the strongest baseline in the general unconstrained setting, which increases to 7.6× when an anchor is provided.
introduction:
Autonomous robots and perception technologies have the potential to transform modern construction.
Tracking construction progress against design intent is one of the most direct levers to reduce project delays and cost overruns [1]. However, doing so requires registering a sensor trajectory captured by a robot or site operator to a prior 2D floor plan.
To this end, camera-based capture is an especially attractive sensing solution given its vast availability, low cost, weight, and energy consumption, as well as providing visual fidelity and human interpretability.
While several works investigate registering dense LiDAR-based reconstruction to floor plans [2, 3, 4], the visual counterpart remains less explored.

In this work, we study the task of aligning a sparse, scale-ambiguous 3D map, as recovered by a monocular VSLAM system [5, 6], to the floor plan of a site under active construction.
Multiple properties compound to make this setting unusually difficult, as shown in Fig. 1.
First, monocular VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, since scale is not observable without auxiliary sensing.
Second, the two representations are highly cross-modal, as VSLAM outputs a sparse, noisy 3D point cloud while the floor plan is a symbolic drawing of design intent.
Third, construction sites are only partially built during capture, so large parts of the plan may not yet physically exist, making it an unreliable prior.
Lastly, such sites are often visually repetitive, consisting mostly of walls, columns, and voids, which both degrades VSLAM quality and removes the distinctive features registration typically relies on.

Existing approaches address at most one or two of these challenges.
Cross-view indoor localization methods [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14] generally assume known metric scale and a fully built environment.
Methods embedding a floor plan directly into the SLAM pipeline [15, 16] similarly assume a known, already-built environment and a metric-range sensor such as LiDAR.
Map-alignment methods such as region decomposition [2] and graph matching [4] require dense metric reconstructions a sparse VSLAM map cannot easily supply.
Recent sparse VSLAM methods instead by-pass dense reconstruction by detecting manually placed visual markers with positions marked a-priori in the floor plan [17].
Learning-based cross-modal matchers [18, 19] can generalize across visually dissimilar modalities [20, 21], but have never been evaluated on this domain.
Thus, no existing method jointly handles unknown scale, sparse representations, the cross-modality gap, and partial construction.

To close this gap, we introduce Reading the Room (RR), a global-local registration approach built around a single energy function.
We propose a robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric objective for cross-modal registration in partially built construction sites.
We then develop a two stage approach to globally initialize and locally refine this (or any other) energy function in feature-degraded and structurally ambiguous environments.
We thoroughly evaluate RR across 3 datasets of active construction sites spanning 33 total sequences.
For practical relevance, we consider two cases, where an initial guess by a site operator is provided as well as the unconstrained global regsitration task, both of which are naturally handled by RR.
We compare RR against several classical and learning-based methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance in both tasks.
In summary, our main contributions are:

We introduce Reading the Room (RR), a novel global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous sparse VSLAM maps against partially built symbolic floor plans.

We introduce Reading the Room (RR), a novel global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous sparse VSLAM maps against partially built symbolic floor plans.

We propose a novel class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function and develop a two stage pipeline combining correspondence-free cross-modal dense feature matching or anchored initialization with local refinement to optimize this energy objective.

We thoroughly evaluate RR across 33 sequences spanning three active construction sites, showing a ≥4.5×\geq 4.5\times improvement in median ATE over the most competitive baselines, providing a first effective solution to this challenging problem.

1. We introduce Reading the Room (RR), a novel global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous sparse VSLAM maps against partially built symbolic floor plans.

2. We propose a novel class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function and develop a two stage pipeline combining correspondence-free cross-modal dense feature matching or anchored initialization with local refinement to optimize this energy objective.

3. We thoroughly evaluate RR across 33 sequences spanning three active construction sites, showing a ≥4.5×\geq 4.5\times improvement in median ATE over the most competitive baselines, providing a first effective solution to this challenging problem.

title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
authors: Matthias Heyrman,Chenhao Li,Ioannis Dadiotis,Marco Hutter
abstract:
Perceptive locomotion policies typically observe a dense robot-centric elevation map, although only the terrain beneath and around the next footsteps informs the control decision.
Learned encoders compress the whole visual input, leaving the policy to work out which inputs matter while learning the baseline locomotion task.
Learning both at once slows training and, without computationally expensive attention mechanisms, makes generalization to new terrain harder.
We instead remove redundant inputs from the elevation map before the policy sees it.
A lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts future footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone, and we sample the elevation map only in small patches around these predicted footholds.
We train the prediction model alongside the locomotion policy, periodically retraining it on new policy rollouts as the robot’s gait matures.
This allows the perception to anticipate where the policy will step, while the policy learns to leverage terrain information around those steps.
With the proposed lightweight preprocessing, the policy reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the training iterations required with the complete map.
It outperforms policies that observe the complete map where footholds are sparse, including in narrow walled corridors, and on unseen terrain, and it matches an attention-based encoder trained at several times the cost.
The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid traversing various obstacles, stairs, gaps, and step-downs beyond the training distribution in both indoor and outdoor environments.
introduction:
Vision is an indispensable tool when traversing unstructured terrain.
People constantly survey the ground ahead of them to plan their next steps and to adjust the trajectory of a foot in mid-air.
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has driven significant progress in legged robot locomotion [1, 2].
Using high-fidelity physics simulators, modern RL algorithms with parallelized environments, and effective techniques to reduce the sim-to-real gap, humanoids can be conditioned on a robot-centric elevation map [3] to traverse rough terrain.

However, this reliance on dense environmental maps introduces fundamental limitations related to sample efficiency, redundancy, and distraction.
Only the small regions of terrain where the feet will next make contact should inform control decisions, yet policies typically sample and process the full map uniformly, even though most of it describes terrain the robot will never step on, such as cells far to the side or directly opposite the commanded velocity direction.
These irrelevant inputs make it hard to learn which regions of the map matter and can distract the policy with terrain features that have no bearing on the next step, while the larger state space makes generalization to different terrains harder and increases the computational cost of the policy.
By contrast, people tend to look at the ground approximately 1.5 seconds, i.e., 2 to 3 steps, ahead of them, focusing on their planned footholds instead of the entire surrounding scene [4].
On more challenging terrains, this look-ahead lets them intuitively adapt a step in mid-air: if a foothold seems insecure or they notice a better spot near the original target, they shift their focus and change the step trajectory.

Existing work primarily aims to reduce redundant information from the full elevation map through learned embeddings that feed the control policy.
Typical encoders compress the full input into a latent vector [2], scale well to complex terrains [5, 6], and transfer to real-world locomotion [7, 8].
However, encoders such as CNNs still have to learn to extract the relevant features from the full map, and thus inherit the redundancy and sample inefficiency of the visual input rather than addressing it.

Attention-based encoders, conditioned on proprioception and the elevation map, weigh terrain features to focus on possible future steps [9], and later work extends them with local and global feature streams [10, 11] and uncertainty-aware terrain estimates [10].
Using egocentric depth images alongside a height scan enables an attention-based anticipatory gaze that better respects onboard compute limitations [12].
These methods learn where to look, but nothing in the encoder structure ensures that the attended features are future footholds; the encoder has to discover the focus implicitly from the task reward.
Other depth-based methods encode the images directly [13, 14].
All of these methods process the entire visual input when deployed and leave it to the policy to ignore what does not matter.
Terrain outside of its next steps can therefore still distract it.

Another approach analyzes the terrain and plans where the robot’s feet should land, a long-standing body of work.
Classical methods select candidate contact regions based on kinematic reachability and terrain geometry [15, 16, 17, 18], and learning-based approaches evaluate candidate footholds based on the height map around the nominal landing position [19] or across the local map under kinematic and collision constraints [20].
These foothold selection methods run as standalone modules that hand a target to a downstream tracking controller.
This requires strongly defined hand-crafted selection criteria for each platform, such as thresholds on the slope, roughness and curvature of a foot-sized patch, its distance to edges, and robot-specific checks of kinematic reachability and leg collision.
These criteria encode the designer’s notion of a safe foothold and must be manually retuned for a new foot geometry or gait.
The module is also not necessarily conditioned on how the downstream controller actually moves, which leaves its output liable to be inaccurate or suboptimal for the gait that executes it.

The mismatch between planner and controller is especially pertinent for modern legged locomotion controllers, which are RL policies trained in simulation to maximize a reward.
RL-based approaches can learn precise foot placement in simulation through a terrain difficulty curriculum and crafted rewards [21, 22] and can learn to track foothold planners [23, 24], use them to shape rewards [25], or track a decoupled learned planning policy [26].
In these cases, however, the foothold serves as a tracking target or a reward that shapes the policy’s actions, not as a filter that shapes the policy’s observations.
Prior work has used predicted footholds to reward safe locomotion using privileged information acquired in simulation during training [14], but the predictions never reach the hardware.

Filtering the elevation map around future footholds before the policy sees it raises two challenges.
First, the filter cannot observe the terrain to decide where to look, as it would inherit the overhead of the full elevation map that it is meant to remove.
It must therefore predict the footholds entirely from the robot’s own state and command, while the policy, like a person, can still adjust its trajectory to choose footholds based on the terrain it sees around each prediction.
Second, where the feet will land is a property of the gait, which the policy is still learning.
A predictor fit to an early, unsteady gait would misplace its patches once the policy improves, and a policy trained on misplaced patches may learn to distrust them.

In this paper, we propose a human-inspired, state-based sampling module that filters the elevation map before the locomotion policy receives any terrain information.
To filter the elevation map without observing it, a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the robot’s next two footholds from its current proprioceptive state and velocity command alone.
We treat only the terrain around these predicted footholds as relevant for locomotion and sample the elevation map in patches surrounding them.
These patches act as the exteroceptive observation of the locomotion policy, creating a state-conditioned representation of the terrain.

To ensure that the predicted footholds, and with them the sampled patches, stay up-to-date as the locomotion policy learns more difficult terrains, we co-train the FPM and the locomotion policy in an iterative training loop.
We train the locomotion policy with RL in simulation and, after a fixed number of iterations, refit the FPM in a self-supervised fashion on the footholds the current policy produces, allowing the perceptual filter to adapt as the policy converges.
We demonstrate that this approach reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the iterations required by other methods using the complete elevation map, at a lower perception cost to the policy and across a variety of rough and sparse terrain styles.
We also show indoor and outdoor hardware experiments, where the resulting policy successfully transfers to a Unitree G1 humanoid (Fig. 1).

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

A self-supervised foothold prediction model (FPM) that accurately predicts the next two footholds from the current proprioceptive state and velocity command, co-trained on policy rollouts during RL training.

A human-inspired perceptive locomotion pipeline that samples the elevation map only around the footholds predicted by the FPM, with insights into its key design choices, such as the prediction horizon and the encoding of the sampled patches.

Simulation and hardware experiments, including comparisons against state-of-the-art elevation-map encoders, that demonstrate the advantages of restricting the policy’s exteroceptive input to the terrain around its next predicted footholds over the complete map.

title: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Jumping in Lunar Gravity
authors: Levin Müller,Oliver Fischer,Marco Trentini,Yusuke Tanaka,Marco Hutter
abstract: Legged robots can extend planetary exploration to rugged and discontinuous terrain that is inaccessible to conventional rovers. In lunar gravity, jumping further expands this mobility by enabling robots to cross obstacles and gaps that cannot be traversed by walking alone. We present a multistage reinforcement-learning approach that produces a single end-to-end control policy for commanded point-to-point jumping under lunar gravity. The resulting policy has a simple architecture and relies exclusively on mission-compatible onboard sensing, making its deployment on a real lunar mission plausible. In simulation, the learned policy performs accurate point-to-point jumps with landing errors smaller than the robot’s body size. We analyze the torque and power demands of lunar jumping and characterize performance degradation under extreme outlier events, including control-update freezes of up to 1 s1\text{\,}\mathrm{s} during flight. Hardware transfer demonstrates that the policy can successfully execute a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading. Furthermore, the measured torque and power profiles are consistent with the simulation results and remain within the robot’s hardware limits.
introduction:
Robotic exploration of the solar system is essential for advancing scientific understanding of planetary bodies and preparing future human missions. While orbiters and stationary landers provide valuable measurements, scientifically relevant targets require mobile surface systems to acquire local observations and interact with the terrain. As interest grows in sustained surface operations [1], infrastructure construction [2, 3], and scientific access to challenging terrain, missions increasingly target sites such as permanently shadowed regions, crater walls, and lunar lava tubes – areas that remain difficult to reach with conventional mobility systems [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Planetary rovers have so far relied predominantly on wheeled locomotion, which provides substantial flight heritage and reliability on comparatively benign terrain, but remains limited on steep, loose, rugged, or discontinuous surfaces [11]. In contrast, recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have substantially improved the ability of legged robots to traverse rough and unstructured terrain, motivating their investigation for planetary exploration.
Beyond robust walking, the morphology of legged robots also enables dynamic locomotion modes such as jumping [12]. For a lunar robot, jumping is not intended to replace walking as an energy-efficient mode of long-range traversal. Still, it can serve as a useful mobility primitive for overcoming obstacles, terrain discontinuities, slopes, and gaps that would otherwise be untraversable [13]. In low gravity, such maneuvers are especially attractive because relatively moderate launch velocities can produce extended ballistic flight phases [12].

At the same time, lunar jumping imposes additional control and deployment challenges: the controller must demonstrate high robustness, particularly during flight and landing, to avoid crashing onto the surface. Specifically on non-redundant system architectures, FDIR may even require the ability to recover from a mid-flight system reboot. In addition, constraints in computing hardware for aerospace engineering favor the development of a low-complexity controller. Although quadrupedal jumping has been demonstrated in both terrestrial and low-gravity contexts, commanded point-to-point jumping for a quadruped in lunar gravity has not yet been sufficiently investigated.

To address this gap, we develop a deployment-lean reinforcement-learning framework for commanded point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity. The key idea is to pair the governing ballistic properties of lunar flight with a multistage control scheme. This provides a versatile training framework to synthesize an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning-based jumping controller within a single multilayer perceptron control policy. The control policy maps onboard-feasible observations to joint-position targets.

Specifically, our contributions are:

We formulate commanded point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity by exploiting the ballistic flight structure to relate the target position and flight trajectory-apex height to the desired launch velocity.

We introduce an end-to-end RL framework that learns the full jumping maneuver using a single deployable control policy, while avoiding dense motion references, online trajectory generation, and policy switching.

We evaluate the resulting controller on the Magnecko[14] quadruped for jumping accuracy, recovery, and robustness to random failures.

We transfer the resulting controller to gravity offloading hardware to evaluate the sim-to-real profile of the torque and power curves.

1. We formulate commanded point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity by exploiting the ballistic flight structure to relate the target position and flight trajectory-apex height to the desired launch velocity.

2. We introduce an end-to-end RL framework that learns the full jumping maneuver using a single deployable control policy, while avoiding dense motion references, online trajectory generation, and policy switching.

3. We evaluate the resulting controller on the Magnecko[14] quadruped for jumping accuracy, recovery, and robustness to random failures.

4. We transfer the resulting controller to gravity offloading hardware to evaluate the sim-to-real profile of the torque and power curves.

title: Joint-Angle Invariance of Jacobian-Based Performance Indices for Serial Robotic Manipulators
authors: Yaohua Zhou,Mingdao Lin,Jiayu Song,Xixin Zhao,Haidong Huang,Jiahu Qin,Xiaocong Li
comment: . Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
abstract: This article investigates the joint-angle invariance (JAI) of Jacobian-based performance indices for serial robotic manipulators. We identify kinematic conditions under which representative performance indices, including manipulability, stiffness, and other Jacobian-derived indices, remain independent of the first and last joint angles. This property allows a systematic reduction in the effective configuration-space dimensionality, thereby simplifying the performance evaluation. The utility of JAI is demonstrated through two application scenarios: workspace performance map construction and task layout optimization. Comparative results show that the proposed JAI-based strategy reduces computational effort and storage requirements without compromising the effectiveness.
introduction:
Serial robotic manipulators have been widely deployed in manufacturing, medical, and aerospace industries due to their large workspaces, structural simplicity, and versatility. The evaluation of the motion/force transmission capabilities relies heavily on Jacobian-based performance indices. The Jacobian captures the instantaneous mapping between joint velocities and Cartesian twists, as well as between joint torques and Cartesian wrenches. On this basis, performance indices are derived to measure various aspects of robot behavior. Notable examples include the manipulability index [1], which characterizes the motion capability, and the stiffness index [2], which evaluates the magnitude of resistance to applied wrenches.

For decades, these performance indices have been applied in robotics. They serve as critical tools in robot design optimization, where geometric parameters are chosen to maximize dexterity or stiffness in targeted regions of the workspace. In trajectory planning, they are used to avoid singularities and maintain desirable kinematic capability. Redundancy resolution strategies frequently incorporate these indices to exploit extra degrees of freedom (DOFs) for enhancing task performance, such as maximizing manipulability. Furthermore, task layout optimization, such as selecting the placement pose of fixtures or workpieces, has been shown to benefit significantly from Jacobian-based performance analysis.

The investigation of performance distribution within the robot workspace facilitates the evaluation of its capabilities. Breitkopf [3] visualized the distribution of manipulability across the entire workspace of a serial robot. Kuang et al. [4] employed a sector space meshing method to construct the distribution of the Jacobian condition number, considering the workspace boundary. Such analyses provide valuable guidance for the design and optimization of robots. For instance, Ginnante et al. [5] utilized a task priority control algorithm to optimize task-oriented robot design, thereby enhancing the kinetostatic performance in desired regions of the workspace. In contrast, Hwang et al. [6] focused on a comprehensive dimensional synthesis based on global performance indices.

Designing trajectory optimization schemes that incorporate Jacobian-based performance indices can effectively enhance the execution capability of robotic manipulators. For redundant robots, manipulability optimization has been widely recognized as a fundamental approach to improving motion capability while avoiding singular configurations. Tan et al. [7] proposed a manipulability optimization method based on singular value analysis, which avoids the instability associated with pseudo-inverse computations. Yang et al. [8] extended the optimization beyond the velocity level and developed a manipulability maximization scheme at the acceleration level. To improve computational efficiency in redundancy resolution, Shen et al. [9] introduced a derivative propagation approach. Further advancements include the optimization of velocity/force manipulability in bilateral teleoperation of coordinated remote redundant manipulators [10]. More recently, cross-domain manipulability transfer has gained attention. For instance, Gong et al. [11] incorporated Riemannian manifold theory to achieve cross-domain mapping of human-robot manipulability ellipsoids via parallel transport. In manufacturing processes such as grinding, polishing, and milling, various stiffness-based trajectory optimization methods have been explored, with the aim of mitigating vibrations during execution [12, 13, 14].

In the field of robotic manipulation and manufacturing, task layout optimization generally refers to the systematic adjustment of the workpiece pose, so as to enhance overall operational performance. Vahrenkamp et al. [15] proposed an extended manipulability measure and applied it to online grasp selection for humanoid robots. For tasks involving the manipulation of large-scale objects, Franceschi et al. [16] introduced a hierarchical optimization framework ranging from global to local levels to optimize work cell layout. In specific process applications, Jiao et al. [17] focused on robotic drilling systems, developing a redundancy optimization model that considers directional stiffness performance. In machining optimization incorporating stiffness thresholds, Liao et al. [18] concentrated on robotic milling, optimizing both the robot redundancy and workpiece setup. Regarding autonomous exploration and planning, Liu et al. [19] established an efficient exploration information system capable of continuously identifying high-manipulability configurations, thereby enabling adaptive layout decisions in unknown environments. Moreover, the adjustment of the robot base constitutes a critical aspect of task layout optimization, with typical applications including manipulator repositioning via mobile platforms for the machining of large components [20].

Jacobian-based performance indices are widely used in robotics, while their dependence on the full joint configuration presents two challenges. First, in high-DOF systems, these indices tend to vary considerably across the joint space, resulting in high computational and visualization costs. Second, the absence of identifiable invariance properties hinders theoretical analysis and limits their applicability in efficient optimization. To address these issues, it is essential to identify structural properties that simplify analysis without loss of generality.

This study introduces joint-angle invariance (JAI)–a property exhibited by specific Jacobian-based performance indices for a class of serial robots, whereby the indices remain independent of the first and last joint angles. This invariance substantially reduces the computational burden in both performance analysis and optimization. The utility of JAI is demonstrated in two application scenarios: performance map construction and task layout optimization, and we achieve notable gains in computational efficiency in both cases.

title: Mixture of Flow Matching and Particle Filter for Proprioception-Based Online Contact Estimation
authors: Seo Wook Han,Min Jun Kim
comment: Author accepted manuscript; (including a cover page), 21 figures, 5 tables
abstract:
In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors.
We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal.
Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously.
To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework.
The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events.
Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method.
In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.
introduction:
Contact information is crucial for robots performing physical interactions.
While collision detection [33, 15, 26] typically provides simple binary information (i.e., contact or no-contact), estimating a detailed contact state that includes contact location and force (e.g., 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} and 𝑭i\bm{F}_{i} in Fig. 1) unlocks a wide range of interactive applications.
For example, such detailed contact information can transform the robot’s body into an intuitive human-robot interface, allowing users to trigger different commands by touching specific locations [9, 20] or to control the robot by leveraging the contact state as a virtual joystick [6].
It also supports interactive control schemes, such as constraining the contact force on the robot’s body [41], and substituting for a dedicated force/torque (F/T) sensor used for admittance [28, 27, 31] or direct force control [22].
Furthermore, this detailed estimation capability enables advanced strategies such as hybrid motion-force control under unknown forces from outside the target region [12], safe navigation through cluttered environments where unexpected contacts can occur [23, 25, 50], and whole-body manipulation of humanoid robots [39, 2, 1].

In essence, all these applications rely on the ability to identify the detailed contact state, which consists of (i) the total number of contacts, (ii) their locations, and (iii) the associated force vectors.
However, accurately estimating the contact state remains a largely unsolved problem.
To address this, researchers have explored two main sensory pathways.
The first approach uses exteroceptive sensors, such as surface-mounted tactile skins [37, 19], to directly obtain rich contact information at the interaction region.
The second relies on proprioceptive sensors, such as joint torque sensors (JTSs) and F/T sensors [13, 36, 21], to infer the contact state from the robot’s internal state.
We focus on the latter approach because these sensors are widely available and integrated into modern robotic systems.
For instance, commercially available platforms such as the Franka Emika Panda, KUKA iiwa and iisy, and Kinova Gen3 are already equipped with JTSs, while F/T sensors can be readily installed (see Fig. 1).

However, due to their sparse placement, proprioceptive sensors provide only indirect information about external contacts, as they capture the resulting internal joint torques and forces.
We need to solve an inverse problem that estimates the contact state that best explain these sparse, internal sensor measurements.
As shown in Fig. 1, our objective is to estimate the contact state, which includes the contact locations on distinct links (𝒓i∈ℝ3{\bm{r}}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}), the corresponding three-dimensional (3D) force vectors (𝑭i∈ℝ3{\bm{F}}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}), and the number of contacts (up to two).
By constraining our scope to scenarios with up to two point contacts, we isolate and tackle the core challenges of the contact estimation problem:

Multi-modality (Singularity):
The primary challenge stems from the inherent ambiguity of the inverse problem.
While the forward mapping (from contact to sensor reading) is deterministic, the inverse mapping is ambiguous; as illustrated in Fig. 2(a), distinct contact states may correspond to identical sensor measurements.
This singularity [42, 44] implies that the contact state might not be reliably determined from a single observation, leading to inherent uncertainty in the estimation.
Consequently, the probability distribution of possible solutions becomes multi-modal.
Due to the uncertain nature of the problem, it is more informative and important to predict the multi-modal distribution, rather than yielding a single deterministic solution.

Temporal Dependency:
Although the ambiguity of inferring contact states from single observations remains an inherent problem, it can be mitigated in specific contexts by leveraging temporal dependency.
For instance, consider the discrete state evolution depicted in Fig. 2(b).
In this scenario, the ambiguity is significantly compounded as the number of contacts increases (e.g., when simultaneously estimating two contacts).
Nevertheless, estimating the second contact becomes more reliable by incorporating past information about the first contact [13].
In the case of continuous evolution such as the sliding contact force shown in Fig. 2(b), knowing the previous contact location simplifies the estimation.
Performing localization around the previous estimate improves efficiency by avoiding the need to explore the entire robot surface [36].
Consequently, leveraging temporal dependency, specifically utilizing past estimates, provides a prior context for inferring the current state.

Contact Event Detection:
Determining the number of active contacts requires identifying discrete transitions, specifically the addition or removal of contacts (see Fig. 2(c)).
While providing a prior context enables effective temporal tracking, its validity strictly depends on the correct discrete state; otherwise, undetected contact events cause the estimator to propagate incorrect past information.
Therefore, robust contact event detection serves as a critical prerequisite for reliable estimation of the complete contact state, including the number, location, and force.

As detailed in Section II, prior work on proprioception-based contact estimation can be broadly categorized into model-based and learning-based approaches.
The former is dominated by particle filter (PF)-based methods [36, 14, 61, 47, 24], while the latter includes deep learning techniques, from probabilistic mapping [32] to diffusion models [13]. Each of these categories exhibits distinct strengths and weaknesses.

While PF-based approaches are well-suited for addressing temporal dependency through recursive belief updates, they often fail to handle multi-modality due to particle starvation [54, 55, 30].
This well-known issue of PFs arises when the particles fail to populate high-belief regions.
In contrast, learning-based approaches excel at estimating multi-modal distributions.
For instance, to capture multi-modality, probabilistic mapping [32] evaluates probabilities for each region of a discretized state space, and generative models [13] learn the underlying data distribution.
These feed-forward approaches, however, are typically non-recursive and trained on temporally independent samples, thus lacking a native mechanism for leveraging temporal dependency.
As for contact event detection, it remains a challenge for both categories of approaches.
Although PFs recursively track contact states, they rely on hard-to-tune thresholds to identify discrete transitions.
Feed-forward learning-based methods struggle to model these discrete transitions, as their non-recursive nature inherently restricts temporal reasoning.

In this paper, we propose a novel framework called ContactFlowFilter that tackles the aforementioned challenges: our approach is built upon a recursive structure of PFs for capturing temporal dependency, while a generative model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events.

As depicted in Fig. 3, ContactFlowFilter updates the contact belief by drawing particles from two complementary proposal distributions: the PF’s temporal prediction and the generative auxiliary proposal.
By preserving the PF’s recursive structure, the proposed method effectively captures temporal dependency, while the generative component complements the PF by representing multi-modal distributions.
Building upon this hybrid framework, we propose a robust method for contact event detection that augments conventional criteria by combining temporal context with generative estimates.

To formally implement the mixture of two proposal distributions, we adopt the dual-sampling concept [54].
We first formulate the PF motion model as Gaussian sampling on the robot surface, providing a basis for integrating the generative model and deriving its importance weights.

The generative component is built upon a novel data representation designed to capture the underlying distribution of contact states.
We utilize a fixed-size array of paired contact points to represent up to two simultaneous contacts, which allows the model to infer the spatial relationships between the points.
This is supported by our proposed observation representation, where spatially aligned robot kinematics data, JTSs data, and base F/T sensor data are mapped as a sequence along the kinematic chain.
A transformer encoder then processes this sequence to extract cross-modal correlations.

To achieve real-time performance for high-fidelity temporal tracking, we employ flow matching [34, 8] as the generative backbone, leveraging linearized probability paths for few-step inference rather than curved diffusion trajectories [17, 52, 35].
We also implement a computationally efficient motion model using pre-processed mesh data [14].

In summary, our contributions are centered on a main framework (C1), which is realized through key technical contributions (C2, C3):

C1)
A novel hybrid framework, ContactFlowFilter, that synergistically combines a generative model and a particle filter to address the key challenges of the contact estimation problem (multi-modality, temporal dependency, and contact event detection) while ensuring real-time performance.
(Validated in simulation (Section VII-C) and real-world experiments (Section VII-D and supplementary video).)

C2)
A spatially aligned data representation and a transformer-based architecture tailored to extract cross-modal correlations, enabling the flow matching model to effectively learn the multi-modal distribution of contact points.
(Validated in Section VII-A.)

C3)
A robust method for contact event detection that leverages a combination of distributions generated by the flow matching model and the PF.
(Validated in Section VII-B.)

We present thorough validation in both simulation and real-world settings.
Comparative experiments confirm that ContactFlowFilter achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.
To assess the estimation accuracy, we employ localization error metrics along with the defined dissimilarity based on the approximated likelihood of the time-dependent belief.
In the real-world experiment, the proposed method achieved the lowest dissimilarity to the target distribution, with localization errors of 0.36 cm\mathrm{cm} and 0.88 cm\mathrm{cm} while maintaining average execution times of 0.69 ms\mathrm{ms} and 2.69 ms\mathrm{ms} for single-contact and dual-contact scenarios, respectively.

The rest of this article is organized as follows.
Section II reviews related research, and Section III presents the preliminaries.
Section IV introduces the baseline PF framework for contact estimation, followed by a discussion of its limitations.
We then present the proposed method, ContactFlowFilter, in Section V and detail its implementation in Section VI.
Section VII demonstrates the experimental validation of the proposed method.
Finally, Section VIII concludes this article.

title: Preserving Operator Intent Under Actuation Constraints: Teleoperation of Manipulators with Coupled Transmissions
authors: Xuhan Miao,Zijin Han,Yutong Shen,Haidong Huang,Shanliushui Gao,Lei Zhang,Xiaocong Li,Chenguang Yang
comment: . Contribution to the IROS 2026 workshop "5th Sensorimotor-Augmented Teleoperation: Human-Interaction-Oriented Paradigm and Real-World Concerns"
abstract: Teleoperation enables intuitive control of remote engineering robots for precision tasks. Existing direct joint-mapping methods have two limitations: independent motor saturation disrupts pitch–roll coordination in differential wrists, while fixed mappings struggle with abrupt tracking changes caused by gravitational loads and actuation constraints. We propose an actuator-constraint-aware leader–follower teleoperation method that jointly models leader gravity compensation, leader–follower joint mapping, and follower differential-wrist control. Specifically, we perform coordinated saturation in motor space according to the available gravity margin and integrate continuous angle unwrapping, feedback-state monitoring, and feasible-reference updates. This preserves the operator’s motion direction, reduces coordination distortion, and suppresses recovery transients during saturation or brief communication failures. Real-robot experiments demonstrate smoother wrist trajectories and more continuous recovery than direct mapping.
introduction:
Teleoperation enables humans to operate robots in hazardous, confined, or contact-uncertain environments, and has become an important interface for remote manipulation and demonstration collection [1, 2]. Compared with keyboards, joysticks, and vision-only interfaces, a leader manipulator directly expresses the operator’s joint motion, reducing cognitive load caused by action planning and coordinate transformation. Recent low-cost leader–follower systems support dexterous manipulation and imitation learning, but commonly rely on independent joint mapping or end-effector tracking, without explicitly modeling transmission coupling, configuration-dependent gravity, and actuator saturation [2, 3].

This issue is particularly pronounced in the engineering manipulator studied here. The leader and follower exchange joint angles, wrist commands, and gripper states through a custom serial protocol. The follower combines heterogeneous motors with a differential wrist, and uses proportional mapping, PID current control, gravity compensation, encoder unwrapping, and feedback timeout protection. In the existing implementation, the differential wrist drives pitch and roll through sum–difference motor commands, followed by independent motor saturation [4]. When one motor saturates, the realized pitch–roll ratio and motion direction deviate from the operator command. Moreover, the distributed treatment of gravity compensation, angle continuity, and feedback loss does not provide a unified model of the available actuation margin. Consequently, fixed mapping cannot capture configuration-dependent capability, while temporarily infeasible commands may accumulate and cause abrupt recovery motions.

We propose an actuator-constrained teleoperation method for manipulators with coupled transmissions. The method maps transmission coupling, gravity demand, actuator limits, and feedback state into a unified actuator-space model. Operator commands are then projected onto the feasible set while preserving local motion direction and pitch–roll coordination as much as possible. A continuous feasible-reference update further prevents command accumulation during saturation or short communication dropouts. The resulting design extends the existing leader–follower hardware and real-time control pipeline, while addressing motion distortion caused by coupled actuation and gravity-dependent capability.

The contributions are threefold:

We formulate the motion distortion induced by differential transmission and actuator-level saturation, and characterize how gravity compensation changes the available actuation margin.

We propose an actuator-space intent-preserving command projection that integrates gravity compensation, joint mapping, and PID current control, thereby reducing coordination distortion near saturation.

We introduce continuous feasible-reference management using encoder unwrapping and online feedback monitoring, which suppresses error accumulation and recovery transients after temporary infeasibility.

title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
authors: Tingwen Du,Haoyu Guo,Hanxue Zhang,Xuanxu Wang,Junting Dong,Chao Gao,Mingfei Han,Tao Lu,Mulin Yu,Chunhua Shen,Xiaojun Chang,Zhihui Li
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance
across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding,
language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful
decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes,
while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting
foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical
architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable
harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution
experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a
fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution
feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate
harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out
testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection,
compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for
history-dependent robotic manipulation.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language
instructions to robot actions, providing a foundation for general-purpose
manipulation (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024).
Long-horizon tasks, however, can require information that the current observation
does not reveal (Koo et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2026). For example, when a robot
must repeat an operation a specified number of times, similar images may call
for different decisions depending on how many repetitions have actually
succeeded. An earlier observation may also contain a cue that is no longer
visible. Such history-dependent decisions require preserving task-relevant
information and tracking execution outcomes over successive interactions.

Existing research provides several foundations for these capabilities.
Memory-augmented policies equip VLA models with mechanisms for retaining and
using historical information, including compact temporal representations
(Koo et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026), memory retrieval, and
recurrent state updates (Shi et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026).
Hierarchical architectures introduce a high-level planning layer that
issues intermediate decisions to low-level executors
(Ahn et al., 2022; Belkhale et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2025; Sridhar et al., 2025) and can
incorporate environment feedback (Huang et al., 2022). Agentic systems further
organize reasoning, actions, and feedback into iterative decision processes
(Yao et al., 2022; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). Recent embodied harnesses
explore external task management (Zhang et al., 2026b; Gu et al., 2026)
and experience-driven adaptation
(Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026).
Together, these developments motivate studying how the high-level planner in a
hierarchical architecture can manage task context and make use of execution
experience.

Our focus is on two connected responsibilities of this planning process.
Within an episode, issuing a command does not establish that the intended
operation has succeeded. In the repetition example, updating progress requires
interpreting subsequent observations and feedback, while retaining information
needed for later decisions. Access to history therefore needs to be accompanied
by an explicit process for maintaining decision-relevant task context.
Across attempts, an execution record must be translated into a reusable change
to influence future planning. This raises a question: how can we support both
ongoing context management and improvements to the planning process from
execution experience? We explore an editable harness around the high-level VLM
as a common mechanism for these responsibilities. The harness organizes context
and feedback during execution, while providing an explicit object for revision
during self-evolution. This also offers a way to investigate experience reuse
when additional demonstrations and manual annotations are costly.
Figure 1 illustrates this design direction.

We present SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), which organizes a VLM as an
agent within an editable harness around a fixed VLA executor. During task
execution, the harness supports sustained context management over long horizons,
guiding the extraction, retention, and updating of task progress and execution
outcomes from observations and feedback. This context supports the
VLM’s subsequent planning.
However, a predefined harness may not anticipate all task requirements,
motivating execution-driven self-evolution to identify and repair its limitations.
Analysis and revision agents autonomously diagnose failures from execution
traces and propose candidate repairs to planning guidance, assessment
criteria, and control rules.
A verifier evaluates these candidates through environment rollouts,
providing feedback for further revision and harness selection.
This process revises the harness without manually constructing additional
demonstration datasets for supervised fine-tuning of the high-level VLM planner.
The selected harness is fixed before held-out testing, while task context
continues to be updated within each episode.

We evaluate SERA on RoboMME, a benchmark for history-dependent robotic
manipulation (Dai et al., 2026). Autonomous SERA achieves 51.38% overall
success, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. These results support an
empirical exploration of agentic planning and the aggregate effect of
execution-driven harness revisions. Our contributions are:

An agentic planning framework that organizes a high-level VLM within an
editable harness for sustained task-context management over long horizons,
tracking task progress and execution feedback to guide a fixed VLA executor.

An agentic planning framework that organizes a high-level VLM within an
editable harness for sustained task-context management over long horizons,
tracking task progress and execution feedback to guide a fixed VLA executor.

An execution-driven self-evolution procedure that autonomously proposes
and evaluates revisions to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and
control rules from rollout feedback, without constructing an SFT dataset.

We evaluate SERA on RoboMME and achieve 51.38% overall
success. Harness self-evolution improves success by 7.00 percentage points
over the initial configuration.
