title: Make it Walk: Computational Design of LEGO Walkers
authors: Siqi Li,Fancheng Gao,Chi-Wing Fu,Peng Song
abstract:
LEGO walkers are walking automata constructed from modular LEGO Technic bricks. They exhibit intriguing locomotion and are also highly reconfigurable through the modular
Technic bricks, making them widely applicable in education, recreation, and robotics research. However, existing LEGO walkers are designed mostly by reusing existing single-actuator walking mechanisms.
Although the locomotion is stable, their fixed walking gaits limit their adaptability and versatility. This paper presents the first computational solution capable of designing LEGO walkers that not only walk stably, but also support a variety of walking gaits.
Our idea is twofold. First, we control the foot motion trajectory of each leg mechanically via a specifically-designed gear-linkage mechanism, in which we incorporate a pair of 3D-printed non-circular gears to work with a LEGO Technic mechanism. Second, we drive each leg by an independent motor and synchronize the timings of multiple leg motions via a simple yet adaptable control algorithm, enabling stable and versatile locomotion. Importantly, we take this modeling as a foundation to co-design the morphology and control of the LEGO walkers to meet the target locomotion and appearance. Leveraging our approach, we created a variety of LEGO walkers, demonstrating various walking gaits and appearances, and fabricated some of them to show their locomotion capability in the real world.
introduction:
Walking automata are mechanical systems designed to produce legged locomotion.
The LEGO Technic system provides an accessible and modular platform for rapid prototyping walking automata, namely LEGO walkers.
These walkers deliver intriguing
locomotion behaviors and have been widely used in
recreational robots [6] and robotics research.
In addition, they serve as effective STEM education tools, nurturing hands-on exploration of the gait principles and stable creeping locomotion.

Existing works create LEGO walkers largely by reusing existing linkage-based walking mechanisms such as Klann linkage [11] and Jansen’s linkage [10]; see Figure  for examples.
Once assembled, such designs are able to walk stably, driven by a single actuator.
Yet, they are specifically constrained to deliver few fixed walking gaits pre-defined in existing walking mechanisms, limiting their versatility and expressiveness.

In this work, we present a new computational solution to create LEGO walkers that can deliver a variety of walking gaits while walking stably.
This problem is non-trivial for two reasons.
First, we cannot rely on existing walking mechanisms, since they generally produce a fixed walking gait.
Hence, the first challenge asks for modeling the morphology of the LEGO walker, including which mechanical parts to use, how to connect them, and also how to actuate them.
The second challenge lies in the vast design space of our problem.
To achieve stable walking with varying gaits, we need to determine not only the geometry and layout of the mechanical parts but also the control and actuation of these parts.

To address these challenges, our key idea is to decouple the trajectory and timing control of each walking leg, simplifying the walker’s morphology and control.
At the leg level, we propose to control the foot motion trajectory of each leg mechanically via a specifically-designed gear-linkage mechanism and incorporate a pair of 3D-printed non-circular gears to work with the LEGO Technic mechanism.
In this way, we can enlarge the design space of the walking gait.
At the walker level, we propose to drive each leg by an independent motor and synchronize the timings of multiple leg motions via electronically controlling the actuation of the driving motors.
By this means, each leg is modeled with its own gear-linkage mechanism, so our LEGO walker can feature a simple and lightweight morphology for delivering stable walking with varying gaits; see Figures  and  for examples.

To design LEGO walkers, we
only need to specify the desired walking gait (including the foot trajectory and footfall pattern) and provide a body frame of the walker.
Then, our computational approach co-designs the morphology and control of the LEGO walker to meet the target walking gait and walker appearance.
In particular, our approach first constructs and optimizes the leg mechanism to approximate the target foot trajectory, then generates the leg layout to match the given body frame, and optimizes the control on the leg actuations for stable walking guided by the gait theory.
At the end, our approach generates all the information necessary for fabricating the LEGO walker, including
the LEGO Technic brick assemblies,
the shape of the non-circular gears for 3D printing,
the assembly instructions, and
the control for the servo motors.
We validate our approach through the design and physical realization of several LEGO-based quadruped and hexapod walkers, demonstrating the practicality and versatility of our approach.

In this work, we make the following contributions:

We exploit a new class of LEGO walkers that integrates mechanical control (for generating leg trajectories) and electrical control (for synchronizing leg motions) for realizing a variety of walking gaits, where the core is a modular and lightweight leg mechanism modeled as a five-bar linkage with two non-circular gears.

We propose an optimization-based approach, capable of efficiently co-designing the morphology and control of LEGO walkers, satisfying the target walking gait and walker appearance, while ensuring stable walking and fabricability.

2. We propose an optimization-based approach, capable of efficiently co-designing the morphology and control of LEGO walkers, satisfying the target walking gait and walker appearance, while ensuring stable walking and fabricability.

title: S-Rolling: Steerable Rolling Gaits for Twistable Snake Robots in Low-Clearance Environments
authors: Qingling Fan,Zhongqiang Ren
abstract:
Snake robots can traverse complex environments with limbless
locomotion, but maneuvering in low-clearance environments remains challenging because a gait must maintain a small swept height while also providing planar steering.
Existing rolling gaits preserve a low swept height body configuration but generally provide limited steering, whereas steering gaits often introduce vertical undulation and require additional clearance.
With that in mind, this paper develops S-rolling, a steerable rolling gait that combines low swept height locomotion with planar maneuverability for twistable snake robots.
S-rolling is designed using an S-shaped planar backbone curve, whose head and tail segments roll with independently controlled angular velocities, producing different motion modes.
We derive its joint space gait equation, in which a central twist joint realizes the relative rotation between the two segments.
We also develop a quasi-static kinematic model relating the segment rolling speeds to the linear and angular velocities of the robot.
Real-robot experiments demonstrate the various motion modes, traversal through a 1010 cm clearance test track, and maneuvering tasks beneath a large workpiece and a car chassis.
In these low-clearance scenarios, S-rolling successfully performs approximately 90∘90^{\circ} and 180∘180^{\circ} heading changes, whereas the baseline rolling arc gait cannot change the robot heading.
introduction:
The paper is motivated by robot navigation in Low-Clearance Environments (LCE), by which we refer to expansive horizontal surfaces that have restricted vertical space (i.e., a ceiling) above them.
Examples of LCEs include the space beneath a vehicle chassis (Fig. 1), and navigating robots in LCEs naturally arises in applications such as exploration or inspection of vehicles or large industrial parts.
Navigating LCEs is quite challenging: on the one hand, the limited vertical space requires the robot to have a small cross section to be able to enter LCEs.
On the other hand, the robot should be easily maneuverable, such as moving back and forth and changing directions in LCEs.

Snake robots, as a class of hyper-redundant mechanisms, enjoy a small cross section and can traverse complex environments such as pipes, narrow passages, and compact spaces with limbless locomotion [1, 2, 3].
However, due to the limited vertical space of LCEs, a snake robot must maintain a small swept height to avoid collision with the ceiling, which makes many existing gaits, cyclic motion in the shape space, for snake robots inapplicable:
To name a few, concertina gaits rely on lateral anchoring and may require sufficient contact with the surrounding walls [4, 5], which may not be available in LCEs.
Sidewinding can generate steerable motion, but its vertical undulation increases the swept height and may collide with the ceiling in LCEs [6, 7].

Possible gaits for snake robots to locomote in LCEs include rolling and rectilinear gaits, which maintain a small swept height.
However, these gaits generally provide limited steering capability [8, 9, 10, 11]: the robot can only move back and forth along a straight line without changing direction, which limits its maneuverability in LCEs.

This paper is interested in enabling the snake robot to achieve steerable motion in LCEs, without losing existing gaits for the snake robot to traverse complex terrains.
To generate steerable motion in LCEs, this paper considers a so-called twistable snake robot (T-Snake) [12] and develops a new S-rolling gait for T-Snake.
T-Snake is a mechanism that can not only bend its backbone as the popular modular snake robot does [13], which allows T-Snake to achieve any gait that regular snake robot has, but also twist about its backbone (Fig. 1(a)), which provides new possibilities for locomotion.
Based on such T-Snake mechanism, we take the view that low swept height and planar maneuverability can be achieved simultaneously by coordinating the rolling motions of different body segments, without introducing additional vertical undulation.
With that in mind, the proposed S-rolling gait leverages an S-shaped backbone curve, which consists of two tangential circular arcs with opposite signed curvatures.
The two segments of T-Snake can roll with independently controlled angular velocities, which thus enables steerable motion in LCEs.

Designing and controlling such new gaits for T-Snake faces the fundamental challenge of coordinating the many degree of freedom (DoFs) of a snake robot to generate effective motion with real-time computation.
To address the challenge, we begin our design of S-rolling using the backbone curve approach [14, 15], which provides an intuitive geometric method to model and design the gait of the snake robot.
Then, we further derive the gait equations, closed-form shape space motion, of S-rolling based on the designed backbone curve, which allows light-weight and fast computation.
With the help of the S-rolling gait, we further derive a quasi-static kinematic model that relates the two segment rolling speeds to the linear and angular velocities of the robot, which allows locomotive reduction of a complicated snake robot to a simple differential drive car, for easy maneuver in practice.

To summarize, the technical contributions of this paper include: (i) the development of S-rolling gaits, which include both the design of the backbone curve and the further derivation of gait equations, and (ii) the quasi-static locomotive reduction of T-Snake as a differential-drive car based on S-rolling that enables easy maneuver in LCEs.

For verification, we conduct real-robot experiments with T-Snake hardware.
We first demonstrate forward and backward translation, clockwise and counterclockwise in-place turning.
We then evaluate the gait on a test track containing 1010 cm clearance passages.
Finally, we demonstrate two practical tasks beneath a large workpiece and a car chassis, with clearance heights of 1515 cm and 1313 cm, respectively.
Compared with the rolling arc gait [8], which cannot change the robot heading in these tasks (Fig. 1(c)), S-rolling successfully performs approximately 90∘90^{\circ} and 180∘180^{\circ} heading changes while maintaining low-clearance locomotion.

title: Linear Twisting Sidewinding Gaits for Twistable Snake Robot Motion Planning on Complex Terrains
authors: Qingling Fan,Zhongqiang Ren
abstract:
Sidewinding is an efficient gait for snake robots to locomote on various terrains, by undulating the backbone curve and shifting the contact segments along it.
However, relying solely on undulatory motion limits the locomotive capability of snake robots, and combining it with twisting motion can improve their speed and robustness.
This hypothesis has recently been verified by the rolling vector approach, which locomotes the robot like a differential-drive car.
Yet its twisting is concentrated in a short buffer segment, imposing most of the workload on the two twist joints in the middle, which can often overburden the motors and limit its locomotion.
With that in mind, this paper develops a new family of twisting sidewinding gaits that distribute the workload over the entire body with our proposed linear twisting function.
Under matched turning speed and total output power, our gaits reduce the peak output power of a single twist joint by 42%.
Real-robot experiments show that, with the reduced workload, our new gaits can locomote the robot in various terrains that the existing rolling vector approach cannot.
Besides, our new gaits can move up to 49% faster than conventional sidewinding without twisting.
introduction:
Snake robots are hyper-redundant limbless robots that can traverse complex environments [1, 2, 3] such as sandy slopes, pipes, and compact spaces, using versatile gaits, which are cyclic motions in the shape space.
Among these gaits, sidewinding is regarded as highly efficient and robust in many terrains [4, 5, 6, 7].
During sidewinding, the snake keeps its body lifted except for a few static contact segments, and undulates its backbone curve both horizontally and vertically to continuously shift these segments, transporting itself using the friction at contact.

While being highly efficient and robust, sidewinding is still relatively slow to traverse even flat ground, and may get trapped on uneven terrains.
In contrast, the rolling motion of wheels is way faster on many complex terrains.
We take the view that relying solely on undulatory motion limits the locomotive capability of snake robots, and that combining it with rolling motion can improve both efficiency and robustness without losing the various gaits.
This hypothesis has been partially verified in simulation by the recent literature [8], which considers locomotion of a twistable snake robot (T-Snake), a modular snake-robot mechanism that can not only bend but also twist about its backbone curve.
A rolling vector approach [8] is proposed to coordinate the motion of joints, which kinematically reduces the T-Snake to a differential-drive car.
This rolling vector approach twists by assigning different rolling speeds to the head and tail segments, bridged by a short buffer segment.
As a result, the twisting is concentrated within the buffer segment, and burdens the two twist joints in the middle of the body, while leaving the others almost idle (Fig. 1(a)), which can often overload the motors in the buffer segment and limit its locomotion capability.

To coordinate the large number of joints while avoiding such uneven workload, this paper proposes a new linear twisting approach that distributes the twisting motion over the entire body.
Specifically, we let the twisting vary linearly along the backbone curve, and refer to the resulting gaits as linear twisting sidewinding (LTS).
Following the backbone curve approach [9, 10], this linear twisting leads to a family of gaits:
When the twisting is uniform along the whole body, the entire robot rolls like a wheel during sidewinding, which we call rolling sidewinding.
When the twisting varies along the body, different parts of the robot roll at different speeds, which turns the robot, and we call this gait twisting sidewinding.
In twisting sidewinding, the point where the rolling speed is zero acts as the turning center, and it can be placed anywhere along the body.

Since the twisting of the LTS is spread over the entire body, all twist joints share the load.
On our hardware implementation of the T-Snake, we compare the two gaits under similar angular velocities and similar total output power during in-place turning.
Under this fair comparison, the two most-loaded twist joints of the existing rolling vector approach carry 96.8%96.8\% of the total power, while those of our LTS carry only 45.1%45.1\% (Fig. 1(b)).
The LTS reduces the peak output power of a single twist joint by 42%42\%, leaving a larger margin before a joint motor saturates (Fig. 1(c)).
Besides, our LTS with evenly distributed workload enables the robot to locomote on various complex terrains.
We compare our LTS against conventional sidewinding without twisting on four types of outdoor terrains, and our LTS moves the robot faster than conventional sidewinding, reducing the traversal time by up to 49%49\% for a fixed travel length (Fig. 1(d)).
Real-robot experiments also validate the translating and turning motions of the proposed gaits.

title: Distance Field Driven Reinforcement Learning for Reactive and Robust Collision Avoidance
authors: Taiga Ikeshima,Sheila Sutjipto,Lan Wu,Francisco J. Naranjo-Campos,Taiki Ishigaki,Taisuke Kobayashi,Teresa A. Vidal-Calleja,Eiichi Yoshida
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
abstract: Robust and reactive collision avoidance remains a central challenge for deploying Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies on real robotic manipulators, particularly when transferring behaviours learned in simulation to the physical world. This paper presents an RL framework that integrates the Euclidean Distance Field (EDF) directly into the observation space, providing the agent with continuous geometric cues that support stable and responsive avoidance behaviours. By leveraging the rich spatial information encoded in the EDF, the method enables a streamlined reward formulation that achieves effective obstacle avoidance both with and without Artificial Potential Field guidance. The proposed approach is validated on a 7‑DoF redundant manipulator, demonstrating zero‑shot transfer from simulation to real hardware. Despite being trained exclusively with randomised static objects, the deployed policy generalizes to previously unseen real environments and exhibits robust online avoidance of dynamic obstacles. These results highlight the potential of EDF‑based representations to mitigate the sim‑to‑real gap and support reliable and real-time collision‑aware behaviour in complex and changing environments.
introduction:
Generating motions that allow a robot to safely reach a target position while avoiding obstacles remains one of the fundamental challenges in mobile robotics and manipulation. As robots are increasingly deployed in cluttered, dynamic, and unstructured environments, the ability to reactively determine collision‑free actions from real‑time sensory data has become necessary for robust autonomy.
This need for reliable, responsive obstacle avoidance is especially pressing where the robot must continuously resolve its motion when presented with incomplete spatial modelling.

A classical solution to real‑time obstacle avoidance is the Artificial Potential Field (APF) method [1], which generates control actions by combining attractive and repulsive potentials. While APF is computationally efficient and reactive, it is known to suffer from local minima and non-reachable goals in the presence of obstacles, restricting its applicability in more complex environments.
Beyond reactive-based strategies like APF, collision avoidance has also been addressed using offline motion planning by sampling-based methods such as Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM) [2] and Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT) [3]. While these sampling-based approaches can navigate complex spaces, they often incur significant computational overhead and lack the real-time reactivity for operating in dynamic or unmodelled environments.
As an alternative method, optimisation-based motion planning [4] has been proposed, formulating collision avoidance as a constrained optimisation problem and directly computing a trajectory.

Recent advances in machine learning have introduced alternative strategies for navigating complex environments. Deep networks can encode the structure of the environment for collision‑free trajectory prediction [5], while Reinforcement Learning (RL) [6] has enabled robots to acquire reactive behaviours directly through interaction with their simulated environment. Hybrid frameworks seek to leverage the benefits of combining traditional methods and RL. For instance, Schneider et al.  [7] integrated guidance from APFs into deep RL to mitigate the local‑minima issue inherent in classical potential fields. However, their method relies on the assumption that accurate spatial information regarding obstacle location and geometry is readily available. Xu et al. [8] proposed a hybrid architecture in which a deep RL policy produces avoidance actions that guide an APF planner online, enabling real‑time motion generation in cluttered scenes. They further extend the potential‑field formulation to account for link‑level proximity for full‑body collision avoidance. Li et al. [9] similarly combine RL with APF by learning situation‑dependent scaling factors that modulate the magnitude of the field, improving robustness in cases where standard APF formulations struggle. These works highlight the appeal of APF‑RL combinations: APFs provide structure and computational efficiency, while RL introduces adaptivity and reduces the need for manual tuning.

In practice, obtaining precise and consistent environmental information is nontrivial and remains a primary source of the sim-to-real gap for RL-based methods, as sensing and modelling can introduce noise and uncertainty that simulations fail to capture.
Policies trained entirely in simulation may behave unpredictably when deployed if real‑world perception deviates from the training assumptions. So far, depth camera images and point clouds from LiDAR have shown a relatively small sim-to-real gap, but ad-hoc tricks are still needed to bridge the gap. Although domain randomisation [10] helps by exposing the policy to varied conditions during training, reliable scene understanding remains essential for robust deployment.

To minimise these perceptual discrepancies, Euclidean Distance Fields (EDFs) have the potential to provide a robust representation for bridging the reality gap in reactive motion planning.
Unlike raw point clouds, which are susceptible to sensor noise, or traditional geometric modelling of the environment, which often results in conservative behaviour, an EDF provides a dense spatial signal representing the distance to the nearest obstacle at any given point in the workspace. For example, Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) have been utilized for manipulator collision avoidance [11, 12]. Despite its potential usefulness for learning, to the best of our knowledge, the distance field representations have not been well exploited with RL.

An advantage of the distance field is its ability to be generated in real-time [13]. By training RL policies on EDF-informed observations, an agent can learn to navigate based on the underlying spatial structure of the environment rather than specific pixel-level features or predefined location information. In this work, we propose to exploit EDFs with RL to reduce the sim-to-real gap, as the distance gradients provided by an EDF in the real world can be mapped consistently to the idealised fields encountered during training, ensuring more predictable and robust behaviour on real hardware. Fig. 1 illustrates an example experiment for real-time collision avoidance using RL with EDF, trained in simulation and transferred to the real robot.

The contributions of this paper are then as follows:

A novel RL framework that incorporates real-time Euclidean Distance Field measurements directly into the observation space, enabling the policy to learn reactive and robust collision‑avoidance behaviours

title: A2I-Calib++: A Kinematics-Driven Anti-noise Active Calibration Framework for Whole-Body Multi-IMU Systems on Legged Robots
authors: Fangyu Jiang,Chaoran Xiong,Kehui Ma,Zhen Sun,Zeyu Zhang,Ling Pei
abstract:
Recently, multi-node inertial measurement unit (multi-IMU) systems have shown promise for robust odometry in legged robots.
Multi-IMU fusion can improve legged robot odometry but requires accurate spatiotemporal calibration among the sensors.
Existing multi-IMU calibration methods, designed for aerial or handheld platforms, face challenges on legged robots because routine locomotion may provide insufficient excitation, while foot slips, impacts, and vibrations introduce measurement disturbances.
To address these challenges, we propose A2I-Calib++, a kinematics-driven anti-noise active calibration framework for body-mounted IMUs covered by the robot kinematic model. It estimates temporal offsets, extrinsic rotations and translations, and inertial biases through temporal correlation search followed by analytic spatial and bias estimation, without artificial calibration targets or complex parameter tuning for the target IMU. A2I-Calib++ comprises three core modules:
1) a Noise-Isotropy-Inspired Trajectory supported by a finite-horizon conditioning proposition that generates sufficient excitation to limit noise sensitivity; 2) a constraint-aware Adversarial Motion Priors controller that combines the anti-noise excitation with a rolling-contact reward for contact-aware execution; and 3) a contact-constrained virtual IMU that fuses pre-calibrated calf IMUs and joint kinematics under a rolling-contact model to construct the calibration reference.
Furthermore, evaluations on both simulation and real-world quadruped platforms demonstrate notably reduced noise sensitivity and simulation calibration errors compared to conventional methods, together with repeatable real-world calibration and improved proprioceptive odometry accuracy for legged robots.
introduction:
Reliable state estimation of legged robots[1, 2, 3] constitutes a fundamental prerequisite for executing complex tasks in embodied navigation[4]. Recently, multi-IMU-based odometry has garnered considerable attention due to cost effectiveness and power efficiency[5, 6, 7].

Distributing IMUs across a legged robot and fusing them with joint encoders
can improve base state estimation
[6, 7, 8]. However,
spatiotemporal misalignment among inertial nodes introduces inconsistent
kinematic constraints and systematic odometry drift
[9], making multi-IMU calibration essential.

Meeting this requirement on legged platforms remains difficult. Passive
targetless methods[10, 11] relying on human intervention suffer from insufficient kinematic excitation, leading to enlarged sensitivity to IMU measurement noise
caused by foot slips, impacts, and vibrations.
Existing observability-aware methods
[12, 13] mainly assess collected data
or provide qualitative motion guidance, rather than directly designing
excitation to improve the numerical conditioning of the calibration
system. A2I-Calib[14] actively calibrates temporal offsets,
extrinsic rotations and gyroscope biases of calf-mounted IMUs, but
extending active calibration to body-mounted IMUs additionally requires
extrinsic-translation and accelerometer-bias estimation.

To address these challenges, we present A2I-Calib++, a kinematics-driven anti-noise active calibration framework for whole-body multi-IMU systems on legged robots.
Our main contributions are as follows:

An active calibration framework that recovers the full set of spatiotemporal parameters with temporal correlation search and analytic spatial estimation (search and solve), requiring no additional artificial targets or complex parameter tuning.

A kinematics-driven anti-noise mechanism that combines an anti-noise reference excitation generated by the Noise Isotropy Proposition (NIP) with a contact-constrained virtual IMU (VIMU) reference formed by multi-leg fusion to reduce calibration noise sensitivity.

A constraint-aware Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) controller that learns the reference motion’s state-transition distribution and incorporates a rolling-contact task reward to generate contact-aware calibration motions for legged-robot execution.

Comprehensive validation across simulation and real-world quadruped platforms, demonstrating notable reductions in
noise sensitivity, high simulation calibration accuracy, repeatable real-world calibration, and lower proprioceptive odometry drift compared with a state-of-the-art (SOTA) calibration method.

title: PRISM: Learning Realistic Depth via Physics-Grounded Noise Disentanglement with Semantic-Geometric Collaboration
authors: Xiujian Liang,Jiacheng Liu,Mingyang Sun,Qichen He,Anda Cheng,Cewu Lu,Jianhua Sun
abstract:
Real-world physical sensing exhibits complex, heterogeneous noise patterns that deviate significantly from idealized simulation, posing a fundamental bottleneck for sim-to-real transfer. Existing sensor modelings typically treat depth noise as a monolithic black-box process, overlooking the distinct physical mechanisms that govern different error modalities. In this work, we introduce a physics-grounded paradigm that disentangles monolithic noise into two complementary modalities: sensing invalidation and measurement inaccuracy, enabling a tailored treatment of noise sources based on their physical origins. Building on this insight, we propose PRISM, a tripartite framework that distills 3D Visual Foundation Model features as rich spatial-semantic priors for physics-based reasoning. To address the inherent sparsity and class imbalance of invalidation regions, we develop Hierarchical Positive-Prioritized Supervision, integrating multi-scale positive-weighted objectives with a positive-preserving dynamic hard mining strategy to enforce precise artifact delineation. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves state-of-the-art fidelity in noisy depth synthesis. Furthermore, downstream robotic experiments show that PRISM facilitates a 92.1% average success rate in the real world, marking a significant improvement over monolithic baselines. Our project page is available at: 

https://shawnleung-sii.github.io/prism-icml2026/.
introduction:
Simulation-based training has emerged as a cornerstone of robotic learning, offering unparalleled advantages in safety, scalability, and data availability, enabling the exploration of complex manipulation and navigation tasks at scale(Mittal et al., 2023). However, the deployment of simulation-trained policies remains fundamentally bottlenecked by the sim-to-real gap(Jia et al., 2025). Among all sensing modalities, depth perception stands out as particularly susceptible: while simulated depth is geometrically pristine, consumer-grade sensors exhibit complex, heterogeneous noise patterns(Fig.1a). Unlike the visual gap in the RGB, the depth gap introduces functional distortions that directly corrupt geometric reasoning, misleading downstream perception and control(Wang et al., 2022).

To bridge this geometric gap, prior efforts have bifurcated into two primary paradigms. Explicit analytical modeling relies on predefined heuristics(Borrego et al., 2018) or differentiable ray-tracing (Zhang et al., 2023b) to simulate light transport. While theoretically rigorous, these methods often suffer from limited generalization beyond specific sensor models or rigid calibration requirements. Conversely, implicit data-driven modeling employs image translation (Shen et al., 2022) or diffusion models (Zhou et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) to learn noise distributions from data. Crucially, despite their methodological divergence, both paradigms typically model depth noise as a monolithic stochastic process. By indiscriminately conflating distinct physical mechanisms into a unified representation, they fail to reproduce the spatially correlated artifacts inherent to physical sensing, often hallucinating noise in clean regions or failing to predict structural voids.

We argue that effective noise modeling should be grounded in the physical mechanisms of sensor degradation, which are intrinsically linked to scene semantics. Real-world depth corruption follows structured physical regularities: specular surfaces (e.g., metal, mirror) cause regular reflection resulting in Sensing Invalidation, whereas transparent or translucent materials (e.g., glass, plastic) induce refraction or sub-surface scattering, leading to Measurement Inaccuracy. Unlike monolithic models that indiscriminately conflate these mechanisms, PRISM establishes a physics-grounded noise disentanglement paradigm. We posit that this bimodal decomposition is a pragmatic macroscopic taxonomy supported by sensor physics, necessitating specialized components to model their statistical and physical properties of each error source.

To operationalize this insight, we propose PRISM (Physics-Reasoned Implicit Sensor Modeling), a semantic-geometric collaborative framework designed to ′refract′ monolithic sensor noise into physically motivated modalities. The framework is instantiated as a tripartite synergistic architecture following a structured pipeline: Reason →\rightarrow Disentangle →\rightarrow Generate.
First, the Semantic-Physics Reasoner (SPR) leverages a frozen 3D VFM (e.g., DepthAnything(Lin et al., 2025), MoGe2(Wang et al., 2025b)) to extract semantic-aware features that act as physics priors identifying non-Lambertian surfaces.
These priors are then injected into the Bimodal Noise Disentangler (BND), which fuses semantic context with simulation geometry to implicitly predict the pixel-wise probability of invalidation and transform into a region mask. Crucially, instead of predicting noise directly, BND formulates disentangled representations that condition a Noise Residual Generator (NRG). NRG employs a diffusion-based process, inspired by (Xu et al., 2025), to synthesize high-fidelity residual maps, ensuring generated artifacts are not only statistically plausible but also geometrically consistent with the underlying scene structure.

Furthermore, training this framework presents a unique optimization challenge: invalidation regions are spatially sparse (often <10%<10\% of pixels). Standard losses inevitably collapse under this extreme class imbalance underweighting these rare but critical events. To counter this, we develop H-PPS (Hierarchical Positive-Preserving Supervision). Unlike conventional hard example mining discards rare signals, H-PPS combines multi-scale boundary constraints with recall-prioritized mining protocol.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

1) Physics-Grounded Disentanglement: We fundamentally reframe depth noise modeling from a monolithic stochastic process to a physics-grounded taxonomy. We identify Sensing Invalidation and Measurement Inaccuracy as two physically motivated modalities, providing a theoretical basis for treating signal loss and signal bias separately. 
2) Semantic-Geometric Collaboration: We propose PRISM, a unified framework that distills the rich physical common sense of 3D Visual Foundation Model to drive noise synthesis. By explicitly aligning semantic priors with geometric distortion, we achieve noise generation that is not only visually realistic but physically consistent with scene. 
3) Sparsity-Aware Optimization: We address the sparsity and imbalance in modeling sensing invalidation through Hierarchical Positive-Prioritized Supervision. By integrating multi-scale positive weighting with a positive-preserving dynamic hard mining strategy, we solve the optimization dilemma of learning sparse, boundary-sensitive artifacts. 
4) SOTA Fidelity and Sim2Real Transfer: Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves state-of-the-art fidelity in noisy depth synthesis. Critically, in downstream robotic manipulation tasks, our method facilitates a 92.1% average success rate in the real world, marking a 53.2% absolute improvement over raw simulation.

title: Integrating Flow Matching and Model Predictive Control for Safe Robot Navigation
authors: Philipp Holzmann,Maik Pfefferkorn,Joao Carvalho,Ali Younes,An Thai Le,Georgia Chalvatzaki,Jan Peters,Rolf Findeisen
abstract:
Learning-based path planners based on diffusion and flow matching can generate diverse trajectories from demonstrations but typically lack mechanisms for constraint satisfaction and collision avoidance during deployment.
This work proposes a framework that combines flow-matching-based path planning with model predictive path-following control to integrate data-driven path generation with real-time, constraint-aware execution.
The flow-matching model captures multimodal path distributions, while the predictive controller adapts motion online to satisfy state and input constraints and avoid obstacles using updated local sensor information.
An event-triggered re-planning scheme incorporates predictive control solutions into subsequent path generation, promoting collision-free navigation in environments with previously unseen obstacles.
Simulation results for mobile robot navigation demonstrate robust performance across cluttered environments.
The framework provides a systematic approach to combining flow matching with predictive control for adaptive, data-driven navigation.
introduction:
Recent advances in robot control for complex tasks have been driven by increasingly capable machine learning algorithms and the availability of high-performance computing resources [28, 19, 11].
Machine learning enables expressive control policies that often outperform classical methods in high-dimensional and multimodal settings, particularly when trained via imitation or reinforcement learning.

To handle multimodal data distributions, recent work has applied deep generative models based on diffusion [20] and flow matching [29, 30], originally developed for image synthesis, to robotics domains including imitation learning [12, 43], offline RL [24], grasping [47, 10], and motion planning [7, 9, 8, 31, 39, 13, 5]. These models are particularly attractive for their ability to represent complex, multimodal trajectory distributions and to generate diverse candidate motions from demonstration data, including different paths from the same initial point.
In this article, we use a variant of flow matching the shortcut model [18], which offers fast sampling [44].

One central challenge in learning policies from demonstrations is the lack of guarantees for collision avoidance during deployment.
For example, a generative model trained on human-demonstrated trajectories may produce paths that become unsafe when new obstacles are introduced or when dynamics or constraints (e.g., velocity limits) change.
Nevertheless, the data remains valuable as a reference for a lower-level controller that can safely adapt to it.

To this end, we combine the deep generative planner with a model predictive path-following controller (MPPFC) [34, 16, 15], which tracks and locally reshapes the generated path to ensure safety, cf. Fig. 1.
Unlike tracking model predictive control (MPC) [42, 17], MPPFC treats path progression and velocity as optimization variables, enabling adaptive motion profiles and reactive behavior in dynamic environments.
By enforcing input and state constraints, including collision avoidance and actuator limits, MPPFC ensures constraint satisfaction even if the reference path must be temporarily deviated from.

Previous works have used simpler generative models, focused on unimodal settings and control-theoretic guarantees [37, 36, 35, 21, 41].
Since combining diffusion and flow matching generative models with predictive control offers a large potential [23], this has been explored by a series of works: [52] uses a diffusion model to learn multi-step predictions and warm-start MPC optimizations; [33] parameterizes MPC feedback using diffusion; [22] applies diffusion models to solve nonlinear MPC problems; and [51, 27] explore diffusion rollouts for model predictive path integral control (MPPIC).
Relatedly, [23] uses diffusion to generate subgoals for long-horizon control with MPPIC.
However, because of the underlying MPC methods used, these works do not guarantee safety or path-following.
In contrast, our approach combines flow-matching for reference generation with MPPFC for local safety and reference tracking, overcoming the limitations of the current methods.
By using MPPFC to track and refine paths generated via flow matching, we ensure constraint satisfaction — particularly collision avoidance — and enable real-time adaptation.
In this sense, the MPPFC shows similarities to predictive safety filters [38, 49, 48].
However, in contrast to standard safety filters that modify unsafe inputs to ensure safety, we directly apply MPPFC as the main controller, using its structure to dynamically shape both path execution and progression.

The main contributions of this work are:
(1) a framework that combines a flow-matching-based path generator, learned from human demonstrations, with MPPFC to enable constraint satisfaction and collision avoidance during execution;
(2) a bidirectional coupling in which flow-generated paths guide MPPFC and its predictions bias the flow planner during event-triggered re-planning;
(3) a systematic evaluation demonstrating collision-free path-following in environments with multiple obstacle configurations not observed during training.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section II outlines the problem setting. Section III introduces the generative model used to learn path distributions from demonstrations. Section IV details the MPPFC formulation and its integration with the planner. Section V presents simulation results, and Section VI concludes the paper.

title: Payload generalization on feedforward control actions for trajectory tracking in robots with rigid and elastic joints
authors: Giorgia Pazzi,Giorgio Simonini,Michele Pierallini,Paolo Salaris,Giorgio Grioli,Manolo Garabini,Franco Angelini
comment: . Accepted for publication in Control Engineering Practice
abstract:
Industries employ robots for repetitive tasks due to their high precision and performance, typically achieved through feedforward control actions based on an accurate robot description. However, an exact dynamic model can be difficult to obtain, especially for robots with elastic elements or when the payload changes.
Learning-based feedforward approaches are promising for trajectory tracking under model uncertainties, but typically face generalization issues when task parameters vary.
This paper proposes a novel method to generalize the feedforward control action with respect to payload parameters, independently of the underlying controller.
Firstly, the minimal number of example objects needed for payload generalization is derived.
Then, an algorithm is proposed to execute the same trajectory with a new payload, given only its parameters, without knowledge of the robot’s dynamic model and even in the presence of elastic joints.
The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is validated in simulations and experiments on tracking tasks with different robots and controllers.
Two sets of experiments are performed: on a standard Franka Emika Panda robot, and on a Franka Emika Panda robot equipped with an elastic wrist.
introduction:
Robotics proved to be a key technology in logistics and manufacturing (Liu et al., 2024), demonstrating exceptional effectiveness in performing repetitive tasks such as pick-and-place operations (Lobbezoo et al., 2021; Surati et al., 2021), unwrapping pallets (Gabellieri et al., 2022), handling fragile items (Angelini et al., 2020c; Pagliarani et al., 2024), and even throwing goods and objects (Zeng et al., 2020).

The ability of robots to transform such industries comes from their safety during human-robot interaction tasks and their excellent tracking performance (Palleschi et al., 2021).
Safety is increasingly achieved thanks to the physical adoption of elastic elements within the robot joints, leading to the so-called articulated soft robots (Albu-Schaffer et al., 2008; Della Santina et al., 2020). However, this progress comes at the expense of increased complexity in robot modeling and description.
In scenarios where the robot’s dynamic model is known with uncertainties, adaptive control techniques can be employed to estimate and compensate for unknown parameters.
Such schemes exploit the linearity of the manipulator dynamics with respect to the dynamic parameters, which they estimate online, from the known model structure, to compute the control torque (Slotine and Li, 1987); recent formulations even recover the exact parameters without requiring persistency of
excitation (Arteaga, 2024).

However, such feedback-based techniques often require high gains that stiffen dynamics, undermining the compliance of soft robots (Pierallini et al., 2022), and although recent adaptive computed-torque schemes mitigate this by enabling low feedback gains (Simonini et al., 2025), they remain feedback- and model-based.
Additionally, adaptive control must re-initialize parameter estimates when the robot’s dynamics change, leading to transient phases of suboptimal performance (Middletone and Goodwin, 1986).
The same parameter linearity also underlies load identification, where the payload inertial parameters are estimated offline from measured joint torques and motion (Atkeson et al., 1986): this is the inverse of the problem addressed here, which instead exploits known payload parameters to generate the corresponding feedforward torques.

In contrast, good tracking performance is often achieved by feedforward control actions (Liu et al., 2019), which are computed either from the perfect knowledge of the system’s dynamics (Chhatoi et al., 2023) or through learning-based techniques (Chen et al., 2025).
Since the former approach relies on exact system modeling, it becomes particularly challenging in many real-world scenarios. For this reason, the latter model-free and learning-based control strategies have been increasingly investigated in recent years.

An example of this class of controllers is Iterative Learning Control (ILC) (Arimoto et al., 1984; Chen et al., 2020; Pierallini et al., 2025), which offers a powerful solution for improving the transient performance of systems that operate repetitively over a fixed time interval, finding application mainly in industrial robotics (Tayebi et al., 2008; Saab et al., 2022). Unlike classical control techniques, ILC leverages previous iteration data to minimize the tracking error in a model-free, data-driven fashion (Bristow et al., 2006).

Despite their promising performance, learning-based methods, particularly ILC, struggle to generalize pre-learned control actions to new scenarios.
Indeed, any slight change in the scene, such as the need to perform a different trajectory or move different payloads, leads to the use of a new control action and, since the model of the system is not entirely available, this is not trivial to achieve, and it requires the repetition of the entire learning phase whenever the task changes (Li et al., 2022; Angelini et al., 2020a).

Several studies have addressed the issue of generalization in learning-based controllers. For instance, the authors in Mengacci et al. (2021a) proposed solutions to generalize the learned control action in terms of stiffness profile. In Angelini et al. (2020b), De Luca and Farina (2002) a procedure is developed to scale and generalize learned control actions to execute desired trajectories at varying velocities.
The problem is further examined from the perspective of final point (Freeman et al., 2010) and trajectory generalization in Angelini et al. (2020a).
However, none of these solutions generalizes the control action with respect to the payload’s dynamic parameters, nor in a feedforward fashion for robots that may even present elastic joints, which is a key feature in many pick-and-place tasks to execute precise, safe, and fast operations.
In many applications, such as manufacturing or logistics, robots repeatedly manipulate several objects, each with a different mass, inertia, or geometry. Conventional feedforward learning-based controllers typically require re-learning whenever some task parameters change, e.g., the manipulated object, leading to a time-consuming process that limits scalability.

This paper develops a novel method to generalize feedforward control actions, acquired with any controller, for tracking a desired trajectory with different payloads, Fig. 1.
To this end, it is first demonstrated that the number of examples required to generalize the feedforward control action corresponds to the number of dynamic parameters defining the object, plus one.
An algorithm is then introduced, capable of executing the same trajectory for a new payload based solely on its given parameters.
The core idea is to collect feedforward control actions for a small set of example objects. From this data, a regressor matrix is computed, enabling the estimation of the feedforward control required for any new object with known parameters.
This makes the method easy to implement in industrial settings where such parameters are usually available or measurable.
Additionally, this purely data-driven, controller-independent approach requires no prior knowledge of the robot’s dynamic model and can improve tracking performance in real-world applications, even when elastic elements are present in the robot’s structure.

The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated for both rigid and soft articulated robots, showcasing its ability to operate independently of the manipulator’s structure and controller while relying solely on the dynamic parameters used to describe the payload.
Specifically, experiments are also conducted on the Franka Emika Panda manipulator, equipped with a variable-stiffness actuator wrist and the SoftClaw11
1
qb-softclaw.

This paper is organized as follows.
In Section 2, the problem, the system model, and the payload description are defined.
The proposed payload generalization approach is detailed in Section 3, and Section 4 provides an extensive validation of the approach, including simulation results and real-world experiments.
Finally, conclusions and future research directions are discussed in Section 5.

title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
authors: Qinghang Liu,Conglin Wang,Zongsheng Li,Boyong He,Han Gao,Pengcheng Wang,Tao Sun,Lige Liu,Chang Liu
abstract:
Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember
task-relevant information beyond its short observation window.
Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant
information from history and reason over it at execution time,
placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address
this challenge, we propose PAL (Plan first, Act
Later), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language
robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a
semantic-event memory, and an executable subtask_list. A
high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual
observations into the subtask_list. At execution time, the
VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the
subtask_list and passes it to a low-level
vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write
to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data
generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and
then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate
training data that better match the state distribution encountered
during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent
benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL
achieves a 56.05% success rate, outperforming the strongest
baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51%. In real-world experiments
across four manipulation tasks, PAL reaches 60.83%
overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00%) and FrameSamp-Modul
(28.33%). These results show that proactively writing
future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves
long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made substantial progress
toward general-purpose robot control
(Intelligence et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2024). By grounding language
instructions in visual observations and actions, VLA provides
a flexible interface for solving diverse manipulation tasks in generalizable open-world. However, many
existing policies still rely on a Markovian or near-Markovian view of the
world: the action to execute is assumed to be recoverable from the current
observation or a short window of recent frames. This assumption becomes fragile
in memory-dependent settings, where successful behavior may depend on historical information observed much earlier. For example, repetitive
manipulation requires remembering progress (Yang et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a) and active exploration requires
retrieving the location or state of an object discovered earlier when the robot revisits
the scene (Shah et al., 2026; Sridhar et al., 2025).

To address these memory-dependent challenges, recent works augment VLA models
with a memory bank that retains task-relevant information from past
observations. At execution time, the model retrieves relevant entries from the
bank to support stable long-term decision making
(Torne et al., 2026; Sridhar et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026). Although this
avoids repeatedly processing the raw history, the high-level model must still
search across a large memory bank and infer the next subtask at inference time. Such
banks often contain redundant information, making it difficult for the model to
fetch the required information and lead to more task failures.

One key observation is that:
Evidence for defining a future goal are available before executing the goal.
As illustrated in
Fig. 1, the task requires the robot to press the button
and then pick up the highlighted cube. While the robot is still pressing
the button, the model can store the future subtask “pick up the cube” in the
subtask list when the cube is highlighted. When the transient highlight
disappears, the robot can simply retrieve the stored subtask for execution,
without re-identifying which cube to pick up. This pattern occurs in many memory-dependent
robotic tasks, where the future plan can be determined once the necessary
evidence becomes available.

Motivated by this view, we propose Plan First, Act Later (PAL), a hierarchical
memory pipeline for VLA long-term decision-making. It comprises a three-level memory system:
a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable
subtask_list. These three memory components have distinct roles: the
visual buffer retains recent observations, the semantic-event memory maintains
task-relevant events, and the executable subtask_list stores
future-relevant subtasks text instructions. At each query, a high-level vision-language model
(VLM) updates the event memory and the subtask_list, then selects the subtask to execute for the low-level VLA. This design
has two benefits: (1) first, streaming memory updates incrementally compress the visual
history, reducing the context required
for long-horizon reasoning; (2) second, the stored subtasks can be directly retrieved without searching across a large memory bank for subtask inference.

To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we propose
a two-stage training pipeline. The pipeline combines dense update-timing
supervision with self-labeling and a task-grounded verifier, allowing the
training data to better reflect the model’s execution rollout distribution.
Evaluation results on RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026), a benchmark of long-horizon, memory-dependent manipulation tasks,
show that PAL achieves a 56.05% success rate, compared with
44.51% for the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul. In real-world
manipulation experiments across four tasks, PAL reaches 60.83%
overall success, outperforming MemER (45.00%) and FrameSamp-Modul
(28.33%), demonstrating the practical benefits of our approach.
Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce PAL, a hierarchical memory architecture
with a streaming-style reasoning mechanism for VLA long-term decision-making. It progressively
transforms streaming visual observations into semantic events and executable
subtasks, providing a structured memory for diverse
long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks.

We introduce PAL, a hierarchical memory architecture
with a streaming-style reasoning mechanism for VLA long-term decision-making. It progressively
transforms streaming visual observations into semantic events and executable
subtasks, providing a structured memory for diverse
long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks.

We develop a two-stage training pipeline that enables the model to
learn reliable hierarchical-memory update behavior. It produces accurate
and timely memory updates, yielding reliable executable subtask lists for
long-horizon reasoning.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of PAL through evaluations on
long-horizon, memory-dependent manipulation tasks, where it delivers
consistent gains over competitive VLA and memory-augmented methods in both
simulated and real-world settings.

1. We introduce PAL, a hierarchical memory architecture
with a streaming-style reasoning mechanism for VLA long-term decision-making. It progressively
transforms streaming visual observations into semantic events and executable
subtasks, providing a structured memory for diverse
long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks.

2. We develop a two-stage training pipeline that enables the model to
learn reliable hierarchical-memory update behavior. It produces accurate
and timely memory updates, yielding reliable executable subtask lists for
long-horizon reasoning.

3. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PAL through evaluations on
long-horizon, memory-dependent manipulation tasks, where it delivers
consistent gains over competitive VLA and memory-augmented methods in both
simulated and real-world settings.

title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement
authors: Jia Deng,Zizhe Wang,Xin Lu,Yi Huang,Zehao Jia
abstract: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43–46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.
introduction:
Space robots are expected to work with less direct supervision. On-orbit servicing combines approach, capture, and manipulation of client spacecraft, and free-flying robots such as Astrobee serve as test beds for autonomy inside the International Space Station (ISS) [1]. Language and vision–language models offer a natural interface for such tasks: they can map an operator’s request to a sequence of pre-verified skills [2] or, in end-to-end form, to robot actions [3, 4]. Space-specific agent frameworks now apply this interface to on-orbit servicing [5]. These systems are usually evaluated with large models on terrestrial computers; SpaceMind, for example, uses Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B throughout [5], a model whose weights alone would far exceed the memory of current flight computers.

Running the model onboard removes the dependence on communication windows, round-trip delays, and limited link bandwidth, but onboard compute is scarce [6]. Perseverance’s primary computer, for example, is a radiation-hardened RAD750 running at up to 200 MHz with 256 MB of DRAM [7]; its global localization instead runs on a commercial Snapdragon 801 from the Ingenuity helicopter base station [8]. Language models are now reaching orbit. An AI assistant that combines ground and onboard models was delivered to China’s space station in July 2025 [9], and ASTREA ran a 1.54-billion-parameter Qwen2.5 model quantized to 4 bits on a flight-qualified, CPU-only system-on-chip in an external ISS payload, with response times from about 40 s to over 8 min [10]. For onboard language models, compression is therefore a prerequisite rather than an optimization.

For flight use, the relevant question is not only how small a model can become but also what the compressed model must preserve. We identify three properties. First, the artifact must fit a fixed memory budget and use a storage format that the onboard runtime supports. Second, it must be a static object that can be versioned, verified, and rolled back like other flight software. Current machine-learning guidance for space engineering does not yet cover large language models [11]; until it does, the preparation process has to make these properties explicit. Third, its behavior must stay close to that of the full-precision reference that was validated on the ground. The third property suggests measuring compression error where the validated behavior is defined: at the model’s output distribution.

Standard post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models (LLMs) applies one quantizer family throughout a model. GPTQ uses approximate second-order error compensation [12], AWQ protects activation-salient channels by equivalent scaling [13], and SignRound, implemented in AutoRound, optimizes rounding and clipping [14]. These families embody different error models, and CALM has shown that choosing a quantization algorithm per Transformer block can help [15]. CALM scores candidates by linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) between intermediate representations [16]. Representation similarity is a reasonable heuristic, but it is not the quantity that an acceptance test of the onboard model would examine.

We therefore treat compression as a ground-segment preparation step (Fig. 1) and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible homogeneous checkpoints. Each linear module is assigned to one quantizer family, and every candidate substitution is scored through the final next-token distribution of the partially assigned model. In its default fidelity mode (QSelect-KL), the procedure is label free and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference strictly decreases; the rule has no tuned threshold. An optional target-adapted mode (QSelect-TA) adds a target-answer likelihood term for missions that can provide a small labeled set, with fixed margins that bound the KL increase allowed at each step. Scoring with the acceptance quantity itself, rather than a cheaper proxy, is affordable in this setting: a one-pass module-wise selection takes one to a few GPU-hours on the ground for the models studied, excluding candidate generation, is paid once per model release, and never changes the bit width or storage format of the result. The memory limits that make compression necessary also keep onboard models small, and the selection cost shrinks with the model.

Experiments on three open models from 3B to 8B parameters at 3 and 4 bits show four things. Composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. Final-output scoring yields lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs of a matched scaffold and lower KL than a local reconstruction criterion in all four tested settings. Module-wise decisions mainly lower 3-bit perplexity, at several times the ground time of layer-wise decisions, and extra passes add little. Packed artifacts are 63–70% smaller than BF16, as for any single-family model at the same bit width, and an analytic breakdown shows that unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43–46% of what remains at 3 bits. All experiments use general-domain language-modeling and reasoning benchmarks on a ground GPU; we do not evaluate space-domain tasks, flight hardware, or radiation effects.

Our contributions are as follows.

A requirements analysis for compressing onboard language models for space robots. It states five requirements—fixed format and budget, a static artifact, behavioral fidelity to a ground-validated reference, scarce mission labels, and bounded ground compute—and maps them to design choices and to the evidence reported here (Section III).

QSelect, which builds on CALM’s per-block algorithm selection [15] with a final-output score, finer decision units, a threshold-free and label-free fidelity mode, and an optional target-adapted mode (Section IV).

An empirical study on three open models that compares QSelect with single-family PTQ, representation-similarity, local-reconstruction, and whole-model selection; characterizes the trade-off between ground time and fidelity; and analyzes packed artifacts for onboard deployment (Sections VI and VII).

1. A requirements analysis for compressing onboard language models for space robots. It states five requirements—fixed format and budget, a static artifact, behavioral fidelity to a ground-validated reference, scarce mission labels, and bounded ground compute—and maps them to design choices and to the evidence reported here (Section III).

2. QSelect, which builds on CALM’s per-block algorithm selection [15] with a final-output score, finer decision units, a threshold-free and label-free fidelity mode, and an optional target-adapted mode (Section IV).

3. An empirical study on three open models that compares QSelect with single-family PTQ, representation-similarity, local-reconstruction, and whole-model selection; characterizes the trade-off between ground time and fidelity; and analyzes packed artifacts for onboard deployment (Sections VI and VII).

title: Relational Geometry Forcing for World Action Models
authors: Yuan Xu,Yixiang Chen,Qisen Ma,Jiabing Yang,Peiyan Li,Kai Wang,Jianhua Yang,Jianlou Si,Jun Huang,Jing Liu,Nianfeng Liu,Yan Huang,Liang Wang
abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions.
However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation.
Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models.
Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features.
To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features.
Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution.
Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module.
Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.
introduction:
Robot policies for manipulation require accounting for interaction-induced scene changes when generating precise action trajectories.
World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate predictive world modeling into action learning by coupling future visual prediction with action generation (Ye et al. 2026b; Li et al. 2026b; Kim et al. 2026; Bi et al. 2025).
Typically, WAMs include a video expert to predict future RGB frames and an action expert to generate action chunks, while scene geometry receives no direct supervision (Yuan et al. 2026; Ye et al. 2026a).
Accordingly, limited geometric perception of the physical scene remains a key challenge for WAMs in precise manipulation (Shridhar, Manuelli, and Fox 2023; Ze et al. 2024).

Recent geometry-aware WAMs address this challenge by adding explicit geometry branches to the video–action framework, as illustrated in Figure 1(a).
These branches introduce depth or 4D prediction as additional training objectives (Guo et al. 2026; Ma et al. 2026; Li et al. 2026d; Zhang et al. 2026a).
We therefore ask whether geometric priors can directly regularize the video and action representations of WAMs without explicit geometric reconstruction.

Representation alignment offers an alternative to explicit geometric modeling by directly supervising intermediate WAM features.
REPA aligns diffusion features with pretrained visual representations (Yu et al. 2024), while subsequent methods use geometric targets from pretrained 3D foundation models to supervise video generators and robot policies (Wu et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025).
As illustrated in Figure 1(b), these methods primarily use pointwise alignment to regress intermediate features in WAMs toward dense geometric targets from 3D foundation models.

However, pointwise alignment assumes that each WAM feature and its geometric target encode comparable content.
Video alignment satisfies this assumption because both representations describe local image regions.
In action alignment, compact action features instead summarize trajectory transitions, whereas dense geometric targets describe scene content.
Directly regressing action features toward scene-level geometric targets therefore conflates representations with different roles.
Consistent with this analysis, extending pointwise alignment to the action expert reduces task success below the unaligned baseline (Figure 2b).

To address this problem, we introduce Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors to WAM features without explicit geometric reconstruction.
As illustrated in Figure 1(c), RGF aligns pairwise relations among WAM features with those induced by a frozen 3D foundation model, avoiding direct feature regression.
Matching these relations does not require WAM and 3D features to share the same dimensionality or embedding space (Park et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2026b).
Using frozen VGGT features as supervision (Wang et al. 2025), RGF transfers scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to video features through intra-frame and cross-view objectives, while its action-temporal objective couples action dynamics to geometric scene evolution.
All auxiliary components are used only during training, leaving inference unchanged.

Experiments on LIBERO (Liu et al. 2023), RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al. 2025), and real-world tasks on a Franka robot show that RGF achieves competitive performance across single-arm and bimanual manipulation.
On the real robot, RGF further generalizes to unseen objects, background distractors, and height changes.
Moreover, RGF yields consistent gains across diverse WAM paradigms.
Qualitatively, Figure 2(a) shows that the RGF similarity map peaks near the ground-truth cross-view correspondence.

Our contributions are as follows:

We identify a representation mismatch in pointwise alignment between dense geometric targets from 3D foundation models and compact action features in WAMs, explaining the performance degradation observed when this alignment is extended to the action expert.

We propose Relational Geometry Forcing, which transfers geometric priors into WAM representations by aligning intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations, without explicit geometric reconstruction or additional inference modules.

Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world tasks validate RGF, demonstrating competitive performance, generalization to unseen real-world conditions, and consistent gains across WAM paradigms.

1. We identify a representation mismatch in pointwise alignment between dense geometric targets from 3D foundation models and compact action features in WAMs, explaining the performance degradation observed when this alignment is extended to the action expert.

2. We propose Relational Geometry Forcing, which transfers geometric priors into WAM representations by aligning intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations, without explicit geometric reconstruction or additional inference modules.

3. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world tasks validate RGF, demonstrating competitive performance, generalization to unseen real-world conditions, and consistent gains across WAM paradigms.
