title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
authors: Chun Gu,Xiaofei Wei,Yiming Chen,Bozhou Zhang,Juntong Zhang,Xiatian Zhu,Li Zhang
abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.
introduction:
Modern robot manipulation increasingly relies on large pretrained robot foundation models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. A common post-training paradigm adapts these pretrained priors to a target task using offline human teleoperation data [1, 7], producing an initially deployable policy. However, real-robot failures often arise in off-demonstration states induced by the policy itself, including contact-rich interactions, recovery situations, and precision-critical configurations. Covering such rare but deployment-critical states by simply collecting additional offline teleoperation episodes is inherently data-inefficient [8, 9, 7].

Human-in-the-loop learning offers a natural mechanism for covering these policy-induced states, as human operators can intervene during failures or challenging recovery behaviors. However, existing approaches often treat deployment primarily as a provider of expert action labels for supervised learning: human-intervention segments are used as demonstrations, while policy-generated segments are discarded or treated as unlabeled data [8, 10, 11, 12]. This limits data efficiency, especially when most deployment experience is generated by the policy itself. Moreover, offline-only post-training methods [10, 11, 13, 12, 14] typically follow a collect-train-deploy cycle, preventing them from immediately incorporating deployment experience and thereby slowing adaptation under distribution shift.
Online reinforcement learning leverages both human interventions and policy-generated rollouts, bringing policy updates closer to deployment [15, 16]. However, these methods often rely on value functions or critics trained from sparse episode-level success-or-failure feedback. Such weak supervision makes it difficult to stably evaluate high-dimensional action chunks, increasing both training complexity and instability. Other systems reduce this burden by updating only small policy modules or by shifting annotation away from real-robot rollouts [15, 17, 18]. While effective in constrained settings, these design choices limit the potential of online post-training to improve large robot foundation models across diverse manipulation tasks.
Existing methods therefore lack a mechanism for promptly incorporating deployment-time intervention and execution signals without deferring learning to a subsequent offline training round or relying on difficult-to-estimate value functions.

Our central insight is that, once a pretrained policy is warm-started on a target task, deployment need not be a data-collection stage before the next offline retraining round. It can instead serve as a continual learning process that produces structured training signals. Human interventions and policy executions reveal what the current policy can accomplish and which state regions still require repair. Deployment data should therefore be organized as provenance-structured online experience rather than flattened into additional expert demonstrations.

Building on this insight, we introduce TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system for pretrained manipulation policies. As shown in , TIDE places the robot, the human operator, and the learner in a single deployment loop: the robot executes action chunks generated by the current policy, the operator intervenes only when necessary, and the system records the executed action at each step together with its provenance, i.e., whether it was produced by the human or the policy. Provenance records execution source only; it is not a reward, correctness label, or quality score. The learner continuously updates all trainable policy modules using both offline task data and the growing online dataset, and returns updated checkpoints to the robot at episode boundaries. Rather than treating mixed online episodes as homogeneous expert demonstrations, TIDE restructures them into pure-provenance chunks. These labels enable provenance-conditioned supervised training without a separate reward model, critic, or action scorer.

We validate TIDE on four real-robot manipulation tasks spanning precision contact, deformable-object manipulation, constrained placement, and recovery from policy-induced states. Across these tasks, TIDE improves no-takeover task performance over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations. It performs comparably to the Fixed Policy baseline while making updates available during deployment. The observed intervention ratio also decreases over deployment, indicating lower human-supervision burden without serving as an autonomous-performance measure.

This paper makes three main contributions: (1) TIDE, a human-in-the-loop online post-training system that keeps real-robot execution, human takeover, learning, and policy redeployment in one session; (2) provenance-conditioned joint optimization of all trainable policy modules, turning mixed human-policy deployment data into structured source supervision; and (3) real-robot evidence across four manipulation tasks showing improved no-takeover task performance and a declining observed intervention ratio.

title: DepState-JEPA: Learning Depth-Grounded State Representation for Visual Perception and Manipulation
authors: Xiujian Liang,Liuyuan Na,Zehao Du,Jiacheng Xu,Weixi Song,Mingyang Sun,Xingjun Ma,Cewu Lu,Jianhua Sun
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes. Guided by this intuition, we introduce DepState-JEPA, a dual-stream RGB–Depth joint-embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState.
Built on V-JEPA 2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality-private features for decoding.
Ray-conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action-conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features.
Robot-state readouts provide recursive proprioceptive inputs; object-trajectory supervision and calibrated forward kinematics shape state learning through motion targets and joint–TCP consistency.
Comparisons show stronger RGB-encoder transfer after RGB-D adaptation, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth content, metric coordinates, and future-state matching, with additional control gains from FK regularization.
introduction:
Learning visual world models enables anticipation of action outcomes (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Maes et al., 2026).
For manipulation in real-world space, this requires relating the current spatial arrangement to
the changes an action may cause. Consider a robot reaching for a cup:
RGB reveals its appearance and context, while depth locates the cup and
gripper relative to the table in three-dimensional space. Anticipating the reach then requires
reasoning about how this arrangement will change, not merely recognizing
the cup. This raises a broader question: how can the geometry revealed by depth inform a robot’s predictions of how its actions will change the scene?

RGB JEPAs predict representations rather than pixels (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024):
V-JEPA 2 supports action-conditioned planning (Assran et al., 2025),
while V-JEPA 2.1 strengthens dense visual features (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026).
Depth-related JEPAs offer complementary designs. LeMuMo-JEPA combines RGB
and aligned depth features within a common Transformer for multimodal
perception
(Cornelissen et al., 2026).
Locate 3D’s 3D-JEPA predicts masked point-cloud features enriched by lifted
2D features, rather than maintaining separate RGB–depth streams
(Arnaud et al., 2025); JEPADepth predicts depth from RGB with auxiliary
latent supervision, rather than encoding measured depth (Grigore & Popa, 2026).
These designs target multimodal perception or geometric estimation, but do not establish a common state interface between spatial understanding and action-driven evolution. This motivates our work:

Can complementary observations ground a spatially queryable, temporally predictive shared state representation while retaining modality-private features in separate decoding paths?

To answer this question, we introduce DepState-JEPA (Fig. 1),
a joint-embedding predictive architecture centered on DepState,
a depth-grounded shared latent state connecting RGB–depth observations,
spatial readout, and action-conditioned transition. Built on V-JEPA 2.1, an independent
Depth-Video branch provides complementary observations and metric
grounding for both streams. DepState aggregates shared information,
while private paths preserve modality-specific detail for decoding
rather than forming separate evolving states. This common interface
supports reading missing spatial content and forecasting representations
after robot actions.
Representation learning uses images and video; robot prediction
initializes DepState from a single RGB-D frame and evolves it under
actions and proprioception, without accessing future RGB-D images.

Specifically, visible metric depth and camera intrinsics place both streams in metric 3D
coordinates; shared–private projections and learned aggregation form
a compact, geometrically grounded DepState. Ray-conditioned readouts
query local shared features without target depth; private features
supply modality-specific decoding detail. After action-conditioned transitions,
the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features with fixed
initial private memory. Robot-state readouts supply recursive proprioception;
object-motion supervision shapes the state. Calibrated forward kinematics
couples independent joint and end-effector predictions, propagating
consistency gradients into the transition alongside direct physical supervision.

Training proceeds in two stages: 1) RGB-D adaptation learns
DepState from images and video clips via masked shared-feature completion
and dense modality-feature prediction, exploiting spatial and temporal
context. 2) Robot post-training learns
action-conditioned transitions and physical readouts using future-state
and feature targets, physical supervision, and kinematic regularization,
while RGB-D replay retains the adaptation objectives. Evaluation
(Sec. 4) spans
spatial understanding, multi-step forecasting, and manipulation, with
controlled ablations testing the roles of geometry, feature sharing,
and kinematic consistency.
Our contributions are threefold:

Dual-stream RGB–Depth Video JEPA framework.
We introduce DepState-JEPA, which connects spatial understanding and action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState. Independent RGB and depth encoders capture complementary observations, while metric depth grounds both streams in a common 3D coordinate frame.

Dual-stream RGB–Depth Video JEPA framework.
We introduce DepState-JEPA, which connects spatial understanding and action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState. Independent RGB and depth encoders capture complementary observations, while metric depth grounds both streams in a common 3D coordinate frame.

Unified DepState construction and prediction pipeline.
We aggregate shared RGB–depth features into DepState, retaining private features for modality-specific decoding. Ray-conditioned readouts predict missing features without target depth and are reused after action-conditioned transitions to predict future features, with initial private memory fixed throughout rollout. Robot-state readouts supply recursive proprioception; object-trajectory supervision and joint–TCP consistency provide complementary training signals for state evolution.

Empirical gains and controlled component analysis.
RGB-D adaptation improves RGB-encoder transfer; the full pipeline supports feature prediction and manipulation. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth and metric coordinates, private decoding for visual accuracy, and future-state matching for control performance.

We introduce DepState-JEPA, which connects spatial understanding and action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState. Independent RGB and depth encoders capture complementary observations, while metric depth grounds both streams in a common 3D coordinate frame.

2. Unified DepState construction and prediction pipeline.
We aggregate shared RGB–depth features into DepState, retaining private features for modality-specific decoding. Ray-conditioned readouts predict missing features without target depth and are reused after action-conditioned transitions to predict future features, with initial private memory fixed throughout rollout. Robot-state readouts supply recursive proprioception; object-trajectory supervision and joint–TCP consistency provide complementary training signals for state evolution.

3. Empirical gains and controlled component analysis.
RGB-D adaptation improves RGB-encoder transfer; the full pipeline supports feature prediction and manipulation. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth and metric coordinates, private decoding for visual accuracy, and future-state matching for control performance.

title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
authors: Josh Qixuan Sun,Xiaoying Xing,Yurun Chen,Huaiyuan Weng,Wentao Zhu,Mark Crowley
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions.
Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal.
However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history.
We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed.
We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches.
Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history.
We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution.
Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
introduction:
In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) (Krantz et al., 2020), vision-language-action (VLA) models (Zhang et al., 2024) map visual observations and instructions to actions.
Success rate measures whether an agent reaches the goal but does not establish whether it follows the instruction.
Route-fidelity metrics (Jain et al., 2019) assess the similarity between the generated trajectory and the ground-truth trajectory, providing an indirect measure of instruction following.
However, these metrics still cannot establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions, as it may instead rely on visual cues or navigation history alone.

Language interventions, i.e., changing the language instruction and observing how the local actions or navigation performance change, provide a more direct test of language dependence.
NavTrust (Jiang et al., 2026) and Contrast Sets (Anwar et al., 2025) rephrase instructions and assess changes in navigation performance.
However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged.
R2RIE-CE (Taioli et al., 2024) modifies instructions by injecting direction, object, and room errors.
However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them.
Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them.
We therefore ask not merely whether the model’s behaviour changes, but whether changing the instruction to describe another feasible route makes the model more likely to choose the corresponding actions.
We keep the agent’s state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix fixed.
In Figure 1, both turning left and continuing up the stairs are feasible, and the remaining instruction specifies which branch to take.
We use instruction-action binding to describe the requirement that the model assigns higher probability to the actions required by the instruction.

We introduce NavBind, a controlled diagnostic built through cross-route
recombination of route-instruction examples drawn from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
Using fine-grained route-language alignments, we retain one example’s
completed instruction prefix and combine it with either its original suffix
or a compatible suffix from another route.
The resulting full-instruction pairs specify different executable
branches under the same replayed history and agent state, yielding
3,252 contexts with reference action sequences for both branches.

Within each fixed context, we first ask: does changing the instruction
change the action sequence the model generates?
We then ask: does the model assign higher probability to the actions
for a branch when instructed to take that branch rather than the other?
We test this by comparing the likelihood of each reference action
sequence under the two instructions.
This comparison can reveal changes in action preference even when the
generated sequence stays the same.
Finally, we examine the visual response: do attention heatmaps and
gradient-based attribution heatmaps highlight different image regions
under the two instructions?

We evaluate four navigation VLAs on NavBind: Uni-NaVid
(Zhang et al., 2025), StreamVLN (Wei et al., 2025), JanusVLN
(Zeng et al., 2026), and FutureNav (Zhang et al., 2026a).
We find that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
(Table 1).
It also shows that models respond more strongly when the instructions
contrast opposite turns than when they contrast forward movement with a turn.

Our contributions are:

We construct NavBind by recombining instruction segments
across routes into full instructions for two feasible branches.
Each pair preserves the agent state, history, and
completed instruction prefix, and provides reference action
sequences for both branches.

We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated
sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods
to assess preferences for the instructed actions, and attention
and gradient-based attribution heatmaps to track spatial changes.

We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how
language affects local decisions alongside navigation success.

sequences for both branches.

2. We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated
sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods

3. We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how

title: SMR: Learning streaming motion retargeting for humanoids from human semantic
authors: Chun Gu,Juntong Zhang,Jingyu Li,Li Zhang
abstract:
Retargeting human motion to humanoids requires preserving motion semantics
while accounting for the robot’s physical constraints. Kinematic pipelines
prescribe a robot trajectory through geometric matching, without establishing
whether it can be executed under the robot’s dynamics. Prior physics-supervised
neural methods train bidirectional full-sequence models on physics-refined
kinematic trajectories, remaining tied to prescribed kinematic solutions and
requiring noncausal context. We propose SMR, a streaming neural motion
retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts. We convert human
motion into robot-aware task-space targets for body landmark positions,
orientations, and velocities. Physics experts track these targets directly in
simulation under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. We train a single
strictly causal Transformer on their executed state trajectories that complete
the motion and pass semantic and physical validity checks. At each incoming
frame, the student uses only current and past human observations to generate a
robot motion reference for a downstream whole-body controller. Experiments
demonstrate that semantic-conditioned
physics experts generate motion with higher semantic fidelity and physical
validity than direct optimization-based retargeting, while the resulting
streaming retargeter achieves improved closed-loop performance over kinematic
and physics-refined baselines under a common whole-body controller.
introduction:
Large-scale human motion datasets such as AMASS, LAFAN1, and BONES-SEED provide
a rich source of whole-body motion for humanoid learning and control
(Mahmood et al., 2019; Harvey et al., 2020; Bones Studio, 2026). Transferring these
motions to robots requires more than geometric matching because humans and
robots differ in morphology, joint structure, mass distribution, contact
mechanics, and actuation. For streaming applications such as live teleoperation,
retargeting must satisfy two requirements: preserving human motion semantics
in physically executable robot references, and generating those references from
current and past human observations.

The first requirement depends on how robot motion is generated for supervision.
Kinematic retargeting pipelines use inverse kinematics or geometric optimization
to construct robot trajectories
(Penco et al., 2018; Darvish et al., 2019; Araujo et al., 2025). Although these methods
can incorporate contact and collision constraints, geometric agreement alone
does not establish dynamic executability. Using the resulting trajectories as
neural supervision can tie the learned mapping to solutions selected by the
kinematic solver. Physics-supervised methods such as NMR (Zhao et al., 2026)
refine these trajectories through simulated tracking, but still use the
prescribed kinematic motion as the expert’s tracking target. This motivates
specifying the motion to preserve directly through robot-aware task-space
semantics and using the resulting physical execution to generate robot
supervision.

The second requirement is causal inference from a live human stream.
NMR’s learned retargeter (Zhao et al., 2026) uses bidirectional modeling over a
complete motion sequence and therefore depends on future observations. This
prevents use in a streaming setting where the reference at time tt must
be generated from observations available up to tt. The challenge is therefore
to retain the benefits of physics-based supervision while learning a causal
retargeter.

To address these challenges, we propose SMR, a streaming neural motion
retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts. We represent
human motion as robot-aware task-space targets for body landmark positions,
orientations, and velocities. The experts track these targets directly in
closed-loop simulation, using robot state and limited future semantic context
to generate motion under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. IK is
used only for initialization, rather than to prescribe a tracking trajectory.
We retain executed state rollouts that complete the motion and pass semantic
and physical validity checks, and use them to train a single strictly causal
Transformer. At each incoming frame, the student generates a robot motion
reference for a downstream whole-body controller using only current and past
human observations. As summarized in Table 1,
SMR is the only compared method combining dynamics-grounded supervision with
real-time teleoperation.

Experiments show that semantic-conditioned physics experts generate motion
with higher semantic fidelity and physical validity than direct
optimization-based retargeting. Under the same frozen whole-body controller,
SMR achieves improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined
baselines. We further demonstrate whole-body motion execution on a physical
Unitree G1 using SMR-generated references.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) we formulate physics-based retargeting around robot-aware human semantics, allowing experts to determine the robot trajectory instead of refining a prescribed kinematic solution; (2) we distill privileged expert rollouts into a single causal retargeter that generates streaming motion references from human observations, without robot-state inputs or future frames; and (3) we demonstrate improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined baselines under a common frozen controller, alongside whole-body motion demonstrations on a physical Unitree G1.

title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
authors: Junha Chun,Youngjoon Jeong,Taesup Kim
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones.
We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it.
Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy.
We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold.
Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models.
In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy.
Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) have recently become a major paradigm for a robotic foundation model (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Pai et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2026).
They inherit the representations and rich spatiotemporal knowledge from generative backbones with scalable pretraining, predict the future with world modeling objective, and generate actions from the features from the reasoning process.
It has been shown that they improve generalization to out-of-distribution scenes by predicting how the world changes.

However, recent researches question whether the capabilities of WAMs come from explicit test-time prediction or enriched representations from the world modeling, and whether video prediction is a good representational prior or objective for world modeling.
FastWAM finds that representational gains from world modeling, rather than explicit future generation at test time, is the main contributor of WAM’s performance (Yuan et al., 2026).
Furthermore, ImageWAM shows image editors as backbones led to significant improvements to the policy generalization from edit-aware representation which contain task-relevant visual changes and is evidenced by attention maps (Zhang et al., 2026b). We therefore ask:

Which geometric structure makes a backbone’s representational prior useful for WAM generalization, and how does policy adaptation transform that structure?

Understanding this question is necessary to explain why some inherited representations support stronger generalization. Inspired by the baseline WAMs and fundamental questions about their representations and performances, we start by analyzing the representational geometry of in- and out-of-distribution observations.

Throughout the paper, we introduce nuisance orthogonality, which characterized the geometric separation between feature displacement from visual variations and the empirical in-distribution manifold.
High nuisance orthogonality therefore measures a potential for disentangled representational prior which presents in the generative backbones before policy training.
We show that nuisance orthogonality is highly related to the generalization performance of WAMs, across visual variations and models, allowing prospective diagnostics of world models.
Furthermore, we present nuisance suppression after policy training, a suppressing behavior of residual displacement so that the policy can remove nuisance information, improve scene retrieval, and enable robust action generation.

Our contributions are as follows:

A geometric characterization of representational priors: Nuisance orthogonality, the fraction of feature displacement orthogonal to the empirical span of in-distribution data, quantifying whether a backbone separates action preserving visual changes from directions that distinguish clean scenes.

An evidence from nuisance orthogonality to policy robustness: Across world model comparisons, higher nuisance orthogonality is associated with stronger downstream visual robustness motivating a diagnostic for assessing world model backbones before WAM policy training.

An analysis on how representations reshape after policy adaptation: We introduce nuisance suppression to measure how representation space change after adaptation, showing that more robust policy exhibits stronger and more consistent nuisance suppression.

1. A geometric characterization of representational priors: Nuisance orthogonality, the fraction of feature displacement orthogonal to the empirical span of in-distribution data, quantifying whether a backbone separates action preserving visual changes from directions that distinguish clean scenes.

2. An evidence from nuisance orthogonality to policy robustness: Across world model comparisons, higher nuisance orthogonality is associated with stronger downstream visual robustness motivating a diagnostic for assessing world model backbones before WAM policy training.

3. An analysis on how representations reshape after policy adaptation: We introduce nuisance suppression to measure how representation space change after adaptation, showing that more robust policy exhibits stronger and more consistent nuisance suppression.

title: SimPT: An Automated Simulation Framework for Intervention-Based VLA Post-Training
authors: Caicheng Wang,Zipeng Ye,Zhexuan Zhou,Zilong Huang,Xi Zhang,Yuchen Xie
abstract:
Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision–language–action
(VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision
and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and
development. We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a
simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training
by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy
training, and standalone evaluation. To automatically determine
intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled
Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state
and retains stable snapshots during policy execution. After a rollout
fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots,
starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as
needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four
post-training methods, RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO, across seven
RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Relative to a fixed-interval snapshot
baseline, the Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts by 75.0% and
increases recovery success from 93.4% to 98.9%. Using SimPT, we develop
RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting and
low-pass filtering of value predictions. This refinement increases the
overall success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials.
In real-robot HIL post-training, it increases the success rate from 72%
to 96% across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. These
results demonstrate the utility of SimPT for exploring and developing
VLA post-training algorithms.
introduction:
Generalist vision–language–action (VLA) policies map visual observations
and language instructions directly to robot actions
[1, 2]. When these policies
encounter states outside the demonstration distribution, or
out-of-distribution (OOD) states, they may produce inappropriate actions
[3]. Such errors can drive the robot further from the
demonstration distribution and compound over time [4].
Human-in-the-loop (HIL) robot learning addresses this problem through expert
takeover, using corrective demonstrations to update the policy
[5, 6, 7]. However, developing
HIL algorithms on physical robots requires substantial human effort to
collect corrections and repeated hardware use for evaluation. Environmental
variation further complicates reproducible comparisons
[8]. These costs and sources of variability limit systematic
exploration and development of HIL post-training algorithms.

Simulation offers controllable scenes, repeatable trials, and scalable data
collection for developing and evaluating HIL algorithms before hardware
experiments
[9, 10].
Platforms such as RoboTwin [11] and SIMPLER
[8] support demonstration generation, policy evaluation, and
sim-to-real research, while automated HIL post-training remains comparatively
underexplored. IntervenGen extends simulation-based data generation to
corrective behavior by expanding a small set of human interventions into
synthetic recovery trajectories, but relies on human experts to determine
when and how to intervene in the initial recovery demonstrations
[12].
Automating these decisions in simulation requires selecting suitable recovery
states along a failed policy rollout and determining how an expert should
complete the task from those states. Both depend on task progress.
Vision-language models (VLMs) can monitor execution, but repeated visual
queries incur inference overhead [13]. CuRobo-based scripted
experts can execute predefined task sequences from initial states
[14], but the motion planner itself does not infer
task progress or select corrective actions for states reached by the policy.

Motivated by these challenges, we introduce SimPT, a simulation
framework that integrates policy rollouts, automated corrective data
collection, policy training, and
standalone evaluation to support the exploration and development of VLA
post-training algorithms (Fig. 1). To guide recovery, an agent
compiles task information into an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph.
During policy execution, the graph tracks task progress through fixed checks
on privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots without further
agent queries. After rollout failure, SimPT attempts expert recovery from
snapshots at more advanced task stages and falls back to earlier ones as
needed. A CuRobo-based expert resumes
execution from each restored state, and successful recovery trajectories
are retained for policy post-training.

Using SimPT, we implement and compare HG-DAgger [6],
RECAP [15], DPO+SFT [16], and
FlowPRO [17] on seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. In
independent data collections, the Progress Graph requires 75.0% fewer
recovery attempts than a fixed-interval snapshot baseline. We further use
SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines
cross-fitting (CF) and Butterworth low-pass filtering (LPF) of value
predictions. This combined refinement increases the overall
success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. Applied
to real-robot HIL post-training, it increases success from 72% to 96%
across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task.
Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce SimPT, a simulation framework that automates the
intervention-based VLA post-training workflow to support systematic
algorithm exploration and development.

We develop the Agent-Compiled Progress Graph to track task progress
and retain stable snapshots during policy execution. After rollout failure,
expert recovery starts from more advanced task stages and falls back to
earlier ones as needed.

We compare four post-training methods on seven RoboTwin tasks
and use SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF. By combining cross-fitting and
low-pass filtering, this refinement improves policy success in both
simulation and real-robot HIL post-training.

1. We introduce SimPT, a simulation framework that automates the
intervention-based VLA post-training workflow to support systematic
algorithm exploration and development.

2. We develop the Agent-Compiled Progress Graph to track task progress
and retain stable snapshots during policy execution. After rollout failure,
expert recovery starts from more advanced task stages and falls back to
earlier ones as needed.

3. We compare four post-training methods on seven RoboTwin tasks
and use SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF. By combining cross-fitting and
low-pass filtering, this refinement improves policy success in both
simulation and real-robot HIL post-training.

title: State-Dependent Objective Coordination for End-to-End Balance and Navigation
authors: Xuhao Huang,Xitao Xu,Yuxin Zheng,Yunfan Ren,Zheng Gong
abstract: Traditional robotic navigation systems separate mapping, planning, and low-level control through cascaded modules, introducing computational overhead and accumulated latency. End-to-end reinforcement learning offers a compact unified policy that maps onboard observations directly to control actions. However, on inherently unstable platforms such as two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robots, navigation progress and obstacle avoidance can conflict with attitude stabilization in a strongly state-dependent manner. We propose a lightweight state-dependent objective coordination method for integrated navigation and control. A pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient β⁡(s)∈[0,1]\beta(s)\in[0,1] adjusts the relative contributions of balance stabilization and navigation objectives during training, without extra control hierarchies or auxiliary attitude-stabilization controllers, such as proportional–integral–derivative (PID) or linear–quadratic regulator (LQR) controllers. To support zero-shot deployment, simulation training models execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. Gradient analysis reveals persistent directional interference and state-dependent variation in the objectives’ relative scales. Comparisons with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies show that PPO+β⁡(s)\beta(s), where PPO denotes proximal policy optimization, achieves 98% and 95% success rates with small attitude excursions on the fixed obstacle map and the randomly generated high-obstacle-density map, respectively. Zero-shot hardware experiments further demonstrate bounded attitude behavior and consistent obstacle avoidance using only onboard observations. Training and evaluation code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
introduction:
Real-world robot deployment increasingly requires compact control policies that satisfy multiple objectives within a single dynamical system under limited onboard computation and strict latency constraints. In strongly coupled robotic systems, these objectives may induce state-dependent conflicts, where an action that improves one objective can degrade another. Modular or hierarchical frameworks usually handle such interactions through interfaces between perception, planning, navigation, and low-level control [1, 2, 3]. However, when multiple objectives share the same control inputs and are jointly constrained by system recoverability, interface-level coordination may lead to inconsistent or overly conservative behavior.

We study this problem on a two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robot that must maintain attitude stability while performing goal-directed obstacle-avoiding navigation. Navigation progress, obstacle avoidance, and attitude stabilization all act through the same wheel-torque commands. Near the upright state, excessive emphasis on stabilization may suppress effective navigation. At larger attitude deviations, aggressive navigation and avoidance actions may reduce recoverability and increase the risk of falling. Therefore, the appropriate balance between stabilization and navigation varies with the current attitude state.

A fixed reward coefficient applies the same objective weighting across states and therefore cannot explicitly adapt to state-dependent attitude risk. A large stabilization weight may be overly conservative near the upright state, whereas a small weight may provide insufficient stabilization as attitude risk increases. Structural alternatives, such as stage-wise training, hierarchical control, and policy composition, do not necessarily adjust this trade-off according to the current attitude state.

To address this issue, we propose state-dependent objective coordination through a state-conditioned scalarization coefficient β⁡(s)∈[0,1]\beta(s)\in[0,1]. During training, β⁡(s)\beta(s) adjusts the relative contributions of balance stabilization and navigation progress according to the robot’s pitch magnitude. Navigation receives greater relative emphasis near the upright state, while stabilization is progressively emphasized as the pitch deviation grows. The coefficient is used only for reward construction during training. At deployment, a single end-to-end actor maps onboard observations directly to wheel torques without online reward computation, policy switching, or an auxiliary stabilizing controller.

We further incorporate deployment-relevant discrepancies into simulation training, including execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. The resulting actor is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and directly transferred to the physical robot without policy adaptation, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate simultaneous balance and obstacle-avoiding navigation as a state-dependent objective coordination problem and introduce a pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient β⁡(s)\beta(s) for training a unified end-to-end policy.

We empirically analyze the interaction between the balance and navigation objectives through gradient direction and relative scale, and compare the proposed method with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies.

We demonstrate zero-shot transfer of the learned actor from simulation to a physical two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robot under matched obstacle-avoidance tasks.

1. We formulate simultaneous balance and obstacle-avoiding navigation as a state-dependent objective coordination problem and introduce a pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient β⁡(s)\beta(s) for training a unified end-to-end policy.

2. We empirically analyze the interaction between the balance and navigation objectives through gradient direction and relative scale, and compare the proposed method with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies.

3. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer of the learned actor from simulation to a physical two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robot under matched obstacle-avoidance tasks.

title: Learning to Absorb Corrections: Critic-Weighted Residual Flow for Vision-Based Insertion
authors: Yiqing Yuan,Zhi Li,Jinrong Yang,Mingshan Sun,Mei Yu Zhi,Yong Zhao,Liangliang Ren,Hui Cheng
abstract: Vision-based insertion requires correcting alignment errors while retaining useful behavior learned from demonstrations. We present ACT–Flow, an online learning framework that couples an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided warmup, ACT absorbs successful executed actions through behavioral cloning, while residual targets are recomputed relative to the updated prior. A chunk-level critic learns from successful and failed interactions and evaluates final composed actions. Its estimates weight generated residual candidates for flow matching, complemented by supervision from successful real executions. Candidate scoring is confined to training; deployment uses RGB observations and samples one residual per action chunk. We evaluate the framework on power-plug, USB, and key insertion, together with cable routing and needle threading. Results show a five-task mean success rate of 66% at 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, exceeding the strongest baseline by 18 percentage points at this checkpoint. Evaluations at matched checkpoints with the residual disabled show ACT’s mean success increasing from 16% to 76%. Component ablations further support the complementary roles of behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.
introduction:
Vision-based insertion requires a robot to correct alignment errors during execution. Inserting a power plug, USB connector, or key can fail when small position or orientation errors persist, or when the target moves after the initial approach. Demonstration-trained policies, including Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) [1] and Diffusion Policy [2], provide effective action priors. However, limited demonstrations cannot cover every state encountered during deployment, and deviations from the training distribution can compound [3]. This motivates a policy that can both correct execution errors and incorporate successful corrections into its learned behavior.

Existing methods obtain corrective guidance from demonstrations or human intervention. DOME [4], MILES [5], and AutoSERL [6] use demonstrations to guide visual alignment, recovery, or automatic intervention. HIL-SERL [7] incorporates human corrections into reinforcement learning (RL), while CR-DAgger [8] learns residual policies from compliant corrections. Demonstration-guidance mechanisms depend on available reference behavior, while human corrections require operator effort. Beyond obtaining guidance, a further question is how the robot should represent corrections and retain the useful behavior they produce.

Residual adaptation provides a natural representation: a base policy supplies nominal behavior and an additional policy learns corrections [9, 8, 10, 11]. FlowDAgger [12] similarly steers a frozen generative policy through its latent variables. A frozen prior provides a stable basis for adaptation, but successful corrections remain in the additional module rather than becoming part of the prior itself. The central question is: how can a robot learn effective insertion corrections from interaction and absorb successful corrected behavior into an improving action prior?

Joint prior–residual learning raises two issues. Updating the prior changes the residual needed to reproduce a successful action, making historical labels inconsistent. Critic estimates rank corrections but cannot replace observed successful actions as supervision. Learning must combine these signals while tracking the evolving prior. Retaining successful executed actions provides a stable reference: their decomposition can change as the prior improves, while their role as observed targets is preserved.

We present ACT–Flow, an online framework for vision-based insertion that coordinates an adaptive ACT prior with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided demonstration and correction warmup, successful executed actions update ACT through behavioral cloning (BC), while residual targets are recomputed against the updated ACT to preserve consistent supervision. To combine value guidance with observed successful behavior, residual learning couples critic-weighted flow matching (FM) [13] on generated candidates with FM on successful executions. The critic learns from both outcomes and scores composed actions.

We evaluate three insertion tasks—power-plug, USB, and key insertion—plus cable routing and needle threading. Comparisons and ablations examine adaptation, behavior absorption, and residual supervision. Our contributions are:

An online learning framework for vision-based insertion connecting an ACT prior and residual flow policy through anchor-guided initialization, online correction, and successful-experience feedback.

A behavior-absorption mechanism that updates ACT from successful actions and relabels residual targets under the current prior, keeping correction supervision consistent as the base policy changes.

Critic-weighted residual flow learning that combines value-weighted fitting of generated corrections with FM supervision from successful executed actions.

Comparisons on three real-world insertion tasks and two additional manipulation tasks, supported by component ablations and diagnostics of base-policy improvement, residual contribution, and critic ranking quality.

1. An online learning framework for vision-based insertion connecting an ACT prior and residual flow policy through anchor-guided initialization, online correction, and successful-experience feedback.

2. A behavior-absorption mechanism that updates ACT from successful actions and relabels residual targets under the current prior, keeping correction supervision consistent as the base policy changes.

3. Critic-weighted residual flow learning that combines value-weighted fitting of generated corrections with FM supervision from successful executed actions.

4. Comparisons on three real-world insertion tasks and two additional manipulation tasks, supported by component ablations and diagnostics of base-policy improvement, residual contribution, and critic ranking quality.

title: PHD-Hand: A Printable Humanoid Dexterous Hand with Linkage-Driven 3-DOA Digits
authors: Neel Adwani,Muhaiminul Islam Akash,Saffia Ouali,Ethan Liu,Cong Wang
comment: Submitted and Accepted at IEEE-RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids 2026). . Supplementary video:this https URL
abstract:
Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work.
As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention.
Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication.
Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge. Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer. This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation. In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.
introduction:
This paper discusses the design of linkage-driven dexterous humanoid robot hands.
With the recent breakthroughs in perception and reasoning powered by artificial intelligence (AI), replicating the dexterity of human hands is increasingly considered the last physical bottleneck that holds back the robotics industry.
Having humanoid dexterous hands not only allows robots to seamlessly handle objects in our daily lives, but also enables robot learning of hand skills directly from native human demonstration.
Other than resembling the appearance of human palm and digits11
1
            
            
          In human anatomy, the thumb is not a finger - i.e., a regular human hand has five digits, including one thumb and four fingers.,
a humanoid robot hand ideally should have at least three degrees of actuation (DOA)22
2
            
            
          Because of the complex kinematics of dexterous robot hands, the term “degrees of freedom (DOF)” has been used to indicate quite different meanings in the literature.
Instead, we have found “degrees of actuation (DOA)” to be a more precise term.

per digit.
The “root joint” of a digit should have two DOAs for tilting, while the “upper two joints’’33
3
            
            
          For a finger, the root joint is an MCP joint, and the upper two joints include a PIP joint and a DIP joint.
For the thumb, the root joint is a CMC joint, and the upper two joints include an MCP joint and an IP joint.
To keep the narrative concise and friendly to a broader audience, instead of the anatomical terminology, we use the terms “root joint” and “upper two joints” in this paper.

almost always flex/extend together and share a single DOA44
4
            
            
          The thumb actually moves differently from the fingers, though the difference is not that significant.
.

A straightforward way to build such a digit is to place the actuators inside or on the digits to drive the joints “locally” with a structure similar to serial robot manipulators (e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4]).
This results in a dilemma of the digit either having weak actuation or being oversize and overweight.
It is therefore desirable to have the actuators placed off the digits, which requires additional drivetrain(s) to deliver actuation to the upper two joints.
The most common solution is to use tendon drives.
The design is largely inspired by human anatomy and has been the mainstream choice of dexterous robot hands [5].
However, without self-healing, the complex tendon systems required for dexterity wear out and loosen up quickly, which leads to demanding maintenance and short life span [6].
Performance of tendon-driven hands is often jeopardized by cable fraying, knot slippage, and tension drift [7][8].
In particular, cable rupture is the top failure mode [8].
In addition, tendon-driven bidirectional actuation requires either two actuators per DOA (leads to sizing problems) or closed-loop tendon routing (prone to loosening and slacking) [9].
The absence of bidirectional actuation excludes the hand from performing certain skills.

Compared to tendon-drives, rigid drivetrains do not have weaknesses mentioned above.
They also provide better precision and can bear higher load [10].
Some designs use geared drivetrains to transmit actuation from actuators placed off the digit to the upper two joints.
[11] shows a representative design in this category.
Each of its digits has a 2-DOA root joint and 1-DOA coupled upper two joints.
Actuation is transmitted to the upper two joints using a bevel gear drive coaxially located with the drive shafts of the root joint. Other than the fabrication hassle and inevitable backlash, complexity of the design results in a hand size significantly larger than human hands.

Alternatively, linkage-driven designs have the potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon and gear-based designs [12].
However, integrating three DOAs with linkage drivetrains in one digit (while keeping the actuators off the digit) poses a great challenge for design and fabrication.
There are only a few presentations [13, 14, 15, 16, 17], which share similar designs and have only emerged over recent years.
Among them, the design presented in [13] is both pioneering and most ready for practical use.
It adopts a novel 5-joint linkage drivetrain to deliver actuation to the upper two joints through the root joint (Fig. 1-a, the portion circled in red).
As impressive as the prototype and demonstration are, the nontrivial number of miniature parts (Fig. 1-b) require serious fabrication capability and make it challenging to balance between durability, size, and cost.
The prototype in [13] has a hand length around 218 mm which is 13% larger than average male human hands.
The design is replicated in [14] and improved in [15] with hand lengths of 255 mm and 219 mm respectively.
In addition, the kinematics of the root joint and upper two joints is partially coupled, which complicates the control.
More details of these designs will be examined later in Section II with a summarizing comparison to our work.
Some other designs work around the challenge by strategically reducing the number of DOAs based on human hand synergies - e.g., [18, 19, 20, 21].
Despite being able to realize a decent variety of hand functions, the strategy does not provide the potential of advanced dexterity that the robotics community is currently wishing for.

Our work aims at developing a dexterous humanoid robot hand that

Has five digits with three DOAs per digit (two for the root joint, one for the coupled upper two joints);

Has each DOA bidirectionally actuated with a decent strength, good backdrivability, and minimal backlash;

Can be fabricated at a size very close to human hands with minimal costs using a budget 3D printer;

Has long-lasting durability and requires minimal maintenance.

This paper continues from our earlier publication [22], which introduces the flexure design of the root joint and presents a preliminary prototype of three digits, together with strength test results.
Our prior work suffers from a series of problems, including mechanical interference, non-humanoid topology, and fabrication complications.
The new design in this paper resolves those problems and demonstrates legitimate humanoid dexterity.
In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.

1. Has five digits with three DOAs per digit (two for the root joint, one for the coupled upper two joints);

2. Has each DOA bidirectionally actuated with a decent strength, good backdrivability, and minimal backlash;

3. Can be fabricated at a size very close to human hands with minimal costs using a budget 3D printer;

4. Has long-lasting durability and requires minimal maintenance.

title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
authors: Weizhe Xu,Jialiang Fan,Essien Taylor,Zijun Wang,Russell Joseph,Fanxin Kong
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)
abstract:
Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints.
Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can
provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats.
Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space.
In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge.
Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources.
To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness.
The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment.
We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm.
Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B–14B planners to 70.5–76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85–26.41 W of average power.
Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
introduction:
Robotic task planning converts a high-level goal into an executable sequence of actions [1].
In safety-critical settings, reaching the goal is not enough: every intermediate state must also satisfy requirements such as ordering, mutual exclusion, and resource constraints [2, 3].
A plan that eventually places an object correctly can still be unacceptable if it enters a restricted region, manipulates a fragile object in the wrong order, or violates a required inspection step.
We therefore study safety-constrained task planning: generating plans that are executable and goal-reaching while satisfying explicit trajectory-level constraints.

Classical planners offer a principled solution when a correct symbolic task specification is available.
Systems such as Fast Downward and OPTIC search over states defined by action preconditions and effects [4, 5]; PDDL3 expresses trajectory constraints, and tools such as VAL check a candidate plan against the formal specification [6, 7].
This formal structure provides an auditable safety criterion, but it comes with two practical costs.
First, tasks in complicated environments can induce exponentially growing search spaces as the number of objects and planning horizon increase, making symbolic search difficult to scale [8].
Second, users must provide rigid symbolic inputs and carefully engineered domain specifications.
Imitation and reinforcement learning can amortize planning into compact policies [9, 10, 11, 12].
However, learned policies are commonly tied to particular task distributions, and their outputs do not inherit a formal guarantee without an explicit specification and verifier.

LLM planners offer a complementary strength: they can interpret high-level
task descriptions and directly generate candidate action
sequences [13, 14].
Recent systems ground language into symbolic specifications or integrate LLMs
with planners and formal verifiers [15, 16, 17].
An inference-time verifier can reject an invalid plan
and prompt the model to revise it [18, 19].
However, this process leaves the base planner unchanged, so repeated failures
increase token usage, latency, and computation.
Moreover, general-purpose LLMs can be too large for memory- and power-limited
robot computers.
These limitations motivate a planner that combines safety-aware plan
generation, compact local inference, and flexible task interfaces.

We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework for this combination.
Rather than keeping the verifier only in the inference loop, SLoSa uses formal feedback to change the compact planner itself.
First, SLoSa constructs behavior-changing safety-aware training data by retaining planning instances in which the supplied constraint rejects the baseline plan while a verified alternative remains feasible.
Second, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts compact, quantized LLMs using the verified plans.
Third, verifier-guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the planner with a reward hierarchy that separates unparseable outputs, precondition violations, safety violations, goal failures, and successful plans.
At inference, SLoSa combines local plan generation with verifier feedback to enforce the supplied safety constraints while reducing the tokens spent on iterative repair.

We evaluate SLoSa using three compact open-source LLM backbones across four PDDL domains that cover manipulation, transportation, object transfer, and tool use, together with separately trained planners for safety-adapted VirtualHome and ALFWorld to evaluate the applicability of the same post-training pipeline beyond PDDL-based planning.
The results show consistent improvements from safety-aware post-training
across model sizes, task domains, and input representations.
We further evaluate local inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4080 and a Jetson Orin,
and demonstrate the complete vision-grounded planning pipeline on a desktop
6-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) robotic arm.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework that
improves compact LLM planners through behavior-changing safety-aware data
construction, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning, and
verifier-guided GRPO.

We construct safety-constrained evaluation tasks spanning four PDDL planning domains and two adapted household simulation benchmarks, with formally verified plans and task-specific trajectory constraints.

We conduct extensive experiments across multiple model sizes, task
domains, and input representations, showing consistent improvements from
safety-aware post-training. We further validate local edge deployment,
verifier-guided inference, and physical robotic-arm execution.

1. We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework that
improves compact LLM planners through behavior-changing safety-aware data
construction, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning, and
verifier-guided GRPO.

2. We construct safety-constrained evaluation tasks spanning four PDDL planning domains and two adapted household simulation benchmarks, with formally verified plans and task-specific trajectory constraints.

3. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple model sizes, task
domains, and input representations, showing consistent improvements from
safety-aware post-training. We further validate local edge deployment,
verifier-guided inference, and physical robotic-arm execution.

title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning
authors: Yash Rampuria,Rohan Garg,Daniele Gammelli,Marco Pavone
abstract:
Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry
and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown
environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL
training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing
and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot
deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a
few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated
graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.
introduction:
Progress in mobile robotics has been driven by a small set of design tools that became shared infrastructure, including occupancy grids for planning [1], GPU elevation mapping for locomotion [2], OpenCV for perception [3], PyTorch for learning [4], and massively parallel simulators for RL [5]. Each is valuable because one implementation serves both deployment on a robot and training in simulation, so improvements on either side transfer.

Graphs have long been used for robot planning. A navigation graph stores sparse collision-free nodes connected by traversable edges, and nodes can carry frontiers, traversability, semantics or learned scores. Such graphs underpin classical exploration planners [6, 7, 8] and a line of learned policies that reason over the graph with Graph Neural Networks [9, 10, 11]. Despite this, no shared tool builds and maintains these graphs. Deployment planners construct them inside planner-specific, single-robot code. Learning pipelines rebuild them for every environment on the CPU, so a 16-worker training run spends much of its wall-clock time maintaining graphs rather than learning. GPU graph libraries [12, 13] target fixed graphs consumed by a model, not graphs that grow and are merged and re-scored at every step of a rollout.

To address this gap, we present GGraph, a GPU-resident navigation-graph library that serves as one design tool for both deployment and learning (Fig. 1). GGraph takes occupancy grids or elevation maps as input. It samples collision-free waypoints, merges them incrementally into a persistent world-frame graph with stable node identities, and attaches per-node attributes through a layer system. Shortest paths, connectivity and frontiers are all available as CUDA tensors. The same implementation serves single-robot deployment through ROS 2 and policy learning across many parallel environments.

Building such a library raises some technical challenges. First, the graph changes at every step, as each observation adds a varying number of nodes and edges that must be merged into a graph already covering the explored world. Second, existing graph builders rely on sequential data structures, such as priority queues and per-node objects, that cannot run in parallel on a GPU. Third, learning requires hundreds of such graphs, each growing at a different rate, to be updated together. Fourth, on a real robot the graph must survive loop closure, which moves every node placed since the drift began. GGraph stores each graph as parallel tensors with stable node identities, so adding, merging, pruning and correcting nodes are single vectorized operations. It merges each observation with one batched nearest-neighbor assignment and one line-of-sight kernel over all candidate edges. It also reformulates graph search as edge-parallel Bellman–Ford and pointer-jumping connected components, running one robot or NN environments through the same kernels. The novel contribution of GGraph is to make the navigation graph itself a batched, GPU-resident, loop-closure-aware data structure shared by deployment and learning. To our knowledge, no other library provides this capability. Our contributions are:

An open-source GPU navigation-graph library. An
extensible layer system stores geometric, semantic and learned
attributes per node, and ROS 2 and batched interfaces let the same code
serve deployment and learning (Sec. IV-A).

An open-source GPU navigation-graph library. An
extensible layer system stores geometric, semantic and learned
attributes per node, and ROS 2 and batched interfaces let the same code
serve deployment and learning (Sec. IV-A).

Validation in robot deployment and policy learning. We use GGraph to build 3-D graphs from real-world sensor data, attach frontier and semantic layers, and correct the whole graph after loop closure in one vectorized pass. Used as a batched RL environment, GGraph trains graph-based exploration policies that reach the quality of prior learned policies in a fraction of the training time and outperform baselines on held-out maps, on a ground vehicle in a high-fidelity simulator, and on a real robot (Secs. V-A and V-B).

Scalability benchmarks. Graph updates take just tens of milliseconds as graphs grow to a million nodes, and environment-step throughput scales with the number of parallel robots, reaching 27×\times that of a SoTA baseline (Secs. V-A3 and V-B1).

title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
authors: Jonas Eschmann,Giuseppe Loianno
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: Accepted at Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20×20\times faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
introduction:
In recent years, imitation learning from human demonstrations has become a dominant method for advanced learning-based control of robots. This is particularly the case in the field of manipulation [1, 2, 3] and locomotion [4, 5]. Conversely, for aerial vehicle autonomy, imitation learning from human demonstrations has not experienced comparable widespread adoption. In the case of quadrotors, in particular, two major trends have been imitation learning from (privileged) expert policies [6, 7, 8] and using pre-trained models as vision encoders [9, 10]. The latter promise to bring broader generalization by virtue of having been pre-trained on massive amounts of real-world images collected from the internet.

Imitation learning from human demonstrations and pre-trained vision models are motivated and driven by scaling laws that were first observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) [11]. Early indications hint that similar scaling laws might exist in robot imitation learning [12]. The potential that scaling robot imitation data could bear similarly large returns as LLM scaling, has led to the formation of a large number of commercial robot imitation data creation/curation companies. These companies also bet on monopolizing forces known as the “data flywheels” [13] limiting accessibility while the capital expenditure (CAPEX) requirement for large-scale robot data collection is by itself already a major hurdle for reproducibility and progress in the community.

The alternative is training robot control policies entirely in simulation without requiring real-world data. Not only are methods fully trained on synthetic data more accessible to fellow researchers, but they are also more introspectable. Due to the lack of interpretability of deep neural networks, in general we cannot get strong guarantees for learned end-to-end controllers. The best way to reason about the behavior of the trained control policy is through introspection of the data that went into training it. For vision foundation models [14, 15, 16, 17] this data is usually proprietary, hampering reproducibility, interpretability of the resulting behavior and the opportunity for independent researchers to study effects of modifying the data distribution.

To accelerate the research of vision-based aerial vehicle control we present the following contributions:

HyperDrone: An extremely fast simulator for training end-to-end visual control policies. HyperDrone consists of:

HyperLux: A fast, large-batch ray-tracing renderer for RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception

Highly optimized multirotor dynamics simulation

Sim2Real Transfer of a yaw-control policy trained entirely in simulation

1. HyperLux: A fast, large-batch ray-tracing renderer for RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception

2. Highly optimized multirotor dynamics simulation
