title: COWBOY: A Scalable Sim-to-Real Framework for Learning Contextual Whole-Body Manipulation
authors: Jiahui Yang,Jason Jingzhou Liu,Ray Muxin Liu,Andrew E. Wang,Kenneth Shaw,Deepak Pathak,Ruslan Salakhutdinov
abstract:
Mobile manipulators must adapt not only to objects, but also to the spatial context in which they appear: where to position the base, how to manipulate, and where to look while navigating surrounding scene geometry. To address this, we present COWBOY, a scalable sim-to-real framework for learning such contextual whole-body manipulation. On whole-body dexterous grasping, COWBOY transfers zero-shot to hundreds of objects and diverse in-the-wild scenes, spanning cluttered tabletops, shelves, drawers, and other unstructured settings.
Rather than learning scene adaptation directly with RL in simulation, a vectorized environment-aware whole-body controller (WBC) handles reaching in thousands of scenes by coordinating base-arm motion, collision avoidance, and active vision. Then, local RL experts are trained in local scenes for object interaction and can be reused across thousands of full-scene layouts. We distill these composed WBC–RL teachers into a single vision policy that controls the mobile base, arm, dexterous hand, and actuated camera from point-cloud observations. The resulting policy exhibits contextual whole-body behavior, automatically adapting base placement, camera viewpoint, arm trajectory, and grasp strategy to observed scene and object geometry. Videos are available at cowboy-manip.com
introduction:
Humans effortlessly interact with diverse environments and objects in their daily lives. A person reaching for the same object may move very differently depending on whether it lies on an open tabletop, inside a shelf, behind clutter, or within a drawer. These behaviors rely on whole-body adaptation: people reposition their body, adjust their viewpoint, and coordinate their arms and hands to maintain visibility and avoid obstacles.

Similarly, deploying robots in everyday environments requires policies that generalize not only across objects, but also across the spatial contexts in which those objects appear. For mobile manipulators, this is further complicated by partial observability, since onboard sensors provide only an incomplete view of the scene. From this context alone, the robot must coordinate its base, arm, and camera to reach the object, maintain visibility, and avoid collisions. We refer to this scene-conditioned whole-body reasoning capability as contextual whole-body manipulation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation is a promising approach for learning
contextual whole-body manipulation as diverse training scenarios can be generated at scale. Recent sim-to-real manipulation systems have demonstrated impressive generalization across large object sets; however, they typically do not generalize across diverse environments and are often trained in a single fixed setting [26, 37]. Training mobile manipulation policies across varied environments remains challenging because it requires global scene understanding beyond local object interactions, often over high-dimensional spatial representations. This complicates both policy conditioning and reward specification. The difficulty is exacerbated by the high-dimensional action spaces of mobile manipulators, requiring coordination of the base, arm, and perception.

To this end, we present COWBOY, a sim-to-real framework for training mobile manipulation skills across thousands of diverse environments and hundreds of objects, enabling contextual whole-body manipulation learning at scale. Our framework first proposes a vectorized, environment-aware whole-body controller (WBC) that operates across many scenes on a single GPU. Given only an end-effector goal, the WBC coordinates base-arm motion to reach the target while avoiding obstacles in the scene. It also controls an actuated neck to maintain visibility to the object.

Our WBC enables us to decompose contextual whole-body manipulation into two stages: global free-space reaching and local interaction. First, the WBC brings the end-effector near a target object while avoiding obstacles and maintaining gaze on the object. Then, for each desired manipulation behavior, we train a local RL policy
to learn interactions across hundreds of objects. Since each RL policy only needs to handle one type of local manipulation behavior, policy conditioning and reward specification become tractable. Finally, we distill both the WBC reaching behavior and the state-based local policies into a unified vision-based whole-body policy. Importantly, during distillation, we reuse each local policy by generating thousands of full-scene layouts around the local scene, enabling scalable training across diverse scenes and objects.

We demonstrate COWBOY on whole-body dexterous grasping with a mobile manipulator equipped with a 16-DoF hand and an actuated neck for active vision. COWBOY achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, robustly grasping hundreds of geometrically diverse objects across in-the-wild settings, including shelves, drawers, and cluttered tabletops. The policy generates adaptive, context-dependent behaviors, coordinating approach direction, base placement, camera viewpoint, grasp strategy, and collision-avoiding motion from the surrounding scene. Ablations validate the key design choices of our framework and show that they are critical for robust in-the-wild mobile manipulation.

title: One Policy, Many Styles: Where to Aggregate Preferences for Steerable Humanoid Control?
authors: Ziqian Huang,Yuzhuo Chen,Shimin Zhang,Junyang He,Xinyue Annie Yang,Animesh Garg
abstract: Modern robotic agents are increasingly expected to support steerable control, where a single policy can adjust its behavioral style at runtime under changing user preferences. Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning provides this interface, but conditioning alone does not ensure that a requested behavior change is strong, does not leak into unrelated behaviors, and does not compromise task performance. Our evaluation combines Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) with coverage and utility metrics. We use these measures to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. No aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria. Experiments show that aggregating objectives early produces a wider range of behavioral responses but greater unintended changes in other objectives, while aggregating them later improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.
introduction:
Robotic and embodied agents are increasingly expected to operate under changing user preferences and behavioral constraints. A household robot may need to prioritize speed in one setting, energy efficiency in another, or smooth and safe motion around humans. Rather than training separate policies for every trade-off, an ideal system should support steerable control, where behavior can be adjusted at runtime through a compact and interpretable preference interface.

Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) provides a natural framework for this problem by representing behavior through multiple reward dimensions and conditioning a policy on a preference vector which specifies desired objective trade-offs (Basaklar et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2025). This enables one policy to expose a continuous control interface at test time, but conditioning alone does not guarantee steerability. Increasing one preference may produce little change in the intended behavior, produce unintended behaviors, or compromise the essential tasks that the robot must continue to perform.

This distinction is not captured by aggregate return or Pareto-coverage measures alone (de las Heras Molins et al., 2026).
A useful evaluation should answer three questions: Does the policy respond strongly when a preference changes? Does the change unintentionally affect other behaviors? Does the policy still perform the task reliably without more failures? We therefore formulate preference-conditioned steerability as a multidimensional evaluation problem and introduce a unified suite based on the Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) matrix, Self-PRR, Cross-PRR, Selectivity, and Rank Accuracy. These metrics complement standard utility measures by exposing both intended responsiveness and cross-objective leakage (de las Heras Molins et al., 2026).

pWe compare reward, advantage, and loss-level scalarization within PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) across two independently implemented humanoid-control systems, ProtoMotions (Tessler et al., 2025) and MimicKit (Peng, 2025), to test whether the findings generalize across implementations. Within ProtoMotions, we additionally test PCGrad-based gradient surgery (Yu et al., 2020) as a later aggregation point that resolves objective conflicts directly in gradient space. Reward-level aggregation achieves the widest controllable range in ProtoMotions, whereas later aggregation achieves higher hypervolume in fixed-direction MimicKit. Its weaker cross-objective precision persists across both frameworks, but these experiments do not isolate the cause of their different coverage rankings. A preliminary check in MetaDrive (Li et al., 2023), a driving domain, shows a broadly similar pattern.

Our contributions are:

We formulate preference-conditioned robot steerability as a multidimensional evaluation problem that separates responsiveness, monotonicity, selectivity, task preservation, and failure behavior.

We present a framework that trains preference-conditioned policies under different PPO-based aggregation strategies and evaluates their steerability using the suite above, validated across two independently implemented humanoid-control systems.

We show that the payoff from aggregating preferences early depends on the experimental setting: coverage and utility rankings differ across frameworks, while later aggregation consistently yields higher selectivity and lower cross-objective leakage.

Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Pref-Align-RL-214C/.

title: Navigation Explainability for Object Avoidance with LLMs for Assistive Robots
authors: Courtney Young,Yi Lian,Taery Kim,Sehoon Ha
abstract:
Blind and visually impaired individuals face uncertainty when navigating unfamiliar areas. Whether a cane or a guide dog is used for navigation, this may prove to be challenging.
To mitigate this challenge, we present the Context-Aware Navigation Explanation framework that explains guide dog movements for obstacle avoidance and navigation using a large language model.
This system integrates perceptual context with planned future trajectories to generate natural-language explanations of robot movement.
We deploy the system on a Unitree Go2 platform in indoor navigation scenarios and evaluate how different explanation context configurations affect user trust and explanation satisfaction. Results show a strong positive relationship between explanation satisfaction and trust, and suggest that combining obstacle information with future trajectory leads to the most effective explanations. These findings highlight the potential of context-aware language explanations to improve transparency and trust in assistive robot navigation.
introduction:
Guide dogs can substantially improve the quality of life for blind and visually impaired (BVI) individuals [1, 2]. However, high training costs and short service lives limit access to approximately 2% of the BVI population [3]. To address this gap, researchers have developed guide robots in both wheeled and quadrupedal forms as potential assistive alternatives that can expand accessibility and complement animal guides [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Although these systems have shown promise, successful deployment in real-world environments depends not only on navigation capability, but also on whether users can understand the robot’s behavior, trust its decisions, and interact with it comfortably [9, 10, 11, 12].

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and speech interfaces
create new opportunities for assistive navigation robots to interpret their surroundings and communicate their intent with natural language. This capability is especially important in BVI navigation, where users may not directly inspect the environment or infer why the robot is adjusting its path. However, it remains unclear which natural-language explanations are most effective in helping BVI users understand the robot’s behavior and build trust during navigation.

This study investigates how differences in robot guide dog navigation explanations affect user trust. We hypothesize that changes in the content and quality of LLM-generated comments, driven by different input context configurations, will lead to corresponding differences in trust.

We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework (Fig. 1), which generates real-time natural language explanations of a robot guide dog’s navigation behavior. This framework constructs a structured textual context by integrating detected obstacle information with future waypoints from a navigation planner over a short temporal window, then provides this context to an LLM to generate explanations of the robot’s current intent. By varying the amount and type of information included in this context, we evaluate how context design influences explanation satisfaction and overall system trust through a user study.

Our results show a strong positive correlation between explanation satisfaction and trust, indicating that satisfying explanations are closely associated with increased user trust. We also observe that the condition combining obstacle information and future trajectory, with a moderate explanation frequency, generally received the highest ratings for both satisfaction and trust, outperforming both the no-future-trajectory and higher-frequency conditions. Item-level analysis further reveals that users particularly value explanations that are informative and complete to their goals.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework that integrates perception and future trajectory information to generate real-time natural language explanations for assistive navigation.

We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework that integrates perception and future trajectory information to generate real-time natural language explanations for assistive navigation.

We investigate how different types and amounts of contextual information affect explanation satisfaction and user trust through a controlled user study.

We show that combining obstacle awareness with future navigation intent improves both explanation satisfaction and perceived trust compared to limited-context explanations.

We provide insights into which aspects of explanations (e.g., completeness, usefulness, informativeness) most influence user trust in assistive navigation settings.

1. We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework that integrates perception and future trajectory information to generate real-time natural language explanations for assistive navigation.

2. We investigate how different types and amounts of contextual information affect explanation satisfaction and user trust through a controlled user study.

3. We show that combining obstacle awareness with future navigation intent improves both explanation satisfaction and perceived trust compared to limited-context explanations.

4. We provide insights into which aspects of explanations (e.g., completeness, usefulness, informativeness) most influence user trust in assistive navigation settings.

title: Learning Dynamic Games for Cooperative Iterative Tasks
authors: Mark Pustilnik,Francesco Borrelli
abstract: We consider cooperative and iterative tasks involving multiple agents whose interactions are modeled as a dynamic game with shared constraints. We propose a general learning framework applicable to nonlinear and nonconvex dynamic games that uses previously executed feasible trajectories to construct a sampled joint safe set and player-specific cost-to-go functions. At each time step, the agents jointly select a previously sampled terminal state and a Generalized Nash equilibrium used to reach it. A new solution is adopted only if it satisfies a cooperative acceptance rule agreed upon by the players. The framework accommodates individual non-degradation requirements and selection criteria such as weighted costs and Nash bargaining. We show that the proposed framework guarantees recursive feasibility and characterize conditions under which each player’s cost is non-increasing across iterations.
introduction:
Many robotic systems repeatedly perform cooperative tasks from identical initial conditions, including payload transport and coordinated assembly using multiple manipulators. Previous executions provide trajectory data that can improve subsequent performance. Although
the agents cooperate, each may retain its own dynamics, constraints, and objective, while shared constraints couple their decisions. Dynamic games model these interactions. Learning Model Predictive Control (LMPC) exploits repeated single agent tasks by constructing terminal safe sets and cost-to-go functions from successful trajectories, enabling improvement while preserving recursive feasibility [1]. Extending this principle to dynamic games requires addressing multiple equilibria with different player trade-offs: improving one player’s cost may worsen another’s. Learning must therefore determine both how to improve previously executed trajectories and how the players agree on which new solution to adopt. In this work, we consider cooperative iterative tasks in which the players agree in advance on rules for selecting new solutions.
Cooperation does not require a common objective: each player retains its individual cost function, while candidate solutions are evaluated according to a jointly agreed criterion. Individual non-degradation can determine admissibility, while weighted costs or Nash bargaining (NB) select among admissible candidates. We propose a general learning framework for dynamic games where each agent uses previously executed feasible joint trajectories to construct a sampled joint safe set. At each time step, candidate solutions connect the current joint state to a previously visited joint state, after which the remainder of a trajectory from a previous successful iteration can be reused. Since the terminal state is selected from a finite set of previously sampled states, the learning problem naturally includes a discrete decision layer in addition to the continuous dynamic-game equilibrium computation.

The framework accommodates nonlinear dynamics and nonconvex costs and constraints, starting from an initial successful feasible trajectory. The resulting performance depends on the initial trajectory, sampled states, and candidates returned by the game solver. The contributions of this paper are:

A learning framework for cooperative iterative dynamic games with shared constraints, jointly selecting terminal occurrences and equilibrium candidates using a pre-agreed cooperative rule.

Recursive-feasibility and individual non-degradation guarantees under stated conditions, supported by an explicitly retained feasible continuation.

A nonlinear, nonconvex three-player demonstration comparing equilibrium exploration and cooperative selection under shared collision-avoidance constraints.

title: Flexible Language-Guided Representation Editing for Adaptive Robot Behavior
authors: Audrey Lee,Nathaniel Dennler,Ilia Sucholutsky,Andreea Bobu
comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX.
abstract: Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (Flex), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot’s internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate Flex on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that Flex achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/.
introduction:
Imagine a scenario like in Fig. 1, where a human asks their personal robot to bring them coffee. While the instruction seems simple, executing it well depends on the features, or measurable properties of the environment, that the robot internally uses to represent the task. For example, a user may prefer that the robot stays away from sensitive electronics or that it stays close to the table to avoid damage from spills. Unfortunately, human instructions rarely describe these features explicitly when specifying tasks, forcing the robot to guess which features matter. When the robot guesses incorrectly, the human and robot end up with misaligned representations, and the robot fails to complete the task in the way that the human desires.

A common approach to address the representation misalignment problem is to iterate between specifying features and optimizing reward, often through demonstrations [39, 29]. However, demonstrations carry little semantic information, so the robot can only implicitly recover which features actually matter to the user. In contrast, natural language contains rich semantic content. When a user says, “Don’t spill coffee on my laptop!” their language communicates both what matters about the task (avoiding the laptop) and why that matters (preventing damage). Language contains the semantic content that demonstrations lack. We therefore propose that feature specification is better addressed through language, while demonstrations are better-suited for reward optimization once the right features are known.

Even a simple language correction contains a wealth of information when interpreted in context. However, existing methods fail to leverage this fully, either failing to update the robot’s underlying representation in a generalizable way [41] or continually adding features until representations become redundant and inefficient [39]. None of these methods account for the full space of ways a feature representation can be wrong: it may be incomplete (missing relevant features), over-specified (tracking irrelevant features), or incorrectly abstracted (tracking a feature at the wrong level of abstraction).

We propose Flex, a flexible feature editing pipeline that uses Language Models (LMs) to adapt a robot’s internal representation of task features in response to natural language corrections. As shown in Fig. 1, when the human says “Don’t spill coffee on my laptop!”, Flex identifies the correction’s intent and applies three operations: Add introduces the laptop as a relevant obstacle, Generalize broadens the newly added feature to all electronics, and Mask removes the now-irrelevant bowl feature. This yields a feature set aligned with the human’s true intent. Unlike prior methods that support only a single operation, Flex selectively applies whichever combination of edits the user’s language correction warrants.

title: inr2action: Encoding Robot Episodes as Neural Implicit Representations for Recall and Action
authors: Leann Alhashishi,Christos Margadji,Sebastian William Pattinson
abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean R2R^{2} of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.
introduction:
Robots that operate over extended horizons must remember what they have observed.
When the information that determines the correct action has already left the field of view, a robot without memory can only guess.
In robotic manipulation, the evidence that resolves such a decision can lie seconds, minutes, or in long-horizon deployments hours in the past, and by then the scene itself may no longer show it: a quantity that accumulated over time, a property visible only before it was occluded, a reference fixed at the outset of the episode.
Feeding the entire observation stream back into the policy is not a general answer, as its cost scales with how long the robot has been running rather than with how much of what it saw actually needs to be remembered.
We consider such settings non-Markovian, as the information needed at time tt is distributed across the episode rather than contained in any single frame, a gap that recent benchmarks make explicit [1].
Throughout, memory refers to a persistent representation of information that can be accessed independently of the original input that produced it.

Existing sequence models hold information in one of three places.
The first is transient activations: an LSTM’s hidden state [2] or a transformer’s key-value cache [3] compresses observed history, but the stored information is bound to the current computation, and once the forward pass ends or the context window closes it cannot be queried on its own terms.
The second is explicit external storage, from differentiable memory matrices [4] to retrieval over document collections [5], which decouples storage capacity from model capacity at the cost of memory becoming a record that must be retrieved before reasoning can proceed.
A third and more recent paradigm encodes memory directly into parameters: Titans [6] updates a dedicated memory module’s weights during inference, and GradMem [7] performs test-time gradient descent on learnable memory tokens, both showing that gradient-based optimization at inference time can construct persistent memory for a model.
These methods, however, have been developed primarily for language sequences, and they continually update a single running memory over an incoming stream rather than representing individual experiences as separable memories.

In this work, each robot episode is encoded as its own parameter-space memory: a neural implicit representation (INR) fitted to the episode from a shared meta-learned initialization, whose weights constitute the memory.
A learned projector maps these weights into token embeddings for a language model, which answers natural-language questions about the episode, and the same tokens condition an action decoder that predicts the robot’s next joint command.
No frame is stored, reconstructed, or retrieved at query time.
We evaluate on RoboMME [1], a benchmark of 16 non-Markovian manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory, and show that a memory encoded in this way is legible to a downstream model without frame re-access.
The contributions of this work are:

A formulation of episodic memory for robotics as INR weights, and a tensor-wise projector mapping them into the token space of pre-trained language backbones, yielding, to our knowledge, the first system to answer natural-language questions about a video episode from INR weights alone.

An action decoder of the same weight-tokens that regresses the robot’s optimal next joint command, extending weight-space memory from recall to action.

Matched noise and within-task controls, together with an initialization ablation, attributing both question answering and action decoding to episode content and establishing the shared meta-learned origin as the condition that renders the weights decodable.

title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
authors: Matthew Strong,Ankush K. Dhawan,Julien Poffet,Giuse Pham,Jinho So,Monroe Kennedy III
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Matthew Strong and Ankush K. Dhawan contributed equally. Project page:this https URL
abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine’s tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.
introduction:
End-to-end robot learning maps pixels to actions in closed loop and is a promising route for robots that take on everyday tasks [1], but it is data hungry. Vision-language-action (VLA) models are pretrained on more than a million robot trajectories [2], and Diffusion Policy [3] still needs on the order of a hundred demonstrations per task. Robot data has two costs – every trajectory requires human time, and every new object instance requires data collection on that instance, so hundreds of demonstrations of a single object will not generalize to other objects of the same type.

Teleoperation [4] is physically grounded but difficult to scale, and each alternative does not address every flaw. Demonstration augmentation [5, 6] still starts from some teleoperation and needs privileged state or accurate 3D observations. Simulated collection [7] needs modeled assets and a human in the loop, and handheld grippers [8] require custom hardware and hundreds of demonstrations per task. Human video [9, 10, 11] must first be annotated with states and actions, which requires motion-capture and depth hardware [12] or for rendering the robot into inpainted 2D frames [13], where objects cannot be moved from their motion in video. Imprecise recovered object motion compounds into drifting poses and implausible geometry (Fig. 2) that are insufficient for a source of data.

Real-to-sim-to-real pipelines reconstruct real objects, recover their motion from a video, and render robot demonstrations in simulation with no robot in the loop. Real2Render2Real (R2R2R) [14] showed that one smartphone scan and one RGB video suffice to fine-tune a VLA, but it augments spatially, not semantically. For example, their exact mug and coffee machine in a human demonstration must be present at deployment, and covering more objects means a scan and a demonstration for every pairing. Digital cousins [15, 16] substitute similar simulated assets, but overall similarity does not say where a mug should rest on a new coffee machine. Humans know a mug is lifted by its handle and set on a platform. Given one human video of a mug placed on a coffee machine, why can’t a policy succeed on mugs and coffee machines it has never seen?

The first step is recovering object trajectories. The strongest pose estimators assume a depth sensor [17], and RGB-only trackers drift or fail at initialization on textureless objects. We track each object with a DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splat [18, 19], optimizing its pose against feature, photometric, silhouette, and monocular depth-ranking losses from an initialization seeded on the table plane. The grasp comes from the demonstrator’s hand via HaMeR [20], following the method in Phantom [13].

The second step is augmentation. Beyond perturbing object poses, we add semantic and functional augmentation. Cousins are generated with MV-SAM3D [21] from one or several images (online, AI-generated, or real photos), and distilled with DINOv3 features. A semantic alignment registers each cousin to the demonstrated object, and for functional placement/motion, a weighted alignment registers each functional and target object by its region of interaction rather than its whole body, so augmentation extends beyond single-object pick-and-place.

Finally, an interactive viewer can be employed to build the simulated scene, a camera optimization matches the simulated camera to the real one without AprilTags, and parallel generation in photorealistic IsaacSim [22], or MuJoCo [23], generates over 2,000 episodes in about two hours, after about 25 minutes of setup, with no human in the loop. Among prior methods (Table I), ours is the only one that transfers demonstrations across object instances from a single monocular RGB video.

We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), summarized in Fig. 1. Our contributions are:

An RGB-only 4D object tracker on DINO-distilled Gaussian splats that outperforms prior methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth;

An RGB-only 4D object tracker on DINO-distilled Gaussian splats that outperforms prior methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth;

A semantic alignment of digital cousins for whole objects and functional placement/motion regions, producing demonstrations for every cousin pairing;

Fast, parallel generation in MuJoCo or IsaacSim, enabled by an interactive scene creation tool that ports directly to simulation; and

Nearly 2,000 real rollouts on two robots, where a VLA trained on data from one human video per task matches or outperforms two hours of teleoperation.

title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
authors: Kaichen Zhou,Yuzhen Chen,Hannah Yao,Chonghe Jiang,Rao Fu,Xihang Yu,Wei Dai,Bashar Kabbarah,Haoyu Chen,Ishita Goluguri,Zhiyang Dou,Haonan Chen,Fangneng Zhan,Mengyu Wang,Wojciech Matusik,Antonio Torralba,Paul Pu Liang
abstract:
In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan.
Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task.
We introduce T-WLA, a world–language–action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction.
At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation.
The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch.
Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction.
We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks.
T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks.
Videos and codes are available at the project website.

Keywords: Robot foundation models; Vision–language–action models (VLA); World-action models (WAM); Visuotactile Manipulation; Residual Action Correction.
introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation refers to tasks whose success depends on precisely managing physical contact with objects or the surrounding environment (Hogan, 2022; Lee et al., 2019).
Tactile feedback complements vision by revealing local contact conditions that are difficult to infer from images alone (Niu et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026b).
For example, when inserting a plug into a socket, vision guides alignment and approach, while touch provides feedback on contact and insertion resistance.
Because these conditions can change between visual updates, tactile feedback supports rapid corrections to the ongoing motion.

Despite the importance of tactile feedback in contact-rich manipulation, many general-purpose robot policies rely primarily on vision.
Vision–language–action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision–language backbones to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions (Kim et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).
World–action models further integrate future-state prediction with action generation, linking control decisions to the anticipated evolution of the environment (Zhang et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2026).
Without tactile feedback, these models must infer local contact conditions from visual cues, which may limit their response to visually subtle contact changes during precise manipulation.

Recent work incorporates tactile feedback into robot control through variable-rate expert architectures (Niu et al., 2026), residual adaptation (Wang et al., 2026), and inference-time policy steering (Wu et al., 2026b). We investigate a complementary question: how can fast tactile feedback correct a slow visual policy between visual updates? Our central idea is to generate asynchronous tactile corrections conditioned on persistent visual memory. The visual branch processes RGB observations at 39.7 Hz, producing a base action chunk and a history-aware visual memory at each update. The tactile branch processes touch at 119.1 Hz, combining recent tactile context with the cached visual memory and the active action chunk to predict residual corrections to its remaining, unexecuted actions. This allows contact feedback to refine ongoing motion without waiting for the next visual update or rerunning the visual branch.

We instantiate this idea in T-WLA, a multi-rate architecture for asynchronous visual–tactile control
(Fig. 1).
The visual branch generates an action chunk and a history-aware visual representation, which is cached until the next visual update.
Between these updates, a lightweight tactile editor combines the cached representation with recent tactile observations to produce high-frequency residual corrections to the ongoing action chunk.
This separation allows the controller to respond to changing contact conditions without repeatedly running the visual branch.
During training, future-image and future-pressure prediction regularize the control representations, encouraging them to capture information relevant to subsequent interactions.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Memory-guided asynchronous control.
We propose T-WLA, which uses the same history-aware visual memory to guide base-action generation and tactile correction.
A lightweight tactile editor uses this memory and the active action chunk to correct unexecuted actions between visual updates, without rerunning the visual branch.

Memory-guided asynchronous control.
We propose T-WLA, which uses the same history-aware visual memory to guide base-action generation and tactile correction.
A lightweight tactile editor uses this memory and the active action chunk to correct unexecuted actions between visual updates, without rerunning the visual branch.

Predictive supervision for control.
We regularize the visual memory through future-image prediction and the tactile features through both future-image and future-pressure prediction.
These auxiliary objectives complement action supervision, and their prediction heads are removed at inference.

Evaluation across hand-motion prediction and robot manipulation.
Experiments on EgoTouch and Tachin show improved finger-joint prediction accuracy, while real-robot tests show that T-WLA increases mean task success from 17.0% to 50.0%. Ablations examine the contributions of tactile input, visual history, and predictive supervision.

title: VeriCalib: Verifiable Target-Based LiDAR-Camera Calibration
authors: Xiangcheng Hu,Xieyuanli Chen,Feiyi Chen,Shengli Ren,Shiyang Chen,Guoqiang Ye,Hao Wang,Ping Tan,Steven L. Waslander,Fuchun Sun,Jin Wu
abstract:
Target-based extrinsic calibration estimates the rigid transform between sensors from a few observations of a known target, and its result is commonly assessed by the root-mean-square error of the fitted residuals. However, this scalar error is computed on the same observations and therefore cannot indicate whether to accept the result, re-extract, recollect or add observations.
This paper presents VeriCalib, which formulates extrinsic calibration as a verifiable estimation problem and reports a calibration state.
The key insight is a two-level extrinsic compensation mechanism, in which the extrinsic compensates the rigid part of each observation error at the residual level, and rotation and translation compensate each other at the parameter level. Consequently, the fitted residual can reveal neither an inconsistency between the observations and the model nor whether the estimated extrinsic is reliable in every direction.
Accordingly, we assess the calibration through a structured covariance that jointly propagates the uncertainty of the camera and LiDAR board features with a known-geometry prior, and estimate its scale as a variance component from the residuals. On this covariance, we decouple rotation and translation to resolve the precision along each direction and guide data collection toward the weakest one. Since this precision presumes consistent observations, we further develop within-view and cross-view checks that examine the internal residual and the rigid discrepancy between observations, respectively, with thresholds that hold their significance level under an unknown noise level. We also extend the minimal detectable bias to the extrinsic to bound the smallest detectable fault along each direction. These criteria form a calibration state that indicates whether to accept the result or how to collect the data.
Experiments in simulation and on real-world robot platforms show that the structured covariance predicts the observed estimation scatter, and that weakest-direction acquisition meets a strict rotation requirement with up to 30%30\% fewer observations than D-, A-, and E-optimal designs. Under an unknown noise magnitude, the consistency checks detect faulty observations while removing few fault-free ones, unlike robust estimators with fixed thresholds. Cross-session validation further confirms a verified calibration state.
The code and datasets will be released to support the future research of verifiable state estimation.11

introduction:
Extrinsic calibration, which estimates the rigid transform
between two sensor frames, is a core problem in multi-sensor robotics perception.
Every fused measurement passes through this transform,
and its error propagates into dependent tasks as a systematic bias.
Such a bias degrades perception and planning
in autonomous driving (Bai et al., 2022; Dong et al., 2023),
grasping on embodied platforms (Fang et al., 2023),
and the trajectory and map references used for evaluation (Hu et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025a).
Among sensor pairs, the LiDAR-camera pair is widely adopted,
as it combines 3D geometry with 2D visual
semantics (Lin and Zhang, 2022; Koide et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025).
Its extrinsic is commonly estimated from a calibration target with a known pattern,
such as a checkerboard or a circular-hole board,
which provides well-defined cross-modal
correspondences (Mirzaei et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2018a; Beltrán et al., 2022; Zheng and Zhang, 2026; Hu, 2026).

As there is no external ground truth, the calibration result is commonly assessed by the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of its fitted residuals (Domhof et al., 2019; Zheng and Zhang, 2026), its consistency (Yuan et al., 2021), or covariance (Brookshire and Teller, 2012; Pandey et al., 2015; Yamada and Yaguchi, 2024).
Figure 1 illustrates the gap: on a set with two extraction errors, a conventional pipeline returns a residual, whereas our method identifies the inconsistent observations and reports a calibration state.
Learning-based assessments likewise return only a binary label (Tahiraj et al., 2025) or a conformal interval (Cocheteux et al., 2025), and neither specifies the corrective action that a failed calibration requires. Consequently, a large residual provides no criterion
for choosing among accepting the result, re-extracting the features,
recollecting the observations, and adding observations, and even in mass-production calibration the number and placement of targets are determined empirically.

We formulate this task as the verifiable calibration problem,
which assesses whether the estimated extrinsic satisfies given
precision and detection requirements
and determines the subsequent calibration action accordingly.
Solving this problem involves three challenges.

Independent and nominal noise modeling.
Existing uncertainty-aware calibration methods (Koo et al., 2020; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020; Brookshire and Teller, 2012) model the target features as independent measurements with a nominal noise magnitude. However, the camera features on one board share the estimated board pose, the LiDAR features share the fitted board plane, and the actual noise magnitude varies across sensors and scenes. As a result, the reported precision and the test thresholds do not match the actual uncertainty, leading to overconfident acceptance or to the rejection of consistent observations.

Independent and nominal noise modeling.
Existing uncertainty-aware calibration methods (Koo et al., 2020; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020; Brookshire and Teller, 2012) model the target features as independent measurements with a nominal noise magnitude. However, the camera features on one board share the estimated board pose, the LiDAR features share the fitted board plane, and the actual noise magnitude varies across sensors and scenes. As a result, the reported precision and the test thresholds do not match the actual uncertainty, leading to overconfident acceptance or to the rejection of consistent observations.

Coupled constraint analysis.
Existing observability analyses of calibration (Mirzaei et al., 2012; Lv et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023) verify only that the extrinsic is observable and, like degeneracy analyses in LiDAR registration (Zhang et al., 2016; Tuna et al., 2024), do not account for the compensation between rotation and translation. As a small rotation and a compensating translation yield nearly the same target observations, this compensation masks weakly constrained directions. Data collection is thus left without a criterion for which target pose to add and when the collected poses suffice.

Insufficient model consistency assessment.
Real target observations contain gross errors such as mis-extracted features and wrong correspondences. Existing calibration methods reject them by fixed robust thresholds (Beltrán et al., 2022; Zheng and Zhang, 2026; Wiesmann et al., 2024), without a stated significance level or a bound on the smallest fault that passes undetected, which reliability analyses provide only for individual measurements (Baarda, 1968; Abdul Hafez et al., 2025). A faulty observation can therefore pass undetected and bias the accepted extrinsic, whereas a consistent one can be discarded.

The three analyses depend on one another, since the precision and thresholds rest on the covariance and all three presume consistent observations, whereas existing pipelines address them separately through a scalar residual. We therefore represent the observation as a unified structured measurement factor, its residual together with the covariance and the local Jacobian, and resolve the dependence by first selecting the consistent observations under a robust working scale and then evaluating the scale, the directional precision, and the detection limits on the selected set (Sections 5.5 and 7.2). Figure 2 follows this procedure on the head pair, from the factor of each observation to the calibration state that feeds back into data collection.

This paper presents VeriCalib, which formulates target-based extrinsic calibration as a verifiable estimation problem on the structured measurement factor. We identify the root cause that prevents a scalar calibration residual from revealing the extrinsic state as a two-level extrinsic compensation (Section 4). At the residual level, the extrinsic absorbs the rigid part of each observation error, and at the parameter level, rotation and translation compensate each other, so that neither a small residual nor an aligned projection implies an accurate extrinsic. Whereas geodetic reliability analyzes the redundancy of individual measurements (Förstner, 1987), this mechanism acts on the rigid-body extrinsic and its coupled rotation and translation, and it determines how the observations of a calibration are weighted, which target poses the calibration requires, and which faults it can detect.

Our first contribution (Section 5) is a structured covariance model for target observations, on which every reported precision, threshold, and detection limit rests. Unlike independent feature covariances of nominal magnitude, its shape is derived from the measurement model of each sensor, through the shared board pose in the camera side and the shared board plane with a known-geometry prior in the LiDAR side (Sections 5.2 and 5.3), and its scale is estimated from the absorbed residual components, which alone determine the estimate (Section 5.5). We further quantify the precision gain of the weighted over the unweighted solver (Theorem 1).

As the precision of a calibration is limited by its weakest direction, our second contribution (Section 6) resolves the precision of the extrinsic by physical direction. Marginalizing the compensation between rotation and translation from the information of this covariance yields directional precisions and a weakest-direction score for selecting the next target pose (Section 6.2). Its closed form for the four-hole target further shows that a common increase of the board distance leaves the rotation precision invariant (Section 6.1).

Directional precision holds only for observations consistent with the model. To this end, our third contribution (Section 7) is a model consistency assessment with directional detection limits. A within-view check tests the internal residual of each observation, and a cross-view check tests its agreement with the remaining observations, both at a significance level that holds under an unknown noise magnitude (Sections 7.1 and 7.2). We further extend the minimal detectable bias (MDB) of geodetic reliability (Baarda, 1968; Teunissen, 2018) from individual measurements to the directions of the extrinsic, which is, to the best of our knowledge, the first direction-resolved detection limit for target-based calibration (Section 7.4). The three analyses combine into a calibration state, each value of which indicates the next calibration action (Section 7.5).

The framework requires only a target-specific factor construction, which we provide for circular-hole and checkerboard targets (Section 3.3).
Section 2 reviews related work and Section 3 formulates the problem.
Section 4 analyzes the two-level compensation, and Sections 5, 6 and 7 develop the first three contributions in turn. Section 8 reports the experiments in simulation and on real-world data, Section 9 discusses the results and the scope of the verification,
and Section 10 concludes the paper.

Existing uncertainty-aware calibration methods (Koo et al., 2020; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020; Brookshire and Teller, 2012) model the target features as independent measurements with a nominal noise magnitude. However, the camera features on one board share the estimated board pose, the LiDAR features share the fitted board plane, and the actual noise magnitude varies across sensors and scenes. As a result, the reported precision and the test thresholds do not match the actual uncertainty, leading to overconfident acceptance or to the rejection of consistent observations.

Existing observability analyses of calibration (Mirzaei et al., 2012; Lv et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023) verify only that the extrinsic is observable and, like degeneracy analyses in LiDAR registration (Zhang et al., 2016; Tuna et al., 2024), do not account for the compensation between rotation and translation. As a small rotation and a compensating translation yield nearly the same target observations, this compensation masks weakly constrained directions. Data collection is thus left without a criterion for which target pose to add and when the collected poses suffice.

3. Insufficient model consistency assessment.
Real target observations contain gross errors such as mis-extracted features and wrong correspondences. Existing calibration methods reject them by fixed robust thresholds (Beltrán et al., 2022; Zheng and Zhang, 2026; Wiesmann et al., 2024), without a stated significance level or a bound on the smallest fault that passes undetected, which reliability analyses provide only for individual measurements (Baarda, 1968; Abdul Hafez et al., 2025). A faulty observation can therefore pass undetected and bias the accepted extrinsic, whereas a consistent one can be discarded.

title: Learning-Enhanced Observer for Sensorless Task-Null-Space Compliant Control
authors: Nuo Chen,Ya-Jun Pan,Onur Toker
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives. Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics. Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance. The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.
introduction:
Physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) has received increasing attention due to the need of humans and robots to share the same workspace. Compared with traditional robotic tasks, pHRI requires the robot to achieve two different objectives at the same time. On one hand, the robot should accurately complete its task, such as position, orientation, and force tracking. On the other hand, it should remain compliant when unexpected human interaction occurs to ensure safety. Therefore, an effective pHRI framework should provide accurate task execution, reliable interaction state estimation, and compliant response to human disturbances.

Force control is necessary for robotic tasks which involve physical contact with humans or the environment. In literature, commonly used force control approaches include the direct force control [4], hybrid position and force control [5, 11], impedance control [19], and admittance control [16, 23]. The hybrid position and force control usually regulates motion and interaction force in different task directions, while the impedance and admittance control regulate the relationship between the motion and force. Some recent studies have combined these control strategies to achieve both accurate force tracking and compliant motion. Hybrid force-impedance controllers were developed to achieve force tracking during fast end-effector motions [14] and large force pulling [25]. In [10], a framework to combine force regulation and compliant behavior within a passivity formulation is presented. In [29], an impedance-admittance framework to improve compliance and adaptability in changing conditions is proposed. These studies have shown the effectiveness of hybrid control in different interaction tasks. However, the force regulation and compliant control often require a reliable interaction force measurements from force and torque sensors.

Access to the interaction force is an important part of pHRI. Force and torque sensors can provide direct measurements of external wrench [13, 1], but they often increase the hardware cost and may not be available in all robotic systems. Force/torque measurements often are noisy and need signal processing before applied to the controller. Observers provide an alternative solution by estimating end-effector wrench from robot dynamics and available joint motion [3]. Among them, momentum observers are commonly used because they do not require noisy acceleration [18, 9]. However, the estimation accuracy may be affected by joint friction, unmodeled dynamics, and control errors [15]. To address these limitations, recent studies have applied adaptive [21] and learning-based compensation [17] to improve the estimation performance. Moreover, for redundant manipulators, external disturbances may generate joint motion that does not contribute to the task-space motion [27]. Such motion can appear in the null-space while the end-effector task remains almost unchanged [28]. However, conventional momentum observers are usually constructed using the overall joint motion, meaning that the human null-space motion may be incorrectly reflected in the task-space estimation. This issue is especially important in pHRI, where human applied disturbance cannot be fully rejected but should be handled differently from the task-related motion.

In pHRI, robustness and compliance are often treated as two independent objectives. Robust controllers are designed to reject external disturbances and maintain accurate task execution, while compliant controllers allow the robot to respond compliantly to human and/or the environment interaction. Most existing approaches mainly focus on designing different controllers and switching between them according to different states [2, 26, 8, 31], making it difficult to achieve both tracking and disturbance rejection objectives at the same time. Moreover, many studies on the pose and force control are conducted on 2D-flat surfaces [30, 22, 12], limiting their applicability to real-world tasks. Motivated by these challenges, we aim to achieve the robust end-effector task performance while allowing a compliant motion under human applied disturbance. For a redundant manipulator, human interaction can be accommodated through null-space motion without changing the desired end-effector behavior. The overview of the proposed framework is illustrated in Fig. 1. The proposed framework consists of an observer module and a hybrid controller for simultaneous task execution and compliant pHRI. The observer combines a conventional momentum observer with a task-null-space decomposition and neural-network (NN) compensation to estimate the end-effector interaction force while reducing the influence of null-space human disturbances. Based on the estimated force, the controller integrates position, orientation, and force tracking with task-space admittance and null-space compliant control to generate the commanded torque, enabling a desired robust task-space performance together with a compliant interaction with human.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A new NN-enhanced momentum observer with task-null-space interaction decomposition is proposed for sensorless external force estimation. The NN compensates for observation errors caused by joint friction and model uncertainties. The proposed decomposition separates the estimated task-space force from null-space human interactions. Compared with the learning-based observer in [4] and [17], this design eliminates the influence of null-space disturbances on the NN-enhanced observer.

A hybrid pose and force controller is developed by integrating the Cartesian position and orientation tracking, force regulation, task-space admittance control, and null-space compliant control. Unlike the 2D-flat surface tasks in [30] and [22], the proposed controller enables the simultaneous position, orientation, and force tracking on a 3D-curved surface. Meanwhile, it achieves a compliant behavior to ensure both task robustness and pHRI safety at the same time instead of the need of mode switching as presented in [2] and [31], which may cause instability.

The proposed observer-controller framework is evaluated on a 7-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Franka Emika Panda robot. Experimental results under different trajectories and interaction scenarios demonstrate an improved force estimation performance, accurate pose and force tracking, and effective compliant responses in null-space.

In summary, the proposed approach offers a new and feasible solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements. As a result, the new framework can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which often do not have force/torque sensors. One example is that for underwater robotic manipulators, it is challenging to install force/torque sensors at the end-effector in the underwater environment.

title: Human-Robot Interaction via Meta-Learning Based Mode Recognition and Adaptive Control
authors: Nuo Chen,Ya-Jun Pan
abstract: In human-robot interaction (HRI) tasks, humans may interact with the robot in either an active guiding or passive following state, resulting in distinct control objectives for each interaction mode. Most existing approaches rely on predefined switching thresholds to distinguish interaction modes, but their performance can be sensitive to measurement noise. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. First, a neural network (NN) trained via meta-learning is developed to recognize human intention without manually defined thresholds. By successfully incorporating force-dependent parameters from the controller, the recognition rates are improved from 90.1% to 99.1% for the passive mode and from 79.8% to 97.1% for the active mode. Second, an adaptive meta-learning controller is introduced to compensate for human disturbances and enable online adaptation to varying interaction forces. Third, a multiple-trajectory meta-learning algorithm is designed to jointly learn an environment-basis representation and force-dependent parameters, allowing the controller to deal with unmodeled dynamics efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust and accurate control performance, while providing reliable mode recognition for safe and adaptive physical HRI.
introduction:
Traditional robot control and HRI primarily focus on precise motion planning and execution, relying on closed-loop control methods grounded in system dynamics and high-precision sensor feedback. The rapid advancement of technologies such as deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable advantages in intelligent control, particularly for systems with high degree-of-freedom (DOF) and in complex environments. However, these approaches often rely heavily on large volumes of high-quality training data. By closely integrating robot control with machine learning (ML), a robust technological foundation can be established to achieve efficient, safe, and flexible HRI across diverse application domains.

During physical interaction, robots typically switch between passive and active modes based on system states. Zhou et al. [24] proposed an active-passive compliance strategy for robotic plugging and unplugging of electrical connectors, integrating a passive compliant device and an active compliance controller with an energy-tank mechanism. This hybrid structure mitigates insertion and withdrawal impacts while maintaining force accuracy. Similarly, Bai et al. [1] developed a spherical wrist with hybrid motion-impedance control, combining mechanical compliance with direction-dependent motion control for unconstrained directions and impedance regulation for constrained ones. In manufacturing, Xu et al. [22] presented a hybrid active-passive force control strategy for robotic belt grinding of turbine blades, in which active force regulation and passive compliance cooperate to suppress grinding marks. However, these works rely on manually defined thresholds to achieve both high precision and safe physical interaction. Beyond model-based approaches, Bazanella et al. [2] introduced learning about passivity from data, which is a data-driven framework that identifies system passivity properties directly from input-output measurements via convex optimization, enabling passivity-based stability assurance even for unknown nonlinear systems.

Recent advances in robot control have underscored the growing importance of integrating NN to address challenges associated with nonlinear dynamics, partially known systems, and complex environmental interactions. Yu et al. [23] proposed an NN-based adaptive human-tracking controller for a flexible articulated machine, achieving high-precision control under uncertain conditions by dynamically adjusting control parameters online. Similarly, NN-based strategies have gained significant attention for trajectory tracking in dynamic environments, as they effectively enhance control accuracy while reducing dependence on precise system models [3]. Hybrid frameworks incorporating sliding mode control (SMC) have also proven effective in mitigating uncertainties during robot-environment interactions, thereby improving adaptability in unstructured environments [9]. These hybrid approaches leverage the complementary strengths of data-driven and model-based techniques. However, key challenges such as improving learning efficiency, ensuring generalization, and enhancing robustness remain critical areas for future research [15] -[5]. Efficient computation of the dynamics and their derivatives is essential for real-time control. Recent works have proposed analytical approaches for computing derivatives of rigid body dynamics using spatial vector algebra, which benefit for high frequency control and learning based frameworks [17] -[18].

Although NNs perform well at modeling unknown dynamics, they require huge amounts of precise data. Such data are difficult to obtain in real-world force-related HRI, as humans cannot simultaneously collect multiple parallel data segments or accelerate the data-gathering process as in simulations. Furthermore, force sensors are expensive, and the acquired data often contain significant noise in both real and simulated environments. Meta-learning has emerged as a promising approach to address the challenge of learning from limited data and rapidly adapting to new tasks. It aims to develop a general learning strategy by training across multiple tasks, enabling fast generalization to novel scenarios with minimal data. For instance, model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) [8] and optimization-based meta-learning [16] have demonstrated fast convergence and strong generalization in few-shot and multi-task learning. These meta-learning methods provide robots with enhanced adaptability and decision-making efficiency in complex and dynamic environments. O’Connell et al. [13] demonstrated rapid learning and highly adaptive flight under different wind conditions. Their approach leveraged NN and online learning strategies to model the NN via meta-learning, effectively capturing external disturbance information that affects drone performance. In addition, an adaptive controller was designed to help the drone adjust to varying wind conditions, achieving robust flight control. This work offers an effective solution for autonomous flight in complex wind conditions. Building on this, Xie et al. [21] proposed a hierarchical meta-learning framework for drone control that extends the work in [13]. Their method decomposes tasks into multi-level sub-tasks and applies meta-learning at each level. Both studies highlight the potential of meta-learning for achieving adaptive and robust control. Although the learning algorithm in [13] combines meta-learning with an adaptive controller, it relies on only one trajectory in the training dataset because the NN is highly dependent on the trajectory, which may lead to poor generalization in robotic manipulator tasks.

In physical HRI, the human does not play a fixed role. Instead, the human may either actively guide the robot or passively follow its motion. These two interaction modes lead to different control objectives. In the active mode, the controller should track the human-applied force, whereas in the passive mode, the controller should compensate for the human disturbance to ensure stable and accurate motion execution. However, most existing approaches rely on predefined switching thresholds or external force sensors to distinguish modes and obtain force information. Moreover, pure data-driven approaches lack stability guarantees, while model-based controllers (MBCs) have limited adaptability. These limitations motivate a unified framework that integrates mode recognition with adaptive learning-based control to achieve both adaptability and stability in HRI.

The overview of the proposed work is illustrated in Fig.1. The proposed framework integrates meta-learning based mode recognition and adaptive meta-learning robot control, and it is experimentally validated. The framework employs a meta-learning-trained NN to classify human intention, allowing more stable adaptation to new trajectories. A multiple-trajectory algorithm is developed to train the environment-basis NN and the force-dependent parameters. In addition, an adaptive meta-learning controller is designed to ensure the robustness of manipulator tracking during the human passive mode.

In summary, compared with existing literature in [1], [5], [4], and [14], this paper presents the following contributions:

Compared with [1] where switching thresholds are manually defined, a meta-learning-based mode recognition method is proposed to classify human intention using an NN without thresholds. Compared with conventional NN training, meta-learning enables more stable adaptation when encountering new trajectories.

Compared with [1] where switching thresholds are manually defined, a meta-learning-based mode recognition method is proposed to classify human intention using an NN without thresholds. Compared with conventional NN training, meta-learning enables more stable adaptation when encountering new trajectories.

Compared with the single trajectory case in [4], a new algorithm is developed to train the environment-basis NN from multiple trajectories, allowing the controller to effectively capture unmodeled dynamics.

An adaptive meta-learning controller is designed to compensate for unknown external disturbances and achieves more accurate tracking performance on unseen trajectories compared with controllers in [5] and [14]. The controller integrates data-driven learning with MBC, ensuring the convergence based on Lyapunov method.

The proposed framework establishes a coupling between control and mode recognition. The recognition accuracy improves by incorporating the estimated force-dependent parameters into the mode recognition network. Experimental results in simulation and real robot demonstrate the effectiveness of the control performance and mode recognition in the proposed framework.

title: Warping the Workspace: Expanding Visual Access with Adjustable Reach Mapping for Humanoid Teleoperation
authors: Keigo Minamida,Koya Dendo,Yuto Nakamura,Jun Rekimoto
abstract:
First-person humanoid teleoperation ties access to side and rear targets to operator rotation.
We present coupled visual–motor remapping, pairing a panoramic azimuth warp with its inverse upper-limb yaw transform.
A working prototype implements Global Zoom (GZ) and Focus+Context (F+C).
In a within-subject study (N=8N=8; 72 trials), GZ had the largest completion count (23/24; Fixed: 20/24; F+C: 21/24), whereas F+C was preferred by 6/8 participants.
Thus, completion and preference favored different mappings in this sample.
introduction:
Immersive humanoid teleoperation lets operators act through a remote body from its viewpoint (Darvish et al., 2023; Fritsche et al., 2015). First-person systems commonly preserve a one-to-one relationship among the operator’s view, body motion, and robot motion. This correspondence is easy to interpret, but it also ties access to side and rear targets to large head and torso rotations. Widening the view can expose more of the workspace, but reduces local visual detail.

Panoramic warping offers another possibility: redistributing a 360∘ workspace into the operator’s frontal field of view. However, visual remapping alone breaks the action correspondence that makes first-person teleoperation understandable. A lateral target may appear in front while the commanded arm direction remains lateral, leaving the operator to see and act through different spatial mappings. Rather than treating zoom as a display-only function, we treat the allocation of visual space as part of the action mapping.

Prior teleoperation systems mirror body motion, steer robot cameras, add auxiliary views, or modify control mappings (Fritsche et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2025; Iyer et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). Fisheye, peripheral-compression, and zoom interfaces redistribute visual detail (Furnas, 1986; Orlosky et al., 2014; Mizukoshi et al., 2020). Most closely, Vaughan et al. applied focus+context visualization to mobile-robot navigation (Vaughan et al., 2016). Our approach instead couples a single panoramic view warp with inverse upper-limb yaw remapping for humanoid manipulation, so that displayed and commanded reach directions remain aligned.

We contribute (1) this coupled visual–motor remapping principle and (2) a working humanoid teleoperation prototype implementing uniform Global Zoom (GZ) and non-uniform Focus+Context (F+C). An exploratory study compares their direction-specific task completion and overall user preference.
