title: Real-Time Ground Normal Vector Estimation for Spherical Mobile 3D Mapping using LiDAR-Inertial Odometry
authors: Tim Schubert,Fabian Arzberger,Andreas Nüchter
comment: Proceedings of the International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Automation in Space (i-SAIRAS 26)
abstract:
Accurate ground plane normal estimation is essential for odometry in spherical mobile mapping systems (SMMS), which face challenges from rapid rotations and limited ground coverage.
We propose two RANSAC-based approaches: single-scan estimation with normal vector scoring and multi-step validation, and LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO)-based estimation using a global 3D map.
Evaluated across diverse real-world datasets against terrestrial laser scanner ground truth, results show that LIO-based estimation significantly outperforms single-scan methods in accuracy and robustness.
Integrating ground normal estimates into the motion model improves pose estimation, supporting autonomous navigation in challenging and hazardous environments.
introduction:
Gathering information about the environment has always been a foundational desire of the human species.
Though, the method of doing so has changed significantly over time.
Nowadays, there is no longer the need to take unnecessary risks to explore unknown and potentially hazardous environments.
Instead, unmanned autonomous robotic systems are applied for this purpose.
While this trend in exploration innovation improves safety for humans and enables the acquisition of large datasets in a short amount of time, there is no generally applicable approach, valid for all the different kinds of environments.
On Earth alone, the exploration of different environments requires heavy adaption of the robotic systems that are used, like wheeled robots for planar environments, legged robots for rough outdoor terrain, and unmanned aerial vehicles for places too hard to traverse.
Going beyond Earth to outer space introduces even more challenging environments.
These also include our Moon, which is of major interest for current and upcoming space missions.
Next to the harsh lunar surface, there exist lunar caves or lava tubes, originating from volcanic activity on the Moon [1].
These underground structures are of high interest for scientific missions that try to learn more about the evolution of Luna [2], our solar system’s history [3], and exploring potential human habitats for crewed Moon base in the near future [4].

While there already exist satellite imagery [5] and radar-based analysis [6] of lunar caves by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Mission, onsite autonomous robotic exploration offers a lot more possibilities to gather information about these unique environments, just recently shown by Calvo et al. [7].
Having high resolution 3D maps of these caves would enable a huge step to further understanding their characteristics, which is why Borrmann et al. proposed the Descent And Exploration in Deep Autonomy of Lava Underground Structures project for this very purpose in 2021 [8].
It allows traversal of the challenging lunar cave terrain thanks to its protective outer shell and rolling motion.
The rotation-based locomotion of the SMMS inherently offers a large Field of View during motion and consequently enables building 3D point clouds that cover the entire surrounding environment.
For reliable navigation and mapping by the SMMS, knowledge of the current ground plane the system is traversing on is crucial.
Therefore, this thesis focuses on the problem of computing a reliable and real-time estimate of the ground plane normal vector, as well as integrating it into an existing pose estimation approach.
To achieve successful and reliable SLAM in real-time, the current pose estimate of the robot must be computed as accurately as possible onboard the system.
The lunar environment with a lack of a Global Navigation Satellite System, and rough, non-planar terrain makes this increasingly hard.
While there exist multiple approaches to estimate the current pose, most of them require information about the plane the system is moving on to provide reliable results.
The SMMS filters IMU data to calculate pose data and, by default, assumes a flat ground plane.
With this assumption, the resulting trajectory will not include any information about the movement in the upwards or downwards direction over time, resulting in a pose estimation process restricted to five of the six possible Degrees of Freedom with static height of the system.
Additionally, the process of mapping the surrounding environment and computing a global 3D point cloud using LIO further depends on these pose estimates, which is the basis for reliable SLAM on the robot.
However, the sphere’s kinematic motion model introduces additional challenges to the ground normal estimation.
Its fast rotations and orientation-dependent ground coverage by the LiDAR sensor make straightforward single-scan-based ground normal computation prone to outliers.
Thus, a more robust approach is needed to achieve the full potential of the SMMS for exploring and mapping challenging terrain like lunar caves.
This work proposes a novel method to extract the normal vector of the current ground plane underneath a spherical robot.
This approach uses a global 3D map as input for the ground normal estimation to assure an adequate amount of points and ground coverage for the normal computation.
An existing approach for estimating the ground normal vector, based on single LiDAR scans, is extended with a scoring system and additional validation techniques to improve robustness.
Both processes are evaluated for their accuracy and runtime using different in and outdoor datasets.
Furthermore, the impact of feeding the ground normal vector into an IMU-based pose estimator with motion-acceleration compensation is evaluated, in order to assess its impact compared to the prior approach assuming a flat ground plane.
Finally, the proposed ground normal extraction method allows future algorithms on the SMMS to go beyond the planar ground assumption, enabling the system to traverse more complex cave-like terrain and further improve the mapping of the surrounding environment.

title: Implementation of Dynamic Microsegmentation for a Multi-Robot Network
authors: Vishwam Raval,Jaewon Kim,Ravi Pattabhi,Sandip Roy
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: This report describes a laboratory instantiation of a dynamic microsegmentation function for an Internet-of-Things network, specifically a multi-robot network, using a commercial software-defined microsegmentation tool. Fine-grained dynamic segmentation policies are defined, where segments are adapted based on asset functional and health tags. Automated implementation of the dynamic policies in software is also undertaken. The microsegmentation solution is shown to automatically isolate an indicated threat in real time, while maintaining unaffected operations. The demonstration indicates that microsegmentation can be implemented in IoT networks, in a way that allows for robust operation in the face of threats and disruptions.
introduction:
Internet of Things (IoT) devices in industrial, defense, and critical-infrastructure environments have introduced substantial operational capabilities, with the global IoT device population projected to exceed 29 billion connected endpoints by 2030 [1]. However, this growing dependence on IoT devices has also increased the susceptibility of critical systems to cyber threats, both by expanding the attack surface and by widening the potential impact radius of threats [2]. Embedded endpoint devices frequently operate with constrained computational resources and limited onboard security, making them attractive initial entry points for adversaries [3]. Once a single device is compromised, the open network architectures common in these environments allow attackers to move laterally, disrupt command hierarchies, manipulate sensing or actuation pipelines, and ultimately compromise the physical-world responses of multiple assets [4].

Traditional perimeter defenses are often ineffective in these dynamic and distributed settings [5]. Embedded endpoint devices do not have the resources or operational flexibility to enact strong authentication or firewall systems; once a device is compromised, there is little to prevent it from launching attacks against controllers or neighboring devices, since it is within the trusted zone. Such vulnerabilities underscore the need for defense-in-depth or Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) principles for security, in which no device is inherently trusted and each communication must be continuously validated.

Network microsegmentation – wherein tailored and dynamic/adaptive network security zones are used to limit lateral movement of network attacks – forms a core component of a ZTA. There has been substantial adoption of microsegmentation in enterprise networks, with an estimated total market of about $21 billion in 2025. Microsegmentation solutions have proved effective in limiting lateral movement, and hence limiting risk, in the enterprise space.

While there is a recognition that ZTA and specifically microsegmentation are important technologies for IoT and other cyber-physical systems, their deployment for these systems remains limited. Microsegmentation for IoT networks entails several specific technical challenges:

1) Instantiation of dynamic segmentation rules in real-time for IoT endpoints, given computational constraints, heterogeneity of devices/protocols, and potentially ad hoc connectivity.

2) Detection of anomalies and classification of compromised assets, based on heterogeneous device-level, network-, and physical-world- behavior.

3) Design of dynamic segmentation rules or policies, that maintain operational safety and enhance system resilience.

This work presents an empirical investigation of dynamic microsegmentation for networked IoT devices, specifically a multi-robot network. The work represents a collaboration between ColorTokens, a leading industry microsegmentation vendor with a growing IoT/OT customer base; and the Global Cyber Research Institute (GCRI) at Texas A&M University, which has a research focus on cyber-physical and IoT security. Using a controlled testbed at the GCRI, we have demonstrated a dynamic network segmentation solution that monitors asset cyber-physical behavior, classifies devices by operational and security state, and autonomously isolates compromised robots. Our architecture leverages tag-based asset health classification and API-driven policy orchestration, for context-aware reassignment of devices to restrictive quarantine segments immediately upon detection of malicious behavior.

The primary contribution of this study is the initial practical instantiation of an automated detection-response mechanism that integrates real-time asset health tracking with dynamic network segmentation. This report describes results of the experiment, which demonstrate that compromised nodes can be isolated with minimal delay and without disrupting the availability or communication link of healthy robots. We believe that these findings represent a practical starting point for securing myriad IoT and cyber-physical systems, including autonomous vehicles, distributed industrial sensor networks, and other emerging Industry 4.0 infrastructures.

title: DriveMLP: When Training Strategy Outperforms Model Complexity in Autonomous Driving
authors: Alessandro Canevaro,Julian Schmidt,Hang Yu,Ye Jin,Sajad Marvi,Georg Martius,Julian Jordan
comment: Accepted at 2026 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL)
abstract:
Learning motion planning policies that remain reliable under closed-loop execution is a central challenge in Autonomous Driving (AD).
Imitation Learning (IL) scales well to large AD datasets but suffers from distribution shift, causal confusion, and compounding errors under closed-loop execution.
In contrast, Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically requires handcrafted rule-based rewards and massive simulation.
We study a simple closed-loop IL framework that uses RL purely as an optimization tool, guided by a trajectory-distance reward derived from logged expert data.
We refer to this training strategy as Expert-Guided RL (EGRL).
Through a controlled empirical study we find evidence that the training procedure, rather than model size and complexity, accounts for a substantial part of the performance gains.
We then introduce DriveMLP, a lightweight MLP policy trained with EGRL, as a simple instantiation of these findings. It achieves a score of 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark, a +3.2 point improvement over the previous best IL planner (Flow Planner), with >15×>15\times faster inference.
Code is available at: 
https://github.com/alessandro-canevaro/DriveMLP.
introduction:
Autonomous Driving (AD) planning requires policies that remain reliable in complex multi-agent interactions and during rare, safety-critical events [39].
Despite rapid progress in large-scale learning-based planners, a fundamental challenge remains: how to train models that are robust under closed-loop execution without sacrificing efficiency or scalability.

In practice, Imitation Learning (IL) has emerged as the dominant paradigm because it scales well to large open-loop datasets of human driving.
Recent methods improve closed-loop performance through auxiliary objectives and data augmentation, alongside increasingly expressive architectures.
These include transformer-based [52] planners such as PlanTF [7] and PLUTO [6], as well as generative approaches such as Diffusion Planner [65] and Flow Planner [50].

However, despite the advances, IL fundamentally suffers from distribution shift and causal confusion: models are trained in an open-loop setting, where spurious correlations in the data may be learned, and are then deployed in closed-loop, where compounding errors can push the policy into previously unseen states [11, 33].
A telling example of causal confusion is that Diffusion Planner loses nearly 10 percentage points in closed-loop performance when provided with additional ego-state inputs [65], suggesting that open-loop training can turn useful causal cues into spurious shortcuts.
More broadly, under mild test-time distribution shifts, such as the nuPlan reactive benchmark, where surrounding agents are controlled by rule-based IDM [51] policies instead of replayed logs, open-loop IL methods exhibit substantial performance degradation.
These observations motivate training objectives that expose the policy to its own induced state distribution.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers this closed-loop training signal, but applying it to AD remains challenging [28, 59].
Strong results often depend either on heavily engineered rule-based reward functions, as in CaRL [23], or on simpler, though still rule-based, rewards paired with extremely large-scale simulation, as in GIGAFLOW [9].

A natural alternative is to derive supervision from expert demonstrations rather than hand-designed rules.
Online Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) methods such as GAIL [22] and AIRL [12] learn rewards via adversarial training, while non-adversarial alternatives such as IQ-Learn [14] rely on occupancy matching.
However, both families are computationally expensive and difficult to stabilize at scale [64].
Recent hybrid IL-RL approaches reduce or eliminate adversarial reward learning by analytically deriving demonstration-based rewards, but introduce other forms of complexity.
CarPlanner [62] uses RL as a trajectory candidate generator, requiring a secondary rule-based post-processing module for final selection and refinement.
Peng et al. [41] leverage expert-guided trajectory signals for multi-agent traffic simulation, employing a two-stage training strategy where RL fine-tunes a pre-trained autoregressive policy.
Another approach is BC-SAC [33], which alternates BC and RL updates using safety-related rewards, treating RL primarily as a corrective component.

In summary, recent ego-planning methods rely on demonstration-based supervision using complex architectures that sacrifice inference speed or, orthogonally, on engineered rule-based supervision.

These approaches motivate an empirical question: how competitive can a simple planning policy become when trained in closed-loop simulation with demonstration-derived supervision?
We investigate a practical training recipe and evaluate its performance against SOTA methods on Highway and nuPlan benchmarks.
We further assess whether this recipe enables a lightweight MLP to compete with recent generative imitation-based planners.

Additional related work and references are discussed in Appendix A.

In this work, we study closed-loop imitation through DriveMLP, a lightweight MLP planner trained using standard RL in a non-reactive log-replay simulator.
Training is guided by a reward derived from trajectory deviations from the logged expert, a strategy we name Expert-Guided RL (EGRL).
Our main contributions are as follows:
(1) Through a controlled empirical analysis, we show that performance gains stem largely from the training procedure, rather than increased model size or complexity alone.
(2) We introduce DriveMLP, a lightweight MLP policy trained with EGRL, as a simple instantiation of these findings.
On the evaluated nuPlan reactive splits, it achieves SOTA performance among purely learned imitation-based planners while running >15×>15\times faster than recent generative planners.
(3) We propose an exponential reward formulation for AD building on [40] that provides dense and stable supervision, improving over the Peng et al. [41] formulation.
(4) We show that through closed-loop RL exploration, our model is substantially more robust to action noise and data efficient compared to SOTA open-loop IL.

title: Extending Affordance Segmentation for Wearable Robots to Multi-Object Images
authors: Simone Lugani,Matteo Montani,Paolo Gastaldo,Rodolfo Zunino,Edoardo Ragusa
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: This paper proposes a refinement to existing vision-based portable pipelines for the recognition of graspable object parts. Such pipelines can effectively support automatic grasp selection and preshaping in upper-limb prosthetic devices. However, realistic scenarios in which multiple objects are present still represent a challenge. The proposed method exploits a minor modification to the conventional hardware setup and a custom training approach to extend the applicability of vision-based pipelines. A laser pointer is introduced in the setup as an effective mechanism for object disambiguation. Accordingly, a suitable retraining of the deep convolutional neural networks supporting recognition of graspable parts is implemented. A mixed reality strategy allows the reuse of available high-quality segmentation masks to generate realistic images procedurally, extending the range of scenarios supported by the final device. Experimental results confirm that the proposed pipeline improves target disambiguation accuracy by up to 9% compared with existing solutions, while preserving the computational cost.
introduction:
Upper-limb prosthetics aim to restore motor function and improve the quality of life after amputation, but their effective control remains a challenge. Conventional myoelectric control is often sequential and cognitively demanding, especially for multi-degree-of-freedom prostheses, which limits usability and leads to high rejection rates [1]. Shared-autonomy paradigms, where the prosthesis exploits environmental sensing to assist the user during task execution [2], alleviate these issues.

Vision-based approaches support automatic grasp selection and preshaping[3, 4], but existing systems rely on the user’s ability to frame the target object[5]. This becomes problematic in realistic scenarios with multiple objects, leading to ambiguity in target selection.

We address this limitation by introducing a simple mechanism for object disambiguation in vision-based prosthetic control: a laser pointer integrated into the wearable setup. The pointer, activated via EMG signals, provides an explicit indication of the user’s intended target. This information is exploited by a lightweight affordance segmentation (AS) module implemented with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which identifies the object of interest and extracts its graspable regions, enabling reliable operation even in multi-object environments [6, 7].

The proposed approach preserves the efficiency required for embedded deployment, while improving the robustness of target disambiguation in semi-autonomous prosthesis control. Experimental results demonstrate that the pointer enables accurate target selection and enhances system performance in challenging multi-object scenarios.

title: AOV-GS: Active Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting
authors: Rodion Shkokov,Tatiana Zemskova,Dmitry Yudin
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Robots deployed in human-centered environments need maps that support both geometric
navigation and open-vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set.
A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on
manually annotated segmentation masks or closed-set semantic categories.
Existing geometry-driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive
by-product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on
supervised semantic segmentation.
We present AOV-GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration
using frozen foundation models.
During coarse exploration, AOV-GS re-ranks geometrically promising candidate views according
to CLIP mask-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration
toward semantically informative regions.
Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language-aligned embeddings throughout
mapping, while a lightweight scene-specific language field is fitted offline directly to the
collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open-vocabulary
text-query segmentation on novel views.
In a controlled comparison using the same SAM–CLIP perception stack, AOV-GS improves average
language-field mIoU over geometry-only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica
(34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes).
With CorrCLIP, AOV-GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched
Geometry-based + CorrCLIP baseline.
Novel-view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry-only baseline on both datasets while depth
L1 improves on Replica.
Code is available at github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV-GS.
introduction:
Mobile robots operating in human-centered environments need spatial maps of the environment
that support both navigation and task-level semantic interaction.
In practice this means a map should render high-quality RGB-D views and support queries
such as find the chair or locate the table near the window.
These objectives are coupled through exploration: the viewpoints collected during mapping
determine geometric completeness, object visibility, and the evidence available for
downstream open-vocabulary retrieval.

Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM systems [13, 11]
achieve efficient high-fidelity reconstruction suitable for online robotic mapping.
Active planners such as ActiveGS [10], ActiveSplat [19],
and ActiveGAMER [3] improve coverage through geometry-aware
next-best-view (NBV) selection.
In parallel, foundation-model perception enables open-vocabulary semantics:
Segment Anything (SAM) [15] provides prompt-free instance masks and
CLIP [24] maps mask regions to a language-aligned embedding space.
LangSplat [23] and related methods attach such features to 3D primitives
for text-query segmentation, but typically assume a fixed observation trajectory.

Active semantic mapping closes part of this gap.
ActiveSGM [4] demonstrates that semantic signals can guide exploration in a
3DGS loop, but relies on per-scene OneFormer [7] fine-tuning, which limits
open-vocabulary deployment.
Passive fusion pipelines [8, 22] can improve
semantic quality on pre-recorded trajectories but do not affect online data acquisition.

This paper addresses the following question:
Can a robot actively explore an unseen scene using frozen foundation models,
improve open-vocabulary segmentation through viewpoint selection,
and preserve competitive RGB-D reconstruction quality?

We answer affirmatively with AOV-GS (Fig. 1).
During coarse exploration (stage 0), geometric information gain is augmented with
CLIP-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance masks on RGB views rendered from the
current Gaussian map.
Semantic novelty is measured against a growing keyframe embedding bank and re-ranks the
top-KK geometrically strong candidates.
During refinement (stage 1+), planning reverts to geometry-only behavior as in
ActiveGS [10].
After exploration, per-keyframe CLIP mask embeddings train a sparse language field on Gaussian
primitives, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views.
As in ActiveSGM, candidate RGB views for semantic scoring are rendered from the current
Gaussian map; Habitat supplies the posed RGB-D observation after the selected view is executed.
The experiments nevertheless use ground-truth camera poses as oracle SLAM input.

Our contributions are:

A coarse exploration NBV criterion that re-ranks the top-KK candidates produced by
the geometric planner according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty, steering the robot toward
semantically novel object instances while reverting to geometry-only scoring during later
refinement stages.

An active open-vocabulary semantic mapping pipeline combining online semantic
exploration with offline LangSplatV2 language-field construction, without per-scene
segmenter fine-tuning.

A two-benchmark evaluation showing average open-vocabulary gains over geometry-only
exploration while preserving comparable novel-view reconstruction quality. Under the
matched SAM–CLIP stack, AOV-GS reaches 34.6% on Replica (+1.3 pp) and 23.1% on MP3D
(+1.8 pp); the per-scene Replica results are heterogeneous and are analyzed explicitly.

title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI
authors: Han Hu,He Chen
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
introduction:
Vision language models (VLMs) increasingly form part of the
perception-and-reasoning stack of robotic systems, supporting visual
understanding, task decomposition, and high-level
planning [1]. For robots that share
spaces with people, human activity is a central part of this
understanding: knowing what a person is doing, what they are
interacting with, and which events have just occurred provides
important context for deciding whether, when, and how to act. Activity
understanding therefore connects visual observation with downstream
reasoning and planning in embodied systems.

Robot perception of human activity in the home, however, is constrained by both lighting conditions and privacy concerns. Thermal video captures body shape and motion cues in darkness while revealing less facial and household appearance detail than RGB imagery [2, 3]. This makes it well suited for human activity sensing in bedrooms and other private spaces, where a robot may need to detect a fall or recognize signs of discomfort even when the lights are off. When combined with the language interface of VLMs, thermal observations could support activity understanding at multiple levels of abstraction.

Prior work [3] found that VLMs recognize some thermal
activities but struggle with subtle gestures and movements, while more
recent thermal VLM studies target general thermal image understanding,
such as scene semantics and temperature
cues [4, 5, 6, 7].
Yet overall accuracy scores and isolated failure cases cannot
show where VLMs fail in understanding human activities from thermal
video, nor how much additional observation and reasoning can help. RGB video benchmarks also expose difficulties in fine-grained motion
recognition [8, 9], although the
different visual cues in thermal video limit direct transfer of these
findings. As a result, thermal video-based human activity understanding for HRI still lacks a concrete basis for choosing activity-understanding tasks, configuring
perception pipelines, and prioritizing improvements.

We address this gap through a diagnostic evaluation of seven locally
deployable VLMs on two person-centric thermal video datasets, testing
three aspects of activity understanding: distinctions between specific actions, recovery of action–object interactions and their temporal extent, and the decision between an action answer and backoff. Paired RGB–thermal recordings and controlled changes in observation and inference examine how failures respond to different conditions, and models developed for physical AI or robotics are compared with their general-purpose base-model reference.

Our systematic evaluation yields four key observations:

Recurring action confusions.
Across seven models, five incorrect answer labels account for
42.9% of pooled exact-action errors. We also observe that recurring substitutions involve similar body movements or hand–object configurations, and these confusions from the test clips can cross functional categories, describing physiological events or potentially urgent behavior as routine activities, such as coughing labeled as touching the face and staggering as walking.

Recurring action confusions.
Across seven models, five incorrect answer labels account for
42.9% of pooled exact-action errors. We also observe that recurring substitutions involve similar body movements or hand–object configurations, and these confusions from the test clips can cross functional categories, describing physiological events or potentially urgent behavior as routine activities, such as coughing labeled as touching the face and staggering as walking.

Activity understanding errors.
In long clips, models recover only 30.2%–51.8% of annotated
events with the correct action and object labels, even without
requiring accurate temporal boundaries. For harder joint tasks, their predictions also contain inaccurate temporal boundaries and hallucinated actions involving objects.

Limited intervention gains.
Across the two tested models, pseudocoloring, contrast enhancement, person cropping, denser frame sampling, and additional reasoning change exact-action accuracy by a limited −5.9-5.9% to +5.9+5.9% point relative to their respective paired baselines.

Unreliable abstention.
Models exhibit different answering tendencies but struggle to
balance rejecting unsupported answers with retaining valid ones,
even under explicit instructions. For example, Qwen3.6-27B correctly abstains on only 6.1% of questions without a valid candidate, whereas RoboBrain2.5 answers only 3.2% of questions containing one. We conclude this behavior as unacceptable for practical robotic application.

title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts
authors: Chu Lin,Yi Sun
abstract: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2R^{2} over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task–seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p≈0.002p\approx 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2R^{2} of 0.755–0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
introduction:
World models are used to predict the evolution of embodied systems as they execute actions [1]. Their prediction accuracy may degrade when physical conditions deviate from the training environment. Recent theory connects generalization across multi-step goals to learned predictive world models [2]. Embodied applications require these models to remain useful under changing conditions, such as when a robot handles a different payload or operates with different physical properties. Pearl’s structural causal model (SCM) framework separates structural dependencies from the functions governing those relationships [3]. This separation motivates two questions for a world model: which inputs should a predictor use, and how should its dynamics mechanism compute their effects?

Causal dynamics models, such as CDL [4] and recent structure-distribution approaches [5], learn or estimate dependencies between current state, action, and next state, and use them to restrict irrelevant inputs to the dynamics predictor. Such constraints remove direct prediction paths from excluded shortcut inputs. However, if the OOD shift involves a true causal factor, such as a heavier robot link, the relevant dependency must remain. The computation performed after reading the shifted value is then determined by the mechanism. Input selection alone does not specify how this function should extrapolate. Recent context-aware mechanical models and structured physical world models further motivate examining how parameter information enters the dynamics mechanism [6, 7].

We develop a robot world-model configuration that assigns physical parameters and control inputs distinct roles: link masses enter inertia and dynamics bias through explicit affine coefficients, actions produce torque through the known PD controller, and a neural residual models contact-related effects without directly receiving robot masses. The dependencies are fixed to each finger’s local state and action, with shared object context. We compare this configuration with an MLP and mass-affine dynamics with learned torque under the same input routing. Each model is paired with a separately trained mass-information control: mass inputs are removed from the MLP or fixed at their training means in the structured models. A complementary synthetic experiment uses an intervention-derived mask to evaluate shortcut dependence. Figure 1 summarizes the robot architecture and prediction procedure.

The experiments connect dependency selection to physical parameter extrapolation. Frozen intervention-derived masks reduce mean synthetic OOD RMSE by 60.6%. In CausalWorld, supplying out-of-range link masses to an unstructured MLP or to a recurrent robotic world model sharply degrades prediction, whereas the known-PD mass-affine model improves its median time-averaged joint R2R^{2} over 150 steps from 0.609 for its fixed-mass-input control to 0.727. The median within-run benefit of mass information is 0.121 under the heavy-mass shift, compared with 0.009 within the training mass range. In a shared 100-step benchmark, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent baseline (median joint R2R^{2} of 0.755 with actual masses and 0.768 with fixed mass inputs, versus 0.752), and the known-PD model retains a positive mass benefit in every run.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A mass-informed robot world-model design. We develop finger-local mass-affine dynamics with learned-torque and known-PD variants. Masses enter inertia and bias through explicit coefficients, while torque and residual networks use mass-excluded inputs. Joint integration and a separate object-state predictor generate future trajectories.

Competitive OOD prediction in a shared CausalWorld benchmark. Over a common 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model reaches median joint R2R^{2} of 0.755 with actual masses and 0.768 with fixed mass inputs, compared with 0.752 for the strongest tested RWM configuration, with slightly lower joint NRMSE and object-position RMSE and without using observation history. The accuracy margins are small; the larger difference lies in how the models respond to out-of-range mass inputs, which sharply degrade the MLP and recurrent predictors.

Consistent predictive benefit from out-of-range masses. Separately trained mass-information controls show that the known-PD design improves median 150-step mean joint R2R^{2} from 0.609 to 0.727. Actual masses improve prediction in all ten task–seed runs in both the 150-step ablation and the 100-step benchmark; the latter yields a median paired mass gain of 0.071 (exact two-sided sign test, p≈0.002p\approx 0.002 in each case).

2. Competitive OOD prediction in a shared CausalWorld benchmark. title: RoPT: Robust 6DoF Object Pose Tracking in Video
authors: Yongqing Liang,Yuzhong Chen,Sihang Li,Junsuk Kim,Chase Kidder,Hui-ping Wang,Yunzhi Xu,Raihan Haque,Yubiao Zhang,Chen Feng
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Accurate 6-DoF object pose tracking is essential for robotic interaction, yet conventional monocular pipelines frequently suffer from catastrophic divergence under rapid object motion.
We present RoPT, a robust tracking framework engineered to overcome this limitation by unifying visual perception, temporal kinematics, and global re-localization into a tightly coupled closed loop.
Unlike existing open-loop trackers, RoPT delivers three critical capabilities that fundamentally alter system resilience. First, the visual perception component tracks object masks to robustly handle partial and severe occlusions. Second, a kinematic factor graph regularizes frame-to-frame updates, forecasts forward pose predictions, and drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme to bypass local minima. Finally, an active re-localization module transforms the pipeline into a closed-loop system, making it failure-aware and capable of deterministic self-recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across challenging benchmarks alongside real-world robotic demonstrations, achieving significantly higher tracking survivability under rapid motion.
introduction:
Robust 6DoF object pose tracking serves as a foundational pillar in modern robotics by providing the precise geometric awareness necessary for seamless human-robot collaboration and complex manipulation. 6DoF pose estimation involves determining the full rigid transformation of an object in three-dimensional space, which encompasses its translational position and rotational orientation relative to a defined coordinate frame. While recent breakthroughs in video understanding have significantly advanced 2D object localization and mask segmentation, these methods often operate purely in the image plane. Such approaches fail to provide the full spatial orientation and geometric grounding required for a robot to interact reliably with the physical world. Consequently, a critical discrepancy remains between existing video understanding frameworks and the requirements of robotic control.

The effectiveness of a tracking system depends on the two critical attributes of robustness and failure-awareness. Robustness entails the ability of an algorithm to remain accurate during high-speed motion and significant fluctuations in object appearance. Conversely, failure-awareness requires the system to actively monitor its own tracking state, dynamically quantifying uncertainty so it can flag tracking anomalies before drift compounds irrecoverably. In real-world deployments or data-driven imitation learning pipelines, losing the 6-DoF tracking of a target object is catastrophic, causing a complete breakdown in policy execution and resulting in total failure of the entire manipulation process. Despite these high stakes, conventional frame-to-frame local refinement pipelines [26, 24] fail on both counts.
When subjected to sudden high-acceleration displacements, objects frequently shear entirely out of the local tracking crop, causing visual networks to process background clutter and become trapped in false local minima. Furthermore, because these monocular trackers operate as open-loop systems, they lack the structural capacity to detect their own divergence, leading to permanent task failure. To achieve true tracking resilience under real-world dynamics, a framework must not only anticipate motion through continuous temporal regularization but also possess a deterministic mechanism to self-heal once visual tracking breaks.

To address these challenges, we introduce RoPT, a robust 6-DoF object pose tracking framework designed specifically to bridge the gap between fragile visual perception models and the rigorous demands of dynamic robotic manipulation. While techniques such as mask-based tracking, kinematic filtering, and feature-based re-localization have been explored individually in literature, isolated components are insufficient to handle the compounding errors of high-speed physical interactions. Our primary contribution to the robot learning community lies not in a single algorithmic silver bullet, but in a meticulously engineered, closed-loop system architecture that balances accuracy, resilience, and computational efficiency. We observe that robustness against rapid, erratic object motion, a ubiquitous challenge in contact-rich tasks and teleoperation,
has received disproportionately little attention due to its inherent difficulty. RoPT explicitly tackles this by tightly integrating continuous kinematic velocity forecasting with a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme and a deterministic, failure-triggered self-recovery module. By intelligently routing expensive computational resources only when geometric ambiguity or catastrophic tracking loss occurs, the framework achieves near real-time performance at 18.6 FPS, ensuring it remains practical for latency-sensitive control and imitation learning pipelines.
In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

Resilience to High-Acceleration Dynamics: We propose RoPT, a closed-loop 6-DoF tracking framework that maintains unbroken trajectory consistency during rapid, erratic object motions where existing state-of-the-art trackers catastrophically diverge.

Kinematic Factor Graph-Enabled Multi-Hypothesis: We introduce a continuous temporal graph backend that drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme, allowing the system to gracefully bypass local geometric minima and severely degraded 2D masks.

Failure-Aware Active Self-Recovery: We design a deterministic re-localization module that automatically detects catastrophic tracking divergence and instantly self-heals by matching real-world observations against predictive synthetic CAD renderings.

title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
authors: Hamza Kheddar
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Performance (cs.PF); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enabling adaptive, autonomous, and self-optimizing behavior in modern computing systems, particularly as applications increasingly migrate toward embedded, edge, and heterogeneous hardware platforms. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer compelling advantages for RL deployment, including low latency, energy efficiency, and fine-grained architectural customization, but they also introduce unique design challenges that differ substantially from conventional CPU- and GPU- based implementations. This review presents a comprehensive survey of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms, with a particular emphasis on architectural design, performance measurement, and hardware–algorithm co-design. A broad body of more than one hundred studies is systematically analyzed and organized into major RL families, ranging from model-based Markov decision processes and classical value-based methods to deep RL, Actor-critic (AC), policy-gradient (PG), and multi-agent approaches. The review further categorizes existing works according to abstraction levels, hardware realization strategies, and application domains, highlighting how different RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware substrates. In contrast to prior surveys that focus narrowly on specific algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified perspective spanning both FPGA and IC implementations, encompassing acceleration techniques, reconfigurable hardware approaches, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Detailed comparisons are provided in terms of resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and achieved performance gains. Additionally, this review identifies recurring architectural patterns, discusses practical limitations, and outlines open research challenges and future directions for RL-driven intelligent hardware systems. By consolidating design insights, evaluation metrics, and application trends, this review aims to serve as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of RL and hardware platforms.
introduction:
Recent years have witnessed a growing shift toward intelligent, autonomous decision-making embedded directly within computing systems, with increasing emphasis on assessing the real-world applicability and feasibility of algorithms that demonstrate strong performance under simulation-based evaluations. As workloads become increasingly dynamic and heterogeneous—particularly in networking and edge computing, cyber–security, robotics [8], natural language processing, intelligent sensing, and embedded environments—traditional static control and optimization techniques, such as proportional–integral–derivative control and fixed-rule heuristic approaches [108] or meta-heuristic-based optimization methods [127], often struggle to cope with variability in data rates, power budgets, timing constraints, and environmental conditions. These approaches are typically designed around fixed operating assumptions and lack the adaptability required to respond effectively to non-stationary workloads or unforeseen runtime disturbances.

RL (RL), as a core paradigm within  ML (ML), has gained prominence in this context because it provides a principled framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. By continuously interacting with an environment and updating its policy based on observed rewards, an RL agent can learn to adapt its behavior online, even when system dynamics are partially unknown or change over time. This capability makes RL particularly attractive for modern computing platforms that must balance competing objectives such as performance, energy efficiency, latency, and reliability under tight operational constraints. However, translating RL from software-centric implementations to practical hardware platforms introduces significant challenges. Many RL algorithms rely on iterative updates, stochastic exploration, and memory-intensive computations that are difficult to reconcile with the strict latency, power, and determinism requirements of embedded systems. Implementations based purely on general-purpose CPU or GPU often suffer from high energy consumption, unpredictable execution timing, and limited scalability, which restrict their suitability for real-time or resource-constrained applications.

FPGA (FPGA)s and IC provide an alternative hardware substrate that fundamentally reshapes how ML, particularly RL, can be realized in practice. FPGA provide fine-grained parallelism, customizable datapaths, and reconfigurability, allowing RL algorithms to be mapped onto hardware architectures tailored to specific workloads and constraints. IC-based realizations, including ASIC and SoC platforms, further extend these advantages by enabling deterministic execution, compact form factors, and ultra-low power operation. At the same time, these platforms impose stricter design constraints, limited flexibility after deployment, and increased development complexity compared with software-based solutions. As a result, the intersection of RL with hardware design has evolved into a multidisciplinary research area encompassing algorithm–hardware co-design [64], hardware acceleration [90, 41, 58], architectural specialization [25], numerical precision optimization [5], and system-level control, including digital twin–based frameworks [106]. In this emerging landscape, RL plays a dual role: it can be treated as a workload to be accelerated on hardware, and it can also serve as a control mechanism for the hardware itself, governing tasks such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, resource allocation, scheduling, partial reconfiguration, and energy management. This duality blurs the traditional boundary between learning algorithms and hardware platforms, creating new opportunities as well as new design challenges. Despite rapid progress, the existing literature on RL implementations for FPGA and IC platforms remains fragmented.

Motivated by the increasingly practical shift of RL from a purely algorithmic concept to a hardware-constrained workload, this review consolidates and structures the fast-growing body of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms.
In particular, this survey emphasizes real-time pattern recognition and perception-driven decision-making systems, where hardware constraints critically affect learning efficiency, latency, energy consumption, and deployment feasibility.
Instead of revisiting algorithmic fundamentals, it adopts a hardware-centric lens to clarify how design and implementation choices shape real-world realizations of RL.
The review organizes the literature into coherent categories and distills recurring design patterns, trade-offs, and limitations, thereby clarifying the current state-of-the-art and highlighting open challenges that guide future research at the intersection of RL, pattern recognition, and intelligent hardware.

Several surveys have examined the relationship between RL and reconfigurable or heterogeneous hardware, yet significant gaps remain. The survey in [118] provides an extensive overview of domain-specific RL architectures, with a primary focus on FPGA-based accelerators. However, it does not integrate IC implementations, unified abstraction layers, nor does it cover the complete spectrum of RL algorithmic families such as  SARSA (SARSA),  MC (MC),  AC (AC), and  PPO (PPO). Similarly, the work in [44] concentrates on ML applications within FPGA EDA (EDA) tools. While valuable, its treatment of RL is brief, lacks architectural depth, and does not relate RL methods to accelerator design or runtime optimization. The review in [162] centers on ML techniques for control and monitoring but does not address RL-driven FPGA or IC architectures, nor broader comparisons across RL categories. Additionally, the heterogeneous-chip scheduling survey in [99] identifies RL primarily as a future research direction without analyzing existing RL implementations, hardware mapping strategies, or design-flow implications. Consequently, none of these studies provide a unified RL-centric perspective that spans both FPGA and IC platforms while simultaneously comparing all major RL types, synthesizing research areas and applications, and identifying cross-cutting architectural and methodological limitations. A detailed comparison of our coverage with prior surveys is provided in Table 1.

In contrast, the present review fills these gaps by systematically analyzing more than 120 FPGA/IC-related RL works and providing a unified and hardware-centric synthesis. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

Unified FPGA/IC perspective: consolidates RL-based realizations across reconfigurable accelerators and dedicated IC engines within a single RL-centric view.

Unified FPGA/IC perspective: consolidates RL-based realizations across reconfigurable accelerators and dedicated IC engines within a single RL-centric view.

Comprehensive RL coverage: covers all major RL families (including SARSA, MC, AC methods, and modern deep RL such as PPO) and relates algorithmic classes to hardware realization patterns.

Abstraction levels and toolflows: structures the literature by hardware abstraction levels and design flows, clarifying how implementation choices affect deployability and reproducibility.

Metrics-driven comparison: synthesizes reported evaluation metrics (latency/throughput, resource utilization, and energy efficiency) and highlights best-reported performance and improvements under application-driven constraints.

Research areas and application synthesis: maps the literature into major research fields and provides an evidence-driven synthesis of the most investigated application domains of RL-enabled intelligent hardware.

Table-based visual benchmarking: summarizes most reviewed works in unified tables capturing the target application, best performance/improvement, key limitations, and implementation notes, enabling quick visual comparison.

Cross-cutting limitations and open challenges: distills recurring architectural and methodological bottlenecks and outlines actionable directions for future RL-based intelligent hardware systems.

Finally, while several RL-based FPGA/IC implementations incorporate CPU or GPU, these processors typically serve auxiliary functions—such as orchestration, environment simulation, or data management—whereas the dominant learning and inference workload is executed on FPGA, ASIC, and custom hardware engines, with general-purpose processors contributing minimally to the computational pipeline.

To ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and reproducibility, this review adopts a systematic literature search and selection strategy centered on peer-reviewed studies addressing the implementation of RL on FPGA and IC platforms. The primary search was conducted using Scopus as the main indexing engine, which provides broad coverage of major scientific publishers and digital libraries, including IEEE Xplore, Elsevier ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, Wiley, Springer, and IET Digital Library, among others. To consistently retrieve works at the intersection of RL algorithms and hardware realization, a structured Boolean query was formulated and applied across databases using title, abstract, and keyword fields. The search logic was designed to capture both classical and deep RL methods, while explicitly constraining results to hardware-oriented implementations rather than purely algorithmic or simulation-based studies. The generic query structure can be expressed as:

Selected papers =
FROM (“Title” OR “Abstract” OR “Keywords”)
SELECT (References WHERE
(RL OR DRL OR “Reinforcement Learning” OR “Deep Reinforcement Learning”) AND (FPGA OR “Field-Programmable Gate Array” OR ASIC OR IC OR SoC OR “Integrated Circuit”)) FILTER (Language = “English” AND Year BETWEEN 2015 AND 2026 AND DocumentType = (“Journal Article” OR “Conference Paper”))

The logical operators AND and OR ensure precise targeting of studies that explicitly combine RL with FPGA or IC hardware platforms. The selected time window reflects the emergence of practical RL hardware realizations, from early tabular and  MDP (MDP)-based accelerators to modern deep and AC architectures.

To balance completeness with technical focus, the retrieved studies were further screened using relevance and quality criteria. Seminal RL hardware-acceleration works were retained when they directly supported the FPGA/IC-centered taxonomy, architectural discussion, performance comparison, or application-level analysis of this review. However, earlier works already extensively covered in prior surveys were not repeated exhaustively unless they established a necessary technical baseline or motivated a later research direction. This avoids redundant historical coverage while preserving the foundational context required for the proposed survey.

Redundant studies, papers with insufficient hardware-implementation details, works lacking meaningful evaluation results, and studies only weakly related to RL-based FPGA/IC platforms were excluded. Priority was given to recent studies that provide clear implementation details and contribute to emerging directions such as energy-efficient RL acceleration, quantized RL hardware, FPGA/IC-based runtime optimization, RL-assisted synthesis,  MARL (MARL) hardware, and application-specific deployment.

The remainder of this review is organized as follows. Section 2 provides essential background on FPGA and IC platforms, clarifying implementation abstraction levels and typical toolflows/simulators used in practice. Section 3 presents a taxonomy of RL-based FPGA/IC works (considering RL in a broad sense), organizing the literature by major RL families and highlighting implications for hardware realization. Section 4 synthesizes the major research areas that define RL-based FPGA/IC design and summarizes the dominant directions and recurring design patterns reported in the literature. Section 5 reviews the most investigated application domains of RL-enabled FPGA/IC systems (e.g., networking, information security, intelligent sensing/imaging, and other domains), emphasizing reported improvements and practical constraints. Section 6 consolidates the key challenges and limitations that still hinder scalability and deployment maturity as well as outlines future research directions to advance more robust, scalable, and reusable intelligent hardware systems. Finally, Section 7 concludes the review. A roadmap of the overall review is provided in Figure 1.

1. Unified FPGA/IC perspective: consolidates RL-based realizations across reconfigurable accelerators and dedicated IC engines within a single RL-centric view.

2. Comprehensive RL coverage: covers all major RL families (including SARSA, MC, AC methods, and modern deep RL such as PPO) and relates algorithmic classes to hardware realization patterns.

3. Abstraction levels and toolflows: structures the literature by hardware abstraction levels and design flows, clarifying how implementation choices affect deployability and reproducibility.

4. Metrics-driven comparison: synthesizes reported evaluation metrics (latency/throughput, resource utilization, and energy efficiency) and highlights best-reported performance and improvements under application-driven constraints.

5. Research areas and application synthesis: maps the literature into major research fields and provides an evidence-driven synthesis of the most investigated application domains of RL-enabled intelligent hardware.

6. Table-based visual benchmarking: summarizes most reviewed works in unified tables capturing the target application, best performance/improvement, key limitations, and implementation notes, enabling quick visual comparison.

7. Cross-cutting limitations and open challenges: distills recurring architectural and methodological bottlenecks and outlines actionable directions for future RL-based intelligent hardware systems.

title: PCLA-Bridge: A Framework for Cross-Domain Deployment of CARLA Agents
authors: Masoud Jamshidiyan Tehrani,Jinhan Kim,Paolo Tonella
abstract: Most high-performing end-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are developed for the CARLA Leaderboard, tightly coupling them to CARLA’s APIs, sensor layouts, coordinate systems, and internal clock. Reusing these models on real datasets, alternative simulators, or physical platforms necessitates substantial manual re-engineering. We present PCLA-Bridge, a deployable tool that runs unmodified CARLA Leaderboard agents from any sensor source to any control destination without an active CARLA server. With PCLA-Bridge handling dependency isolation, tensor marshalling, routing, and synthetic timing, integrators only need to provide a minimal interface. We validate the tool across two operational paradigms: offline replay on in-domain CARLA recordings and real-world nuScenes logs, and live closed-loop control across three diverse simulation engines: MetaDrive, AWSIM, and AlpaSim. We analyze the lightweight integration requirements for each platform, highlighting output translation (such as converting agent actions into target trajectory formats) and coordinate-frame transformations, showing that integration requires minimal glue code rather than structural changes. All eight evaluated agents execute across all three simulators without modification, confirming the reliability of PCLA-Bridge and establishing a foundation for systematic sim-to-real, cross-sim, and security testing.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are typically built and evaluated in a single simulator, most commonly the CARLA simulator [1]. Because these implementations assume a specific end-to-end environment, relying on native sensor tensors, routing, temporal synchronization, and coordinate conventions, a published agent becomes tightly coupled to its original execution harness. This coupling hinders code reuse, cross-environment evaluation, and any transition toward physical deployment. Currently, to run a published CARLA agent on real-world logs or within another simulator, researchers must manually re-engineer the agent.

While the PCLA framework [2] decoupled 41 Leaderboard agents from the Leaderboard codebase [3] to enable execution across diverse CARLA environments, those agents remained bound to the simulator itself. This paper offers a tool that removes that dependency. PCLA-Bridge executes unmodified agents without a CARLA server, allowing any data source to drive the agent and any control target to consume its outputs. While an earlier extended abstract introduced this concept using offline replay [4], this paper describes a fully functional tool featuring live, closed-loop operation and documents the practical requirements for integrating new data sources.

The envisioned users are autonomous driving (AD) researchers and software engineering (SE) testers who need to evaluate a published PCLA agent on inputs that the agent’s native simulator cannot produce. These inputs may come from real-world logs, alternative simulators, adversarial perturbations, or physical vehicles. PCLA-Bridge enables this evaluation without requiring the user to modify or rewrite the agent.
